_note: INTERNAL USE ONLY — not part of the public book/website. Private accuracy assessment for every cross-tradition citation, kept for project QA.

entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match — an explicit 'I am the beginning' self-declaration.
Closest match in the whole set — both texts use the exact same alphabet metaphor for divine primacy.
Strong doctrinal match on divine primacy, expressed through a broader set of paired attributes rather than the Kural's narrower 'first' image.
Very close conceptually; the main difference is Isaiah frames it as an argument against rival gods rather than a pure cosmological claim.
Genuine textual basis, but represents a specific, later Vajrayana/tantric development, not classical or Theravada Buddhism, which explicitly rejects a single first cause.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §§210–211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Quote verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the Rishabha identification of 'Adi Bhagavan' is a Jain interpretive tradition, not settled fact, and Jainism holds no creator who is the 'origin of the world', so the fit is to 'first teacher', not first cause.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 340, Raag Gauri Poorbi, Bavan Akhri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verbatim on srigranth.org; the alphabet-and-the-Primal-One device closely matches the Kural, though Kabir stresses that letters cannot capture God where Valluvar stresses priority.
Matches the 'first thing' structure exactly, but Chaos is not a person or object of praise, only an origin point.
Strong structural match on the argument for a first cause; Aristotle's Prime Mover is a rational, impersonal principle rather than a devotional God.

entries.source: Apollo 8 astronauts read the opening of Genesis from lunar orbit
entries.rationale: A well-documented event centred on a first origin of the world, though it reflects one scriptural tradition rather than the kural's non-sectarian analogy.
Very close structural match — both texts explicitly rank ordinary learning below a higher, reverence-based knowing.
Strong match on the core claim ('knowledge alone = nothing'), though Paul's missing ingredient is love specifically, while the Kural's is reverence for God.
Same link between knowledge and reverence, but stated as an observation about scholars rather than a direct claim that learning without reverence is worthless.
One of the closest matches in the whole project — reverence-as-foundation-of-wisdom is essentially the Kural's own claim.
Very close in spirit — both condemn scripture-knowledge divorced from genuine practice/humility.
Verified verbatim; strong thematic fit, though 'right faith' in Jainism is conviction in the tattvas taught by the Jinas rather than worship of a deity's feet.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org (ellipsis marks the omitted middle lines); a near one-to-one match on the uselessness of learning without devotion.

entries.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VIII (the myth of Daedalus and Icarus)
entries.rationale: Matches the danger of applying skill/knowledge without heeding wisdom or restraint, but is not specifically about reverence for a deity.
Thematically aligned (humility as the mark of true wisdom), but Socratic humility is about intellectual limits, not reverence for a divine being specifically.

entries.source: Friar Gregor Mendel's pea experiments at St Thomas's Abbey
entries.rationale: Illustrates learning joined to reverence, but the kural's claim that learning is barren without it is not something Mendel's story directly tests.
Strong, direct doctrinal match on devotion producing ongoing sustenance and protection.
Very close match — both use a growth/attachment metaphor for flourishing that depends entirely on nearness to the divine.
Strong shared imagery, though the Qur'an's point is about firmness of faith/speech more than the specific 'long life' the Kural promises.
Very close match in both structure and specific tree/water/fruit imagery.
Precise match on the mechanism (reverence leads to longevity/flourishing) but a different, non-theistic object of reverence.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book I (Adishvaracharitra), ch. III, 'Description of a samavasarana' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, 1931)
entries.rationale: Quote verified verbatim on wisdomlib; the Kural phrase is also read by Saiva and Vaishnava commentators as a lotus-seated deity, so the Jain identification is one interpretive tradition among several.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1281, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Pauri 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the feet and flower imagery and the promise of lasting peace match well, though in Gurbani the lotus stands for the devotee, not for God's footing, and the reward is spiritual rather than long earthly life.

entries.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VIII (Baucis and Philemon)
entries.rationale: Good thematic match on 'devotion rewarded with long life,' though the reward here is hospitality-specific and the source is Ovid's Roman retelling of Greek material.
Same general shape (aligned living produces lasting flourishing) but not a devotional or theistic framework, so the parallel is structural rather than doctrinal.
Shows devotion yielding durable flourishing in a monument rather than in individual lives, so the fit is partial.
Near-exact match — both name the same pair (craving/aversion) as what a steady, suffering-free person has transcended.
Strong match on the mechanism (fixed attention on God produces unshakeable peace).
Very close doctrinal match — a specific, named class of people promised freedom from fear and grief.
Close match on the promised outcome (fearlessness/freedom from affliction through God's presence).
Strong match on the outcome (complete freedom from affliction/craving), though the mechanism (arahantship) differs from the Kural's devotional framing.

Verified verbatim; the verse describes the dispassionate person directly rather than refuge in a dispassionate Lord, which Jainism frames as following the Jina's example rather than receiving his grace.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Mool Mantar (opening of Japji Sahib), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; nirvair corresponds well to freedom from aversion, but the creed does not itself state the Kural's second claim that refuge in such a God ends suffering.

entries.source: Prodicus, 'The Choice of Hercules', in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-33
entries.rationale: Shares the craving-vs-aversion structure, but the fable is about a moral choice at a crossroads, not a description of an already-attained equanimity.
Strong structural match — both locate suffering in the mind's reaction rather than the external event itself.

entries.source: Marcus Aurelius writes the Meditations on campaign
entries.rationale: Captures the freedom from craving and aversion, but Stoic reason is not the same as refuge in a divine being.
Near word-for-word doctrinal match on transcending both good and bad karma through wisdom.
Shares the 'no longer under the ledger' logic, though Paul's grounds (justification through Christ) differ from the Kural's grounds (wisdom/true understanding).
Close in imagery (deeds transformed), though again tied to repentance from sin specifically, not a general teaching of transcending karma.
Good match on 'the record is wiped,' but tied specifically to repentance from sin, not a broader teaching about escaping the merit/demerit system.
Near-exact conceptual match — explicitly transcending merit and demerit as a pair, exactly as the Kural does.

entries.source: Kundakunda, Samayasara 146, as given in Saman Suttam 201 (English edition, Jain World)
entries.rationale: Wording verified verbatim in the Saman Suttam English translation (verse 201); the Samayasara gatha number 146 follows the standard numbering and was not checked against a separate full Samayasara translation.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 325, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strong conceptual match on good and bad deeds equally binding, though Kabir does not use the Kural's darkness/ignorance image.
Striking 'escape the wheel' language, but the underlying mechanism (Orphic ritual purification) and target (rebirth, not the merit/demerit ledger) differ from the Kural's claim.
Structurally similar (wisdom relativizes the good-evil ledger), but Spinoza's rationalist framework is a world apart from the Kural's devotional, karma-based context.

entries.source: Ashoka turns to the Dhamma after the Kalinga war
entries.rationale: A real shift of understanding, but the kural's metaphysical claim about karma ceasing to cling cannot be shown by any historical event.
Very strong structural match — an explicit sense-mastery allegory with the same stakes (a well-lived life vs. chaos).
Strong match on the self-discipline theme, phrased through an athletic training metaphor.
Near-exact match — restraint of desire explicitly named as the cause of the best outcome.
Strong match on the core value (self-mastery as the highest form of strength).
Near-exact match — explicit sense-by-sense restraint as the direct cause of freedom from suffering.
Verified verbatim (Jacobi notes the verse does not construe smoothly); near one-to-one on sense-mastery, though the Kural's promise of long life is not the Jain goal.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 503, Raag Gujri, Ashtpadi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong thematic fit on mastering a fivefold inner force, but the Sikh five thieves are vices rather than the five sense faculties, and the Kural speaks of God's mastery while Nanak speaks of the seeker's.
Strong thematic match, though Odysseus is deliberately restrained by others rather than self-mastering in the purest sense.
Strong structural match — an independently-arrived-at chariot allegory for sense/appetite mastery.
Illustrates steadfastness on a disciplined religious path; the link between sense-mastery and long life is interpretive.
Good conceptual match — both locate the end of anxiety in transcending the ordinary framework of separate, comparable things.
Very strong match — both promise complete relief from anxiety through a specific relationship with the divine.
Very strong match — both make God the singular, sufficient answer to unrest of mind.
Strong match on the mechanism (transferring the burden to God relieves anxiety).
Solid structural match with a real canonical source, though the object of refuge is plural and non-theistic, unlike the Kural's singular incomparable God.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.6.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the 'beyond comparison' match is strong, but the passage does not itself speak of relieving mental anxiety through refuge.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, Raag Asa, So Purakh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted lines); both elements of the Kural, incomparability and relief from sorrow, appear in the same hymn.
Good structural echo (relief only through a higher power) but the Furies represent guilt over an actual crime, a narrower kind of anguish than the Kural's general 'mental anxiety.'
Strong match: written by a philosopher facing real anxiety, explicitly locating peace of mind in a single, incomparable highest Good.

entries.source: Blaise Pascal's night of fire and the Memorial
entries.rationale: A close parallel of a restless mind finding its anchor in the incomparable, though the sources document the experience and not a measured end to anxiety.
Very strong match — the same ocean-crossed-by-vessel image applied to spiritual liberation.
Strong match on the exclusivity claim (one sole path/mediator to cross over).
Authentic hadith about life-as-a-journey, but doesn't make the Kural's specific claim that only God enables the crossing — a looser fit than the other citations here.
Excellent match on 'a sea crossed only through God's action,' though this is a specific historical rescue rather than a general soteriological claim.
Strong match on the crossing metaphor, though the object (Dharma-as-raft) and destination differ from the Kural's devotional framing.
Verified verbatim; the ocean-of-births image is shared closely, and the title Tirthankara itself encodes the crossing.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 516, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; 'ocean of excellence' matches the Kural's 'ocean of virtue', but the crossing of the world-ocean is not in this verse and is supplied from Gurbani's wider imagery (see Ang 1009).

entries.source: Greek mythological tradition (Charon and the Styx)
entries.rationale: Strong match on the core claim that the crossing absolutely requires outside aid.
Good match on 'the real crossing is toward one's true origin,' though Plotinus's 'the One' is an impersonal metaphysical principle rather than the Kural's gracious God.

entries.source: John Newton survives a storm at sea and later writes Amazing Grace
entries.rationale: A strong match for the two-oceans image, with the caveat that the kural's ocean is worldly existence rather than a real sea.
Strong thematic match (pride negates other genuine virtues/abilities), delivered as epic narrative rather than doctrinal statement about the specific 'eight qualities.'
Strong, direct match — pride explicitly named as what blocks divine favor.
About as close a literal match as exists in this project — an actual refusal to bow, caused by pride, with catastrophic consequences.
Strong, direct match on pride as the specific cause of downfall.

entries.source: The story of Devadatta (Vinaya Pitaka / Dhammapada commentary)
entries.rationale: Good narrative match on 'ability undone by refusal to defer,' though the story concerns a specific rivalry rather than a general teaching about bowing to God.

entries.source: Nemicandra, Dravyasaṃgraha, verse 14 (tr. Sarat Chandra Ghoshal, Sacred Books of the Jainas vol. 1, 1917; text at jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verse 14 checked word for word against Ghoshal's translation on jainworld.com. It fixes the Jain doctrine of the Siddha's eight qualities, but reading the Kural's 'en-gunattan' as a Siddha is a Jain interpretive tradition that competes with Parimelazhagar's Saiva list of eight attributes, and I found no scholarly source for that reading itself.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Saloks 71-72 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; near one-to-one on the useless unbowed head, though Farid's simile is firewood where the Kural's is a dead sense-organ. Farid's verses are canonical scripture in Sikhism.

entries.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VI (the myth of Arachne)
entries.rationale: Strong match — real talent undone specifically by a refusal to honor the divine, closely mirroring the Kural's logic.
Solid conceptual match (refusing the universal order blocks the good life), though 'God's Law' here is the rational order of the cosmos, not a personal deity to be bowed to.
Henry's bowing was political as much as religious and was made to a pope rather than to God, so the fit is loose.
Strong match on the exact mechanism (surrender, not self-effort, enables the crossing).
Strong match on the 'not by your own effort' logic, though Paul's specific context is salvation from sin rather than rebirth.
Strong match on the universal-crossing-with-selective-rescue structure.

entries.source: Gilgul neshamot, the Zohar and later Kabbalah
entries.rationale: Real textual basis in Kabbalah, but this is a mystical minority position within Judaism, not found in the Tanakh and rejected by mainstream Rabbinic/Maimonidean thought.
Strong match — same rare-successful-crossing structure and the same insistence on practice over mere nominal belonging.

Verified verbatim (the verse's refrain 'Gautama, &c.' is omitted); strong fit on crossing the sea of births, though Jainism stresses one's own effort on the path rather than reaching a divine Lord's feet.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1009, Raag Maru, Ashtpadi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks one omitted line); a near one-to-one match on crossing the ocean of births through God alone.

Genuine ancient doctrine of cyclical rebirth and escape from it, matching the Kural's core claim well, though escape comes through ritual/philosophical purification rather than devotion to a personal God.

entries.source: Plato, Republic, Book X (the Myth of Er)
entries.rationale: Strong structural match — an explicit doctrine of escaping the wheel of rebirth through pursuit of the highest good/wisdom.

entries.source: Ibn Battuta sets out from Tangier on pilgrimage to Mecca
entries.rationale: Next-best only: a well-documented journey toward God, but no historical event can show liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
An almost word-for-word conceptual match: the Sanskrit amṛta and the Tamil amizhdham are the same word, both predicated of water.
Strong on rain as life-sustaining gift; adds a theological claim about God's witness that the Kural deliberately avoids.
Very close on rain-as-blessing-and-sustainer; the Kural's specific nectar-of-immortality figure has no exact Qur'anic counterpart.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 7a (Koren–Steinsaltz, William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Unusually close: both traditions independently place rain in the same conceptual register as deathlessness.

entries.source: Saddharma-Pundarika (Lotus Sutra), Chapter 5, "On Plants" (Kern translation, SBE vol. 21)
entries.rationale: The literal rain imagery matches well, but in the sutra rain is chiefly a simile for the Dharma rather than the physical subject.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'Utsarpini' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; a vivid parallel, but in Jainism these rains come from the impersonal turning of the time-cycle, not as a divine gift, and the passage concerns cosmic renewal rather than everyday rainfall.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1281, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted lines); the rain-amrit pairing is genuine, but in Gurbani the nectar is ultimately the Name, a spiritual meaning beyond the Kural's literal praise of rain.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 5.92–94, 199 (ambrosia and nectar of the gods)
entries.rationale: The etymological and conceptual kinship is real and illuminating, but Homer never connects ambrosia to rainfall — the link is comparative, not thematic.
Strong on water as universal sustainer; Thales makes a cosmological claim about origin, while the Kural makes a practical claim about ongoing maintenance.

entries.source: Parakramabahu I builds the Parakrama Samudra reservoir
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of rain as the life-sustaining wealth of a society, though it shows human engineering more than rain itself.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on rain as the producer of food for all who eat; the Gita adds a ritual cause above rain that the Kural omits.
Exceptionally close on rain-makes-food-for-eaters; the verse does not add the Kural's second claim that rain is itself the drink.
The strongest match in the chapter: both texts explicitly name rain as simultaneously the drink and the source of food.
Solid on rain-produces-food; a general Tanakh psalm rather than a distinctively rabbinic source, and it lacks the rain-as-drink half.
Genuine on universal dependence on food, but the Pali canon is silent here about rain, so the rain half of the Kural is missing.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1.3.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; next-best match only, since the Jain text turns the Kural's praise of rain-as-drink into a caution about harming water-beings rather than a celebration.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1281, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks one omitted line); a strong match on rain as the source of food, but it lacks the Kural's second claim that rain is itself the drink.

entries.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter (and the Eleusinian Triptolemus tradition)
entries.rationale: A real parallel on food as gift rather than achievement, but Greek myth assigns that role to grain and the goddess, not to rain.
Matches the priority-of-food claim exactly; Plato is silent on rain, so only half of the Kural's two-step argument is present.

entries.source: The Nabataeans harvest rainwater at Petra
entries.rationale: Fits the dual role of rain as food-maker and drink, though the sources stress the engineering rather than the kural's double claim.
A genuine drought-and-famine narrative, but the emphasis falls on the ritual remedy rather than on hunger itself as the Kural has it.
Strong narrative match on no-rain-then-famine; framed as divine judgement, which the Kural does not invoke.
Close on the thought-experiment of water failing; speaks of groundwater vanishing rather than naming hunger as the consequence.
Very close on rain withheld producing region-wide want; a prophetic Tanakh text rather than a distinctively rabbinic one.

entries.source: Ratana Sutta (Sn 2.1 / Khp 6) and its commentarial background narrative on the famine at Vesālī
entries.rationale: The famine-from-drought link is explicit, but it comes from commentary rather than canonical text, and the focus is on the protective chant.

entries.source: Bhadrabahu–Chandragupta famine-migration tradition (Digambara), as summarised in Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bhadrabahu I'
entries.rationale: Paraphrased from a reputable encyclopedia. I could not consult the Shravanabelagola inscriptions directly (archive.org rate-limited me). The story is a sectarian tradition whose dating and details are historically disputed, and it shows famine's effects rather than teaching anything about rain.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim, but next-best only: Japji speaks of spiritual craving, whereas the Kural is about literal famine from failed rain.
Strong on society-wide famine; Hesiod's moral causation is an addition the Kural's plainly meteorological statement does not make.

entries.source: Thomas Robert Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), Chapter VII
entries.rationale: Very strong on famine as nature's final constraint; Malthus's driver is population growth rather than a failed monsoon.
Very close to a dramatisation of the kural: the failure of rain directly produced mass hunger.

entries.source: Kautilya, Arthaśāstra, Book II, Chapter 24 (Shamasastry translation)
entries.rationale: A genuine classical Indian text linking rainfall directly to whether and what farmers sow; paraphrased rather than quoted because translations of the measurement passage vary.
Very strong on the farmer-waits-for-rain motif; James uses it as a moral simile for patience, the Kural as a statement of fact.
Strong on the farmer's dependence; frames the dependence theologically rather than naming rainfall shortfall as the Kural does.
A real halakhic link between failed rain and suspended planting; the Mishnah's framework is liturgical and penitential, not agronomic.

entries.source: Kasi Bhāradvāja Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.4 (Thanissaro Bhikkhu translation)
entries.rationale: A verified canonical text that pairs rain with ploughing, but it works as spiritual allegory rather than a claim about agriculture.
Verified verbatim; next-best match, since the shared ground is the farmer's dependence on a return, not the failure of rain that stops the plough.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; it shares the farmer, plough and water imagery and Sikh respect for agricultural labour (kirat karni), but it is a metaphor and does not make the Kural's point that ploughing stops in drought.
Strong on rain as the trigger for ploughing; Hesiod describes timing rather than the failure case the Kural addresses.
Explicitly joins rain and ploughed fields; it is a prayer rather than the Kural's flat causal statement, and wording varies slightly across translations.

entries.source: The Dust Bowl drives farmers off the Great Plains
entries.rationale: A strong match, with the honest caveat that poor soil practices as well as drought caused the disaster.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 9.19 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)
entries.rationale: Outstanding match: withholding and sending rain, ruin and restoration, are held together in one statement just as in the Kural.
Very close on rain's twofold effect; Job attributes the choice to God, where the Kural leaves the agency with rain itself.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1013–1014 (Book of Istisqā), narrated by Anas ibn Malik
entries.rationale: A strong narrative match on rain's two faces; summarised rather than quoted, since the hadith runs several paragraphs across two reports.
An unusually precise parallel on rain's destructive and restorative faces; paraphrased because the account is a multi-paragraph narrative.
Honest stretch: the antithetical structure and rain imagery match, but rain here is purely a simile for defilement, not a life-giving force that also restores.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'The sixth spoke' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; strong structural fit of destroying and restoring rain, though on a cosmic time-scale rather than the seasonal flood and drought the Kural has in mind.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 3, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the destroy-and-restore structure is exact, but Gurbani gives it to God rather than to rain, as the Kural pointedly does.

entries.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.253–415 (the flood of Deucalion and Pyrrha)
entries.rationale: Strong on rain as both destroyer and precondition of renewal; the restoration comes from stones rather than from rain itself.

entries.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose 2 (Fortune's wheel)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased rather than quoted because English translations of the wheel passage differ significantly; the parallel is structural, and Fortune is capricious where rain is not.

entries.source: Egypt completes the Aswan High Dam
entries.rationale: Captures rain's double power to ruin and to restore, though the Nile flood comes from distant rainfall rather than local rain.
Very close on rain as the sole trigger of vegetation; framed as praise of a deity rather than as the Kural's bare observation.
Near-identical logic, down to the emphasis on 'every herb of the field'; the only gap is Genesis's added mention of human tillage.
Extremely close on barren-ground-until-rain; the Qur'an dwells on the growth, the Kural on the barrenness.
The blade-of-grass-and-sky image is a remarkably close echo; English renderings vary (some read 'angel' for 'constellation'), and the celestial influence is astral rather than rainfall.

entries.source: Dhaniya Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.2 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)
entries.rationale: Honest stretch: rain and grazing grass both appear, but the sutta never claims that without rain no grass grows.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis §55 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a close observational match, framed in Jainism as a reason for non-harm rather than as praise of rain.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a close match on water as the precondition of all green life, though the surrounding salok is about impurity rather than rainfall.

entries.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, lines 305–309 (Evelyn-White translation)
entries.rationale: Strong on total failure of vegetation; the withheld agent is the goddess's blessing on seed rather than rainfall specifically.

entries.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.250–254 (W. E. Leonard translation, 1916)
entries.rationale: Strong on rain as the direct material cause of green growth; Lucretius argues conservation of matter rather than dependence.
A strong match: loss of pasture after rain failure is close to the kural's own image.
Strong on the up-and-down water cycle; the Rigveda does not add the Kural's specific point about the sea shrinking if the return fails.
Good on the vapour-to-rain circuit; Job celebrates the giving and never contemplates the failure case that is the Kural's point.
Genuine on water as measured and withdrawable, but the sea is not in view and the cycle is theological rather than physical.
Very close on the sea-and-return cycle; Kohelet draws a lesson about futility where the Kural draws one about reciprocity.

entries.source: Upayanti Sutta, Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.69 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)
entries.rationale: Honest stretch: the ocean-and-waters interdependence is real, but it functions purely as a simile for dependent origination and involves no rain.

Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; next-best match, since the sutra concerns souls aiding one another, while the Kural's sea and cloud are not souls in that sense, and no Jain text found treats evaporation and rain this way.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; it matches only the Kural's traditional social reading (taking without returning), not its literal water-cycle image.
Good on ocean as source of all waters; Homer sees only the outward flow and never the cloud's return, which is the Kural's real subject.

entries.source: Aristotle, Meteorologica II.2 / I.9, 346b (E. W. Webster translation)
entries.rationale: Excellent match on the closed evaporation-precipitation cycle; Aristotle is descriptive where Valluvar draws a consequence from it.

entries.source: Pierre Perrault measures rain and river flow in the Seine basin
entries.rationale: Matches the kural's water-cycle insight, but Perrault studied rivers rather than the sea's own fullness.
Very strong on the ritual-rain-food loop; Manu runs the causation from sacrifice to rain, while Valluvar pointedly runs it the other way.
An almost exact parallel — drought halting both daily offering and priestly ritual — from a text Valluvar could not have known.
Honest partial match: the rain-and-worship pairing is genuine, but the causal arrow runs opposite to the Kural's, which is the whole point of Valluvar's verse.

entries.source: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:2 (Koren–Steinsaltz, William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Strong on festival life being structured around rain; the Mishnah has festivals petitioning for rain, not ceasing for lack of it.

entries.source: Vinaya Piṭaka, Mahāvagga III (Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka, the chapter on entering the rains)
entries.rationale: Real and structural link between rain and ritual life, but the vassa is organised by rain's presence, not disrupted by its absence.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Rules for Yatis §1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (Jacobi's 'Pa-g-g-usan' rendered as Paggusan); partial fit, since Jains do not offer worship to celestials for rain, and this ties festival to the rainy season rather than to the rain's success or failure.

entries.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 50-52
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the Hardwar episode (verified in Macauliffe, drawn from the Janamsakhi tradition and hagiographic in detail) links water and worship, but Sikh teaching rejects the very ritual worship whose survival the Kural defends.

entries.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter, lines 310–313 (Evelyn-White translation)
entries.rationale: One of the closest cross-cultural matches in the chapter — celestials losing their sacrifices because the earth has stopped producing.
Paraphrased because English renderings of the passage differ; the parallel is about worship being grounded in material benefit, not about drought halting ritual.

entries.source: Megadroughts contribute to the decline of Angkor
entries.rationale: Drought is one documented contributor among several, and the sources do not record worship ending, so the fit is partial.

entries.source: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2.1–3 (the teaching of the thunder, 'Da Da Da')
entries.rationale: A striking convergence — thunder teaching dāna and dama — though the Upanishad makes rain the teacher of the virtues, not their material precondition; paraphrased because translations of the syllables differ.
Strong on provision grounding generosity; Paul's confidence that the supply will come differs from the Kural's warning about its failure.
Strong on rain as the image and enabler of charity; the verse uses rain as simile for reward rather than as literal precondition.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (Mishnah Yomit, Dr. Joshua Kulp translation)
entries.rationale: Exceptionally close on material provision as the precondition of religious life; the Jewish text does not name rain, and adds a reciprocal dependence the Kural does not.
Genuine pairing of rain imagery with generosity, but rain here is a simile for how merit travels, not the condition that makes giving possible.
Verified verbatim; it pairs giving and austerity with rain, but the causality is reversed, with rain as the gods' response to virtue rather than its precondition.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; it names the same two virtues and makes them conditional on something more basic, but that foundation is the Name, not rain, and Sikhism downplays austerity, which the Kural values.
Weak next-best match: the elements of generosity, water from the sky and worship all appear, but the causal claim of the Kural is absent.
Strong on virtue requiring material means; Aristotle speaks of wealth and friends generally, not of the natural supply that generates them.

entries.source: The Ancestral Pueblo people leave Mesa Verde during the Great Drought
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the sources document migration after drought, not the specific collapse of charity and austerity the kural names.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14–16 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, 1972)
entries.rationale: Strong structural match linking duty and rain in one cycle; summarised across three verses, and the Gita's arrow runs from duty to rain rather than rain to conduct.
Good on rain-and-moral-fruitfulness held together; Hebrews uses the rain figuratively, where the Kural also means it literally.
Very strong on the rain-and-conduct linkage; the dependence runs from conduct to rain, the inverse of Valluvar's direction.

entries.source: Deuteronomy 11:13–17 (KJV, rendering the Hebrew Tanakh; the second paragraph of the Shema)
entries.rationale: Outstanding thematic match on rain bound to conduct; the causation is theological and runs conduct-to-rain, while the Kural runs rain-to-conduct.

entries.source: Vassa Sutta (Obstacles to Rain), Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.197 (Bhikkhu Sujato translation)
entries.rationale: Strong and unusually explicit pairing of unrighteousness with failed rain; the dependence again runs conduct-to-rain rather than rain-to-conduct.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book X (Mahaviracharitra), ch. XIII, 'The sixth spoke' (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; partial fit, since in Jain cosmology both are effects of the declining time-cycle rather than conduct depending on rain, and the same chapter supplies Kural 15's entry.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1282, Raag Malar, Vaar Malar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a strikingly close match tracing rain to food to right living, though Gurbani places the whole sequence under God's will.
Strong on the fusion of justice and agricultural plenty; Hesiod again makes conduct the cause and harvest the effect.

entries.source: Karl Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859)
entries.rationale: Strong on material conditions grounding morality, and it runs in the Kural's direction; Marx's base is the mode of production rather than rainfall.
A neat illustration of water and conduct bound together, though it concerns irrigation water rather than rain itself.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.46 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
entries.rationale: Both are authoritative texts issuing a comparative ranking that puts disciplined renunciation first; the small gap is that Krishna ranks the yogī above the tapasvin, while Valluvar praises the renunciant as such.
Strong: a canonical text exalting wilderness renunciants above the world; the Kural's insistence on disciplined conduct is implied in the passage rather than stated.

Honest gap: the Qur'an praises the humble, night-praying devotee rather than the world-renouncer, and elsewhere (57:27) is explicitly reserved about monasticism, so this is a close cousin rather than a twin.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 6:4 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
entries.rationale: Very close in substance — a canonical rabbinic text commending an ascetic regimen as the highest way; it prescribes the life rather than praising a class of people who already live it.
Near one-to-one: a canonical verse performing an explicit comparative ranking that puts reverence for the perfected renunciant above all rival goods.

entries.source: Namokar Mantra as Saman Suttam vv. 1-2, Mangalasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: A strong, distinctly Jain match for honouring renunciants above all, though the mantra salutes five classes of perfected and practising souls rather than ascetics alone; the jainworld page prints 'inthe', silently corrected to 'in the'.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on praising freedom from desire, tempered because Sikhism rejects formal renunciation (see Ang 467 on wilderness-dwellers), which the Kural's chapter exalts.
Weak, and honestly so: these are an idealised foreign tribe, not chosen renunciants, and Homer's aside is two lines long — Greek myth simply has no established ascetic class to exalt.
Strong conceptual match — an authoritative philosophical text ranking the renunciant highest; paraphrased rather than quoted because the discourse makes the point across many pages.

entries.source: Francis of Assisi renounces his inheritance
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of a renunciant honoured above worldly excellence, though the kural's point about textual consensus is not shown by a single event.

Strong structural parallel (a failed measurement used as a proof of transcendence), but the Upanishad is measuring the bliss of Brahman rather than the greatness of renunciants; paraphrased because English renderings of 2.9 vary widely.
Good rhetorical match — an explicit refusal to finish counting the righteous; the impossibility here is practical (time fails) rather than the Kural's stronger claim of principled uncountability.
Very close — the phrase 'without account' is literally a refusal to quantify, applied to exactly the kind of person the Kural has in view; the Qur'an speaks of reward rather than of greatness.

entries.source: Mishnah Peah 1:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
entries.rationale: The shared idea of 'things without measure' is genuine and unusual, but the Mishnah is defining unbounded obligations, not praising ascetics — a real but oblique correspondence.
About as close as cross-tradition matching gets — same subject (the renounced), same predicate (immeasurability), same rhetorical shape.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.6.3-4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts, but the Acaranga speaks of the liberated soul (siddha) rather than the living ascetic, and of inexpressibility rather than numberlessness, so the fit is thematic and partial.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 273, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 8, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted lines); near one-to-one on immeasurable greatness, though the Sikh figure is a God-conscious householder rather than a renunciant.
The match is with the Kural's simile rather than its point: Homer gives a vivid picture of the uncountable dead, but says nothing about ascetics.

entries.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, Proposition 7 (trans. C.K. Ogden, 1922)
entries.rationale: Honestly a stretch: the shared idea is the limit of what can be stated or measured, but Wittgenstein is doing logic, not praising renunciants, and the resemblance is formal rather than substantive.

entries.source: Mother Teresa receives the Nobel Peace Prize
entries.rationale: The prize honours a renunciant's greatness, but the kural's point that such greatness is beyond counting cannot be shown directly by any event.

entries.source: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1-2 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)
entries.rationale: Very strong: both texts make discernment between a paired alternative the decisive act, and both attach the ascetic's greatness to having made the harder choice.
Close match on the two-orders structure and on acting in the present in light of it; Paul does not single out a renunciant class the way the Kural does.
Strong: the paired this-world/hereafter framing is the same, and the verse's whole point is that the two must be told apart and ranked correctly.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:16 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
entries.rationale: Unusually close: the two-world scheme plus the urgency of preparing in this life map onto both halves of the couplet.
Strong on the two-worlds framing and on taking up virtue now; the verse is addressed to everyone rather than to renunciants specifically.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Close structural match to discern-then-adopt, especially under the birth-versus-release reading of 'irumai', though the Acaranga does not itself speak of 'two' things or of the renouncer's greatness shining in the world.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 272, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 7, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; it matches the 'this world and the next' reading of irumai, but only partially captures the Kural's emphasis on discernment and visible greatness.

entries.source: Plato, Republic X (the Myth of Er, 614b-621d)
entries.rationale: A genuine Greek narrative about knowing both worlds and choosing accordingly, but it is a philosopher's constructed myth rather than traditional mythology, and it centres on justice rather than renunciation.
Strong: an ascetic practice justified explicitly by knowledge of two states of being; the Greek framing is about the soul's separation rather than about release from rebirth.

entries.source: Emperor Charles V abdicates and retires to the monastery of Yuste
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of discerning the two orders and choosing the spiritual, though the sources do not record his inner reasoning.

entries.source: Katha Upanishad 1.3.3-4 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)
entries.rationale: Very strong — same structure (senses as animals, discipline as the controlling instrument, liberation as the destination); horses and reins rather than elephants and a goad.
Strong on the substance of forcible sense-restraint aimed at a final reward; Paul speaks of the body generally rather than enumerating five faculties.
Very close: restraint of the nafs is named as the precondition and Paradise as the consequence, matching the 'seed for the highest estate' structure.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
entries.rationale: Strong on the inner-mastery-as-true-power theme and on the paradox of the smaller force governing the greater; the yetzer is a single drive rather than five sense-channels.
Outstanding match: the ankus-and-elephant metaphor is shared almost verbatim; the Dhammapada applies it to the mind while the Kural applies it to the five senses.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.46-48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895); vv. 42-46 recur in Dasavaikalika Sutra 2
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified in 'Sramanahood'); the elephant-and-goad image and sense-control leading to perfection match closely, though in the story the goad is another person's words rather than the ascetic's own inner firmness.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 516, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the elephant-and-goad image is a near one-to-one match, with the difference that the Guru's knowledge, not personal willpower, is the goad, and the mind rather than the five senses is the elephant.
Genuinely close on sense-restraint as the saving act; the difference is that Odysseus restrains himself externally with ropes rather than internally with firmness of mind.
Very strong and historically striking — Max Müller himself noted the resemblance between this passage and the Katha Upanishad's chariot; the appetitive powers are two horses rather than five senses.

entries.source: Eric Liddell declines to run on Sunday at the Paris Olympics
entries.rationale: A good example of firmness of mind overruling desire, though it concerns ambition rather than the five senses.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (the Vishvamitra and Menaka episode, sargas 63-64)
entries.rationale: Strong: this is almost certainly the body of story Valluvar is gesturing at, and Indra's fear functions exactly as the 'sufficient witness' the couplet names.
Solid on the core idea that fasting confers power, but the Christian text supplies no heavenly witness testifying to that power, which is the Kural's distinctive framing.
The heavenly-testimony structure matches well, but the hadith attests to the fast's acceptability rather than to the ascetic's power, which is the Kural's actual subject.
Structurally very close — heavenly witness, ascetic subject, claim of world-sustaining power; paraphrased rather than quoted because English renderings differ and I did not verify one word for word.
Excellent: subdued senses, divine beings as the attesting party, and the implicit ranking of the liberated human above the gods all line up with the couplet.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.6-58, esp. 9.55-59 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified) and a near one-to-one match; in Jain cosmology Indra is a karma-bound celestial, not a creator, which suits the Kural's use of him as witness, though the Ahalya allusion some commentators find has no Jain counterpart here.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1344, Raag Prabhati, Dakhni, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; it matches the Ahalya reading of the Kural closely, but not the primary reading of Indra as witness to ascetic power, and Gurbani cites Indra only as a cautionary tale.
Fair rather than strong: the divine-certification structure is genuine, but Heracles endures labours imposed on him rather than quenching desire, and he is anything but continent.

entries.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14; cf. Diogenes Laertius 6.32
entries.rationale: Strong on the crucial point — the highest worldly authority testifying to the renunciant's greater power; paraphrased because the wording varies between Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius.

entries.source: Emperor Akbar honours the hermit Salim Chishti at Sikri
entries.rationale: A strong parallel of a sovereign testifying to an ascetic's power, with an emperor standing in for the kural's Indra.

entries.source: Katha Upanishad 1.3.14 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)
entries.rationale: Strong on the shared premise that difficulty is the defining feature of the highest path; the Upanishad urges the effort rather than classifying people by it.
The narrative setting (a renunciation too hard to perform) matches well, though Jesus resolves the difficulty by referring it to divine power rather than by grading people as great or small.
Close on substance: difficulty as the marker of the higher road, ease as the marker of the lower; it rates destinations rather than persons.

Honest partial match — the equation of difficulty with worth is shared, but the Mishnah measures reward rather than sorting people into the great and the small; paraphrased because I did not verify a single English rendering word for word.
Strong: both verses rank people by difficulty of achievement, and the Dhammapada names the specific hard thing the Kural's chapter has in view.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.24-44, esp. 19.36 and 19.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong thematic fit chosen to avoid the self-conquest motif already used in the Buddhism slot, though the Jain text does not draw the Kural's explicit great/small contrast.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong thematic fit on greatness as willingness to do the hardest thing, though Nanak's verse is an invitation rather than the Kural's two-way definition.
Genuinely close on the criterion of greatness, though the labours are feats of strength and endurance rather than the inward ascetic difficulty the chapter is about.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9, 1109a24-30 (trans. W.D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Strong philosophical parallel linking difficulty, rarity and praiseworthiness; Aristotle's hard thing is hitting the mean rather than renouncing the world.

entries.source: Hillary and Tenzing make the first ascent of Everest
entries.rationale: A clear fit for the kural's test of greatness, though the kural is in a chapter on ascetics and Everest is a physical rather than moral feat.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
entries.rationale: Good on the shared premise that the sense-contacts are the raw material of experience and that discerning their nature confers mastery; the Gita's conclusion is endurance rather than possession of the world.
Real but partial: the move of defining 'the world' as sense-appetite is shared, yet John lists three categories rather than five and urges renunciation rather than discernment.
Strong: the verse enumerates sense-faculties and ties them directly to knowledge and responsibility, closely paralleling the Kural's epistemic framing.

Moderate: shares the diagnosis that the senses drive the self, but prescribes an external reminder rather than the analytical discernment the Kural praises, and it names two faculties rather than five.

entries.source: Sabba Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.23 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Excellent: an explicit identification of the world with the sense-fields, which is exactly the premise the Kural relies on; Buddhism counts six bases by including the mind.

Verified verbatim; a strong match for mastery of the five bringing mastery of all, though the Jain verse adds the four passions and speaks of conquest rather than the Kural's discernment of sense-objects.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib, Pauri 28, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on inner mastery as mastery of the world, with the mind in place of the five senses.
A fair thematic echo — knowledge of sensory danger as protection — but Homer supplies a magic herb rather than analytic discernment, and there is no enumeration of five senses.
Genuine but partial: Stoic analysis of impressions parallels the Kural's discernment of sense-modes, though Epictetus focuses on judgement rather than on the five channels themselves.

entries.source: Helen Keller understands the word water
entries.rationale: A vivid case of understanding the senses opening up the world, though the kural concerns an ascetic's discernment rather than learning language.

entries.source: Rig Veda and the rishi-attribution tradition of the Sarvanukramani
entries.rationale: Conceptually very close, and probably part of the intellectual background Valluvar assumes; described as a tradition rather than quoted because it is a framework spread across texts rather than a single citable line.
Strong on the endurance of the sacred word as the mark of the speaker; it asserts the words' permanence rather than using them as evidence of the speaker's greatness.

entries.source: Sahih Muslim 2622 (Book of Virtue, chapter on the virtue of the weak and downtrodden)
entries.rationale: Excellent match: a dusty, propertyless ascetic whose oath God fulfils is precisely the 'man of full speech' the couplet has in view.
Substantively very close on the efficacious word of the righteous; paraphrased rather than quoted because I did not verify a specific English translation word for word.
Very strong: the act of truth is the canonical Buddhist form of 'full speech' whose power certifies the speaker; paraphrased because the episode is a narrative rather than a line.

entries.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara v. 9 (tr. Champat Rai Jain, The Householder's Dharma, 1917)
entries.rationale: Verified against the archive.org scan (OCR 'Ttrihaijikara' read as 'Tirthamkara'); a good fit on the sage-and-sacred-word link, but the argument runs in the opposite direction to the Kural's, and Champat Rai's word 'God' for the apta in nearby verses means a perfected teacher, not a creator.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 982, Raag Nat, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on sacred words as the lasting evidence of the great, though Gurbani identifies the word with the Guru rather than treating it as proof of a person's greatness.

entries.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 300-462; cf. Homer, Odyssey 11.90-151
entries.rationale: Fair: the efficacious-word-proving-the-speaker structure is genuinely there, but Tiresias' authority comes from prophetic gift rather than from ascetic perfection of life.

entries.source: Heraclitus, Fragment DK B92 (trans. John Burnet)
entries.rationale: Strong on the enduring unadorned word as the evidence of an inspired speaker; Heraclitus credits the god in her rather than ascetic attainment.

entries.source: The Diamond Sutra, the world's earliest dated printed book
entries.rationale: A good fit for sacred sayings that outlast their speaker, though the printing shows devotion to the words rather than proving their power.

entries.source: Bhagavata Purana 8.5-8 (the curse of Durvasa and the churning of the ocean)
entries.rationale: Very strong — the ascetic's momentary wrath producing instant, unstoppable ruin is exactly the couplet's claim, and this genre of story is almost certainly its background.
Strong on the instant, unavoidable consequence of offending a holy figure; the text presents it as divine judgement rather than as the holy man's anger, which is a real difference.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6502 (Book of Ar-Riqaq, chapter on humility)
entries.rationale: Excellent: same content (offending the saintly person is catastrophic and unshieldable), though the agency is God's rather than the wali's own anger.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
entries.rationale: Outstanding: an ancient wisdom text explicitly warning that the anger of the virtuous wise is dangerous beyond remedy — the closest parallel in this chapter.

Honestly a weak match, and interestingly so: Buddhism has no equivalent of the destructive sage's curse, so the closest canonical verse is one that contradicts the Kural's premise rather than supporting it.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.19-33, esp. 12.23, 12.28, 12.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; strong narrative fit on the peril of offending an ascetic, but Jain doctrine treats anger (krodha) as a passion a true monk must not have, so it moves the retaliation away from the sage himself, a real difference from the Kural's 'veguli'.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 13, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (ellipses mark omitted lines); close on the danger of wronging the holy, but Gurbani frames it as the consequence of slander and stresses the saint's mercy, where the Kural stresses the saint's anger.
Very strong — one of the clearest cross-cultural instances of the offended-holy-man motif, with the same instantaneous and unstoppable outcome.

entries.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger), esp. I.1 and III.5
entries.rationale: Deliberately a low-confidence, contrastive entry — Greco-Roman philosophy has no doctrine of the efficacious wrath of the holy, and the nearest sustained treatment denies the phenomenon exists.
Zola was not an ascetic and the wrongdoers were exposed over years, not in an instant, so the fit is partial.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
entries.rationale: Very strong: the brāhmaṇa, animals and the outcaste appear in one breath, matching the Kural's 'every living thing' and its detachment of status from birth.

entries.source: Bonaventure, Legenda Major XII.3 (the sermon to the birds); cf. the Canticle of the Creatures
entries.rationale: Strong on universal compassion as the badge of sanctity; described rather than quoted, and Christianity does not use it to redefine a priestly caste the way the Kural does.
Excellent: an explicit ruling that compassion extends to all living beings and is decisive for a person's standing, matching 'ev-uyirkkum' closely.
Good: the same diagnostic (compassion to animals reveals the righteous), though it names a trait of the righteous rather than redefining a priestly title.
Outstanding: identical rhetorical move on the identical contested term, and the surrounding verses (e.g. 405, on renouncing violence toward all beings) supply the Kural's compassion clause as well.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.19-33, esp. 25.23 and 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified); a near one-to-one match on redefining the Brahmin by compassion for all beings, parallel to but independent of the Buddhist Brahmanavagga used in that slot.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on redefining Brahmin status by compassion and conduct, though the Kural's compassion explicitly extends to every living creature.

entries.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV.60-478 (the speech of Pythagoras)
entries.rationale: A real and substantial parallel, though it sits at the edge of mythology proper — Ovid is dramatising a historical philosopher's doctrine inside a mythological poem.
Strong philosophical parallel tying ascetic attainment to universal compassion; paraphrased because the argument runs across many chapters rather than sitting in one quotable line.

entries.source: Albert Schweitzer and Reverence for Life
entries.rationale: Nearly a dramatisation of the kural: compassion toward all life as the mark of the truly virtuous.

entries.source: Mahabharata 18.5, Svargarohanika Parva (Bharata Savitri), trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: both texts assert that wealth and enjoyment flow from righteousness and then ask rhetorically why anything else would be pursued.
Strong structural match on 'virtue first, prosperity follows'; the Kural is non-theistic where Matthew is explicitly about God's kingdom.

entries.source: Qur'an 64:16, At-Taghabun (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Genuine overlap on 'piety is what is best for you', but the Qur'anic 'success' (falah) is eschatological, while Valluvar explicitly promises worldly wealth as well.

entries.source: Mishnah Peah 1:1 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Unusually close — the this-world/next-world double return is the same structure Parimelazhagar reads into 'sirappu' and 'selvam'.
Very close on the two-worlds benefit; the Dhammapada speaks of joy where the Kural speaks of honour and wealth.

entries.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 1.1, as Saman Suttam v. 82, Dharmasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified on jainworld's Saman Suttam page (its typo 'p[enance' read as 'penance'); a strong match on virtue as the supreme good and source of honour, but Jainism treats worldly prosperity as at most a by-product of merit (punya), not one of dharma's goals as the Kural's 'selvam' implies.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on the supremacy of virtuous conduct, but the verse says nothing of worldly wealth, which Kural 31 explicitly claims virtue also yields.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-237, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
entries.rationale: Strong on 'justice produces prosperity'; Hesiod's mechanism is divine reward for a community, whereas Valluvar's is an impersonal claim about individual life.
Exceptionally tight parallel — both explicitly reverse the assumed causality between wealth and virtue.

entries.source: The Cadbury brothers move their works to Bournville
entries.rationale: A clear case of conduct that brought both honour and wealth, though the kural's sirappu also carries a spiritual sense of liberation that no business history can show.

entries.source: Manusmriti 8.15, trans. Georg Bühler (Sacred Books of the East, 1886)
entries.rationale: Almost a perfect structural twin; Manu frames it as active violation where Valluvar frames it as forgetting.
Captures the 'no greater loss' half very well; the 'no greater gain than virtue' half is implied rather than stated.

entries.source: Qur'an 91:9-10, Ash-Shams (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Very strong parallel in form and content; 'success/doom' maps cleanly onto aakkam/kedu.
Strong on the binary structure; Deuteronomy's frame is covenantal and national, the Kural's is individual and universal.
Close on the gain/ruin symmetry, though the Dhammapada emphasises repetition rather than the Kural's 'forgetting'.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 and 10.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified in 'Samsara'); pramada as heedless forgetting closely matches Parimelazhagar's reading of 'marathal' as delusion rather than defiance, though the text has no explicit gain-versus-ruin contrast.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Close structural parallel (forgetting as the cause of ruin), though in Gurbani what is forgotten is God and the Name, whereas in the Kural it is aram itself.

entries.source: Aeschylus, Eumenides, the Furies' choral ode (ll. 490-565)
entries.rationale: Thematically apt on 'forgetting justice equals ruin', but Aeschylus is arguing about institutional punishment, not about personal virtue as the highest gain.
The health/disease analogy reproduces the Kural's two-sided maximum claim closely; paraphrased rather than quoted because translations vary widely.

entries.source: The collapse of Charles Ponzi's scheme
entries.rationale: Illustrates the ruin that follows abandoning virtue well, though Ponzi's fraud was deliberate rather than the forgetful lapse the commentators stress.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.19 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Strong on constancy of right action; the Gita adds non-attachment to fruits, which the Kural does not raise here.
One of the closest matches in the chapter: 'not weary' = ஓவாதே, 'as we have opportunity' = ஒல்லும் வகையான், 'unto all men' = செல்லும்வாய் எல்லாம்.

entries.source: Qur'an 64:16, At-Taghabun (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Direct match on the capacity clause; the 'without ceasing' element is present only implicitly.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 2:16 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Very strong on the capacity/continuity pairing; Avot's framing is about Torah study and communal work rather than good deeds generally.
Close on urgency and continuity; the Dhammapada lacks the Kural's 'according to your means' qualification.

entries.source: Tattvartha Sutra 6.1-3 (Umasvati; cf. tr. Nathmal Tatia, That Which Is, 1994)
entries.rationale: The mind-speech-body triad matches the commentarial gloss exactly, but this is paraphrase rather than a verified quotation, and Jainism holds that even wholesome activity binds karma (as merit), so it does not share the Kural's unqualified call to ceaseless doing.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang (Sarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Good fit on giving according to one's own means, but the verse lacks the Kural's stress on doing good ceaselessly and in every situation.

entries.source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5 (the Twelve Labours of Heracles)
entries.rationale: Honest stretch: the labours are penance under compulsion, not freely chosen everyday virtue — the shared element is only unremitting, adaptive effort.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (1103a-b), trans. W. D. Ross
entries.rationale: Excellent philosophical underpinning for the Kural's 'without ceasing'; Aristotle is explaining character formation rather than commanding action.

entries.source: Chiune Sugihara issues transit visas to refugees
entries.rationale: Very close to the kural's call for unceasing good done with whatever means are at hand.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.16 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Strong on the primacy of mental purity; the Gita still retains bodily and verbal austerities as valid, where the Kural dismisses the rest as show.
Very close on the critique of performative virtue; Matthew's criterion is divine reward rather than the Kural's inner stainlessness.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 1, narrated by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab
entries.rationale: Outstanding match — this hadith is the canonical Islamic statement that inner state, not outward deed, constitutes moral reality.
Strong on inner-versus-outer; the verse is about divine evaluation of a person rather than a definition of virtue as such.
Very close — both verses make the mind the exclusive seat of moral quality and treat outward acts as downstream.

entries.source: Samayasara of Kundakunda, gathas on linga, c. 408-411 (numbering per Amritachandra's recension; varies between editions)
entries.rationale: A strong and distinctly Jain match, including the commentators' point about garb, but I could not find an online English translation to check wording or exact gatha numbers, so this is paraphrase with approximate numbering.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on inner purity versus outward observance; the one difference is that the Japji attributes the cleansing to the Name, while the Kural speaks simply of a mind free from stain.

entries.source: Herodotus, Histories 6.86 (the story of Glaucus of Sparta)
entries.rationale: Thematically excellent on inner stain, but it comes from a historian's oracle-tale rather than myth proper, and its logic is punitive where the Kural's is definitional.

entries.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, opening of Section I, trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott
entries.rationale: Remarkably close in claim and in exclusivity ('nothing... except' mirrors 'அனைத்து அறன்'), though Kant is arguing from autonomy and Valluvar from purity.

entries.source: Wilhelm Röntgen declines to patent X-rays
entries.rationale: Shows purity of motive over outward reward, but the kural's sharp contrast between inner stainlessness and outward religious display is only partly reflected.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.21 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Strong overlap on craving, anger and greed; the Gita's list omits envy and harsh speech, and Valluvar's 'avā' covers both lust and greed.
Covers anger, harsh speech and malice precisely; greed is absent from this particular verse.

entries.source: Sahih Muslim 2564a, narrated by Abu Hurayra
entries.rationale: Paraphrased rather than quoted because the standard English rendering on Sunnah.com is unidiomatic; envy and hatred match well, greed and harsh speech only partially.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Envy and craving match exactly and the list-form is identical; honour-seeking replaces the Kural's anger and harsh speech.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikaya 41, Saleyyaka Sutta (the ten courses of unwholesome and wholesome action)
entries.rationale: Method and content align closely; paraphrased because the sutta's list is long and no single sentence quotes cleanly.

entries.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38-39 (numbering varies by edition), as Saman Suttam vv. 135-136, Samyamasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on jainworld; the four-fault structure and two of its members match, but the Jain list has pride and deceit where the Kural has envy and harsh speech, and the Dasavaikalika verse number differs between editions (8.37-38 or 8.38-39).

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A reasonable but partial match: anger and greed correspond, but envy and harsh speech are not in this passage, and the five thieves are a different list from Valluvar's four.
Powerful on envy alone; it does not address greed, anger or harsh speech, and offers no definition of virtue, so it is a partial match.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (1107a), trans. W. D. Ross
entries.rationale: Envy appears by name and the 'always wrong, never moderated' logic matches the Kural's absolute exclusion; Aristotle's list differs in its other items.

entries.source: Nelson Mandela wears the Springbok jersey at the Rugby World Cup final
entries.rationale: A strong public example of freedom from anger and harsh speech, though one occasion cannot show the steady lifelong conduct the kural describes.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.40 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Very strong on virtue surviving death as an imperishable asset; the Gita does not include the Kural's rebuke of procrastination.
Near-exact on the second line's image; the first line's 'do not defer' has no counterpart in this verse.

entries.source: Sahih Muslim 1631, narrated by Abu Hurayra
entries.rationale: Outstanding match on the imperishable-companion image; the urgency of 'do not postpone' is implicit in the hadith rather than stated.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria); cf. b. Shabbat 153a
entries.rationale: Exceptional match on the anti-procrastination argument; Avot speaks of repentance where the Kural speaks of doing good.
Among the closest matches in this chapter — same claim, same crossing-of-death frame, same warmth of the companionship image.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.27 and 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on both the warning against delay and virtue as the sole protection at death.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir 138 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Very close on the 'do it now' half; the Kural's second half (virtue as the undying companion at death) is matched in Gurbani by the Name, e.g. Sukhmani, Ang 264, and Kabir is a non-Sikh saint whose verses are part of Sikh scripture.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 410-413, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
entries.rationale: Very close on procrastination but Hesiod is talking about agricultural labour, not virtue, and has nothing corresponding to the companion beyond death.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 1 (On Saving Time), trans. Richard M. Gummere
entries.rationale: Sharp match on the anti-deferral argument; Seneca is concerned with time as such rather than specifically with moral action.
Closely fits the urgency of doing good now and the good that outlasts the doer, though the kural's companion is meant in a karmic sense beyond earthly legacy.
Very close doctrinally; both texts are also open to the same modern objection that they naturalise social hierarchy.
Strong on 'judge by observable results rather than testimony'; the content of the fruit differs, and there is no rebirth dimension.

entries.source: Qur'an 6:132, Al-An'am (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Good match on deeds determining rank; in Islam the decisive ranking is at the Judgement rather than visibly in this life, which weakens the empirical parallel.
The proportionality principle matches well, but the Mishnah applies it within a single lifetime and to a specific ritual case, not across births.

entries.source: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta (The Fruits of the Contemplative Life)
entries.rationale: Strikingly parallel in method and even in imagery; paraphrased because the exchange runs over several pages with no single quotable sentence.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.1-20, esp. 13.10 and 13.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on social station as visible karmic fruit, but the Jain story then subverts it, since the prosperous king clings to pleasure and sinks into hell (13.34), and this carries the same modern caveat about justifying inequality that the Kural's commentators raise.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Only a partial parallel: Sikh teaching rejects caste and does not treat social rank as earned merit, so the verse shares the Kural's observation of inequality but not its argument that virtue visibly explains it.
Shares the 'look and compare' structure, but the outcome is direct divine intervention rather than the impersonal ripening of deeds the Kural implies.
Good on the side-by-side comparative method; Plato's point inverts outward appearances where Valluvar takes them at face value.

entries.source: Charles Booth maps London's wealth and poverty street by street
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shows unequal fortunes made directly visible, but the kural's claim that these differences are the fruit of past virtue is a karmic teaching that no historical event can demonstrate, and Booth's maps imply nothing of the kind.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.51 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Strong on the rebirth-ending outcome; the Gita's means is devotional service rather than the Kural's daily unbroken good works.
Honest partial match: good on daily non-wastage, but the entire second half of the Kural, about obstructing the path of further births, has no Christian counterpart.
Excellent on daily constancy; Islam's linear eschatology means the rebirth-blocking half has no parallel.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 2:15 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Good on daily urgency; mainstream Judaism has no rebirth doctrine to match the Kural's second line, so this is a deliberate half-match.
Very strong on the rebirth-ending image; the Buddha's mechanism is insight into craving, not the Kural's cumulative daily merit.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.24-25 and 14.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (Jacobi notes the original reckons by 'nights'); a near one-to-one match on both the unwasted day and the ending of rebirth, though the Kural's road-blocking stone is its own image.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Shares the urgency and the goal of release from rebirth, but the means in Gurbani is the Name and the company of the holy (sangat), not daily good deeds as such.

entries.source: Orphic gold tablets (Thurii and Petelia lamellae, 4th-3rd c. BCE)
entries.rationale: Genuinely shares the escape-from-rebirth goal, which is rare in Greek material, but the means is ritual knowledge rather than daily good works.

entries.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations II.5, trans. George Long
entries.rationale: Good on unbroken daily practice; Stoicism's goal is present integrity, not the closing of a cycle of births.

entries.source: Florence Nightingale's night rounds at Scutari
entries.rationale: Illustrates the daily, unbroken practice of good well, but the kural's promise that such practice blocks rebirth is a spiritual claim beyond history.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.38 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Close on the disqualification of unprincipled pleasure; the Gita grades happiness into three modes where the Kural draws a single sharp line.
Solid on the contrast, though Hebrews concedes that sin's pleasures are pleasures (briefly), where the Kural denies them the category entirely.

entries.source: Qur'an 16:97, An-Nahl (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Strong on 'virtue yields the genuinely good life'; the Qur'an does not add the Kural's negative clause about honour.
Good on 'the virtuous way is the pleasant way', but the subject is ḥokhmah (wisdom) rather than virtue proper, and there is no negative counter-clause.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta (Debtless), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
entries.rationale: Very close, including the honour/blame dimension the Kural adds; paraphrased because the passage's force depends on its full four-part structure.
