Verified verbatim; strong on pleasure outside virtue being pain, but the Kural (per Parimelazhagar) endorses pleasure within domestic virtue, whereas Citta rejects sensual pleasure outright and allows the householder only noble deeds and compassion as a second-best (13.32).

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Good thematic fit, though Gurbani grounds true delight in love of God while the Kural grounds it in aram, and Sikhism, like the Kural, does not reject the householder's lawful pleasures.

entries.source: Prodicus, The Choice of Heracles, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
entries.rationale: Unusually strong for a Greek parallel, matching both the pleasure claim and the honour claim; paraphrased as the allegory runs to several pages.
Exceptionally close in substance; the biconditional is even stronger than Valluvar's one-directional claim.

entries.source: Ben Johnson is stripped of his Olympic gold medal
entries.rationale: A vivid case of gain won outside virtue yielding neither lasting joy nor honour, matching both halves of the kural.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.30 (Bhaktivedanta, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Very close: kārya/akārya is a near-exact Sanskrit equivalent of செயற்பால/உயற்பால.
Nearly one-to-one on both halves; Paul's framing is affective (abhor/cleave) where Valluvar's is categorial.

entries.source: Qur'an 3:104, Ali 'Imran (Dr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Structurally near-identical; the Qur'anic duty is also directed outward at the community, which the Kural does not require.

entries.source: Psalms 34:15 (JPS/Sefaria Tanakh; numbered 34:14 in Christian Bibles)
entries.rationale: About as close as cross-tradition matching gets — sur me-ra va-aseh tov is functionally a translation of this couplet.
The strongest match in the chapter; it even supplies a third clause that ties back to Kural 34.
Verified verbatim; a close structural match to the do/avoid binary, though the Jain criterion is inner restraint rather than the Kural's socially answerable 'blame'.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on the virtue/vice binary defined by action, but the Kural frames what is to be avoided as public blame (pazhi), whereas the Japji frames it through karmic consequence under hukam.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 286-292, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White
entries.rationale: Strong on the exhaustive binary, but Hesiod's emphasis is on the difficulty of virtue rather than on defining duty as such.

Matches the unconditional 'shun what deserves blame' half very well; the positive 'what ought to be done is virtue' half is assumed rather than argued. Paraphrased because translations of the passage vary considerably.

entries.source: Frances Kelsey refuses to approve thalidomide
entries.rationale: A clear example of choosing duty and avoiding blameworthy action, though the kural is a general definition rather than a call to resist pressure.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.77 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: A near-identical doctrine expressed with the same three-other-orders structure; almost certainly the shared intellectual background of the Kural.
Very close on the duty of support; the Kural adds the 'good path' qualifier and a wider circle of dependents than Paul's immediate household.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 893, Book of Friday Prayer
entries.rationale: Strong on responsibility-for-dependents; the hadith's frame is accountability before God rather than the Kural's 'standing on the good path'.
Paraphrase, not a verified verbatim quotation; strong on duty-to-dependents but narrower (father-to-son) than the Kural's threefold circle.
Paraphrase of the sutta's well-known structure rather than a verified quotation; the six-directions scheme matches the Kural's logic closely but counts six groups, not three.

entries.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §94 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
entries.rationale: Wording verified on wisdomlib's Jacobi text. A real Jain parallel for duty to dependants, but it concerns parents only, not the 'three' of the Kural's commentators, and the passage frames household duty as a stage before renunciation.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, closing Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the verse affirms working householder life and its benefit to others, but the 'many saved' is spiritual rather than the material support of named dependants that Kural 41 describes.
Honest next-best match: Hesiod grounds virtue in the household, but his point is not depending on others, which is nearly the inverse of the Kural's point about being depended upon.
Very close in method (duties from relations); Epictetus stresses duties owed *to* the householder as much as by him.

entries.source: Young Anton Chekhov supports his family
entries.rationale: A good picture of one person becoming the support of his dependants, though Chekhov was a son supporting his family rather than a married householder as the kural envisages.
Matches well on non-reciprocal giving as the householder's duty, but the Gita does not enumerate the same three recipients.
Very close on care for the destitute; James has no counterpart to the Kural's duties toward renunciants or the dead.
Strong structural parallel (an enumerated list of dependants); the Qur'anic list omits the dead and renunciants, since Islam has no monastic order.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 49b (Koren-Steinsaltz / William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Extremely close on the distinctive point — duties owed to the dead as well as the living — from an authentically Jewish, not merely biblical, source.
Near one-to-one on the householder-supports-the-renunciant claim, and from the tradition whose renunciant prestige Valluvar is implicitly answering.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 1.47–56 (the thirty-five householder qualities, no. 19), English as given in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism
entries.rationale: The English is Sangave's rendering as published on jainworld.com, not a direct translation of the Sanskrit verse. Jain doctrine does not accept rites that feed or benefit the dead, so the Kural's third dependant (iṟantār) has no Jain counterpart.

entries.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter III, pp. 30-31
entries.rationale: Strong fit on feeding renunciants and the hungry, but it rests on the Janamsakhi tradition (hagiography), and it has nothing to match the Kural's third class, the dead.
Paraphrase of the plot rather than a verified quotation; it captures the duty-to-the-dead strand well but says nothing about renunciants or the poor.
Paraphrase, not a verified verbatim; the principle matches but Cicero's list of claimants is civic rather than the Kural's three specific classes.

entries.source: Emperor Harsha's five-yearly gift-giving at Prayag
entries.rationale: Matches the support of renunciants and the needy well, but a king's public charity is not quite the ordinary householder's duty, and the kural's third group, the dead, is not shown.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.72 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: As close as cross-textual matches get: the same five categories, including the unusual inclusion of oneself.
Strong on the guest-and-god pairing but covers only two of the Kural's five obligations.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, Book of Good Manners (Al-Adab)
entries.rationale: Very strong on hospitality and neighbourly kin duty; no Islamic counterpart to offerings to ancestors, which is a real divergence.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 127a (Koren-Steinsaltz / William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Excellent on the guest-versus-god ranking; like the Islamic parallel it lacks an ancestor-offering element.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.41, Adiya Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
entries.rationale: Strikingly exact overlap of an enumerated fivefold list; the Buddhist list substitutes kings for 'oneself', which AN 5.41 covers in its first benefit instead.

entries.source: Ṣaḍ-āvaśyaka verse for householders, as quoted and translated in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism (jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Next-best match. The duties differ: 'God' here means the Jina, who receives nothing from offerings, and Jainism makes no offerings to ancestors (tenpulattār). Sangave does not name the verse's author.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 332, Raag Gauri Bairaagan, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: this is a deliberate contrast, since the SGGS rejects the ancestor rites and offerings to deities that Kural 43 lists among the householder's foremost duties.
Paraphrase of the narrative rather than a quotation; superb on guest-and-god but silent on kin, ancestors and self.
Paraphrase, not verified verbatim; the graded-obligation structure matches, but Cicero's list is civic rather than the Kural's ritual-domestic five.

entries.source: UNESCO recognises Mexico's Day of the Dead
entries.rationale: Partial fit: it shows several of the kural's five claims (ancestors, the divine, kin) honoured together, but guests and care of oneself are not prominent, and it is a recurring custom rather than a single act.
Very close on shared-versus-selfish eating; the Gita frames the sharing as sacrificial offering rather than social distribution.
Strong on sharing-leads-to-increase; Paul does not address the 'fear of blame in acquiring' half of the couplet.
Near-exact on sharing food despite wanting it; the promise of an unbroken lineage is not part of this verse.
An unusually precise match on both halves — generosity and the unbroken, unbegging lineage.
Good on generosity-and-future-good; the Buddhist reward is a personal heavenly rebirth rather than the Kural's continuing family line.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 1.47–56 (the thirty-five householder qualities, nos. 1 and 3), English as given in V. A. Sangave, Ethics of Jainism
entries.rationale: A close fit for the Kural's first condition. The promise that the family line will never fail has no direct Jain equivalent, and the English is Sangave's rendering.

entries.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 43-44
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on blameless earning and its moral weight, but it is Janamsakhi hagiography and says nothing of the Kural's promised reward, a lineage that never fails.
Very close on blameless acquisition determining the survival of the house; Hesiod does not pair it with the sharing of food.
Paraphrase of Aristotle's analysis rather than a verified quotation; the earn-cleanly-and-share-well pairing matches well, but Aristotle promises no generational outcome.

entries.source: Mitsui Takatoshi opens the Echigoya shop
entries.rationale: Partial fit: blameless earning and lasting continuity are shown, but the kural's second condition, sharing one's food before eating, is not, and a business line is not the same as a family lineage.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.60 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: Close on love-as-the-source-of-household-good; Manu speaks only of the spousal pair, not of virtue alongside love.
Strong on love-as-completion; Paul's frame is the Christian community, which includes but is not limited to the household.
Outstanding match: a two-term pairing of love and moral kindness as the defining content of domestic life.
Very close in sentiment and in the domestic-meal setting; Proverbs contrasts love with wealth rather than pairing love with virtue.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
entries.rationale: Very strong on love-plus-virtue as the substance of married life; the sutta's payoff is future rebirth together, slightly unlike the Kural's 'the reward is the thing itself'.

entries.source: Uvāsagadasāo (Upāsakadaśāḥ) ch. 1, story of Ānanda (tr. A. F. R. Hoernlé, 1890); summary at jainworld.com
entries.rationale: The vow-taking by Ānanda and Śivanandā is confirmed on jainworld.com, but I could not read Hoernlé's text this session. The story is about vows, not marital love as such, so the fit is thematic.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on love as the substance of the household, though it centres on the married pair rather than the whole household and does not name aram (virtue) alongside love.
An exceptionally close parallel — 'there is nothing better in this world' is functionally identical to 'its quality and its fruit are that'.
Paraphrase rather than a verified verbatim quotation, but the conceptual match — virtue-based spousal friendship as an end in itself — is very strong.

entries.source: The von Trapp family leaves Nazi-annexed Austria
entries.rationale: Shows a household held together by love and principle, though the kural's claim that these are their own reward is an inner truth that the family's later success does not by itself prove.
Outstanding match — both texts deflate the prestige of formal renunciation in favour of duty performed in place.
Strong anti-ascetic parallel; the epistle condemns compulsory celibacy outright where the Kural merely calls the ascetic path superfluous.
Near one-to-one: the same argument, the same target, and the same preference for the householder's path.
Paraphrase of the sugya rather than a verified verbatim; the anti-ascetic stance matches strongly, though Judaism's target is self-denial rather than a rival monastic institution.
Honest partial match: Buddhism deflates *external* asceticism but still ranks the homeless life above the household, which is the opposite of the Kural's implication.

Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. Jainism agrees about heavenly reward but still holds that final liberation needs full renunciation (5.20, 5.25), so it does not fully endorse the Kural's 'what more is there?'.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on the redundancy of renunciation for one living rightly in the world; the Sikh verse adds the Guru's grace as the condition where the Kural speaks only of virtue.
Paraphrase of the episode rather than a quotation; the choice-of-home-over-transcendence is a genuinely strong echo, though Odysseus's motive is longing rather than ethical argument.
Strong on the impossibility of a superior solitary path; Aristotle's target is the apolitical individual rather than the religious ascetic specifically.

entries.source: Martin Luther marries Katharina von Bora
entries.rationale: A direct historical instance of choosing household life over the renunciant path, though the religious meaning of this choice is understood differently by different Christian traditions.

entries.source: Manusmriti 6.89 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: Essentially the same sentence: householder ranked first among the recognised religious modes of life.
Strong: household competence as the qualifying credential; the epistle makes it a prerequisite for leadership rather than the highest state in itself.
Very close on domestic conduct as the criterion of being foremost; the hadith narrows the field to treatment of one's wife.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage rather than a verified verbatim quotation; the householder-as-ideal match is strong.
Honest weak match, given as a paraphrase: Buddhism dignifies lay life but explicitly does not place the householder at the head of all who strive.

entries.source: Uvāsagadasāo (Upāsakadaśāḥ) ch. 1, story of Ānanda (tr. A. F. R. Hoernlé, 1890); retold in Jain Story Series, 'Anand Shravak'
entries.rationale: A well-attested canonical episode, confirmed this session only from a modern retelling. Ānanda had by then taken the advanced lay stages (pratimās), so he is an exceptional householder, not an ordinary one.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 730, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on ranking life in the world above ascetic striving, though the hymn does not mention the householder or family by name.
Genuine parallel on the primacy of the hearth in religious ranking, but it honours a goddess of the household rather than the human householder, and Hestia is notably unmarried.
Excellent on the 'live your assigned role according to its nature' principle; Epictetus does not rank roles against each other as the Kural does.

entries.source: Guru Nanak settles as a farmer at Kartarpur
entries.rationale: A strong fit for the householder's life placed at the head of spiritual striving, coming from a tradition that itself honours the householder path.
Very strong: Janaka is Hinduism's canonical case of an active householder surpassing renunciants, and the verse states the guide-others principle directly.
Good on lead-others-by-example; the Gospel does not make the comparison with ascetic practice that gives the Kural its edge.
Very close on the self-and-others double duty of the householder; the Qur'anic frame is eschatological rather than a strength contest with ascetics.
Excellent on the household as the engine of moral instruction, and it is a foundational Jewish text rather than an incidental proof-text.
Near-exact on the two-condition structure; the verse is addressed to anyone rather than specifically to householders.
Verified verbatim. The first half is a close parallel, but the second half keeps the Jain hierarchy, so the Jain claim is narrower than Valluvar's.

entries.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 40 (tr. Dr Jodh Singh)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on the polemic of householder against ascetic; note that the Vaaran are early exegesis, not scripture, and that this translation was verified on allaboutsikhs.com because searchgurbani.com would not load.
Strong on the householder as moral instructor of his kin and on virtue as arduous; Hesiod never compares this to ascetic penance.

entries.source: Musonius Rufus, Lecture XIV, 'Is Marriage a Handicap for the Pursuit of Philosophy?'
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the lecture's argument rather than a verified verbatim quotation, but it is probably the closest philosophical analogue to this Kural in the entire Western tradition.
A good example of a household leading others on the right path; the comparison with ascetic austerity is the kural's own judgement and not something the event can prove.

entries.source: Manusmriti 6.90 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: Very close on the household as the defining centre of religious life; Manu's image is about material support rather than a definition of virtue.
Strong on marriage as honourable per se; the epistle does not take up the comparison with celibate life that the Kural's second clause handles.
Remarkably close on the conditional, slightly sceptical concession to the ascetic path — the same rhetorical shape as அஃதும் … நன்று.
Strong on domestic partnership as the normative good; it is a creation statement rather than a definition of virtue, and says nothing about a rival path.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
entries.rationale: Excellent on the blamelessness criterion applied specifically to householders; the sutta does not equate household life with virtue as such.

entries.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra v. 33 (gṛhastho mokṣamārgastho…), tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917, pp. 18–19
entries.rationale: Verified against the archive.org OCR of Champat Rai Jain's 1917 translation. His edition does not number the verses, so 'v. 33' follows the standard Sanskrit numbering. His own note adds that as a rule the ascetic takes precedence.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 496, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit, but Sikhism goes further than the Kural: it does not grant the ascetic road separate standing as a second valid path, it absorbs detachment into the householder's life.
Honest weak match, given as a paraphrase: it honours domestic life beautifully but never calls it virtue, and Greek epic has no ascetic alternative to weigh it against.
Good on the primacy and naturalness of the household; Aristotle's interest is political genealogy rather than the Kural's identification of household life with virtue itself.

entries.source: Father Damien serves the Hansen's disease settlement on Molokai
entries.rationale: Illustrates the second half of the kural, a blameless renunciant life, but not its main claim that household life is virtue itself.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Vyadha Gita / the story of Dharmavyadha)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the narrative rather than a quotation; extremely close in message, though it ranks the householder above ascetics rather than literally among the gods.
Strong on divinisation through right living; the epistle attributes it to divine promise and grace rather than to domestic conduct as such.
Very close on the 'enter among' formula and on its being earned by earthly conduct toward dependants; Islam would not say a human is reckoned among gods.

entries.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 4:16 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
entries.rationale: Good on earthly living determining a higher station; the Mishnah treats this world as preparatory where the Kural treats living rightly here as already the achievement.
Outstanding: the same identification of good householders with divine beings, and the closing verse adds that such people 'after death rejoice in heaven'.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. In Jainism heaven is still within saṃsāra and is not liberation, which is a real difference in framing from the Kural's climactic praise.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong, close parallel in structure (right living in this world brings honour above); the Sikh version names seva and God's court where the Kural speaks of living well and the sky-dwelling gods.
Strong on right-living mortals joining the divine ranks; Hesiod's golden race qualify by belonging to a lost age rather than by individual household virtue.
Very close on becoming godlike through right conduct; Plato's 'fly away from earth' is more world-renouncing than the Kural's insistence on living well *within* the world.

entries.source: Imhotep, builder of the Step Pyramid, is later worshipped as a god
entries.rationale: Next-best: a real person was literally counted among the gods, but little is known of how Imhotep lived, so the kural's link between right living and this honour cannot be shown.

entries.source: Manusmriti 9.11 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a verse whose content matches the kural's economic-stewardship criterion closely, though Manu frames it as the husband 'employing' her.
Very close thematic and structural match — both are opening definitions of the worthy wife keyed to household provision.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5200 (Book of Wedlock/Marriage), narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the standard sunnah.com English rendering; the stewardship framing matches the kural directly.

entries.source: Genesis 2:18 (King James Version); Hebrew ezer kenegdo
entries.rationale: The Hebrew term for 'helper fitted to him' is almost a lexical twin of the kural's 'life-companion', though Genesis is about marriage's origin rather than household economy.

entries.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one overlap on the household-management and income-preservation criteria; the Sutta adds reciprocal husbandly duties that Valluvar's chapter does not.

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 39 'Chaste Women', st. 2 (= st. 382), English translation in The Indian Antiquary
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text, used because no canonical scripture addresses a wife's household management this closely. Quoted from the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib, not Pope's.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Pauri 3, Rai Balwand and Satta Doom (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on a wife's excellence shown in running the household's provision for others, though nothing is said of living within her husband's means, which is the second half of the Kural.
A real and apt figure, but Arete's authority is royal and political rather than the domestic thrift Valluvar specifies.
Paraphrase; the indoor/outdoor division of labour and the proportionality principle match the kural very closely.

entries.source: Abigail Adams runs the family farm and finances during the Revolution
entries.rationale: Closely matches the kural's picture of a capable partner who fits the household to its means, even going beyond it by enlarging those means.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva §74 (Shakuntala to Dushyanta; trans. K. M. Ganguli, 1883–96)
entries.rationale: Faithful paraphrase of a well-attested passage; marked as paraphrase because Ganguli's exact wording varies between printings.
Strong structural parallel (grandeur vs. character), though Proverbs targets quarrelsomeness specifically rather than the full range of 'manaimaatchi'.

entries.source: Sahih Muslim 1467, Book of Suckling, Chapter: Advice with regard to women (narrated by 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr)
entries.rationale: Near-exact inversion of the same claim; wording follows the standard Siddiqui English rendering on sunnah.com.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 62b (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the Davidson translation; speaks of having no wife rather than an unworthy one, which is a slight shift of target.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.53, Paṭhamasaṁvāsa Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
entries.rationale: Verbatim; Sujato's 'zombie' renders Pali chava (corpse). Note the Sutta is symmetrical — it says the same of a bad husband — where the kural is not.

entries.source: Uvāsagadasāo, Lecture 8 (Mahāsayaga), §§ 233–257, esp. § 234 and § 247 (tr. A. F. Rudolf Hoernle, Bibliotheca Indica, vol. 2, Calcutta, 1888; scan at archive.org)
entries.rationale: § 234 and the phrase from § 247 checked against the archive.org OCR of Hoernle's translation, with obvious OCR slips corrected ('thonsand', 'Mahisayaga'), and the narrative summary follows §§ 238–257. It is a negative example, a bad wife in a rich house, not a positive teaching on a wife's virtue, so the fit with the Kural is strong but indirect.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the logic (outward splendour is empty without inner worth) matches, but the verse is about the soul-bride and God, a spiritual rather than domestic relationship, and the roles are reversed.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 702–705 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White, Loeb Classical Library, 1914)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Loeb text; one of the closest cross-cultural parallels in this chapter.
Widely attested English rendering, though wording varies across translations (Ross, Rackham, Irwin); Aristotle is explaining marriage's basis rather than diagnosing its failure.

entries.source: Queen Victoria withdraws from public life after Prince Albert's death
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the roles are reversed (a queen losing her husband rather than a man lacking a worthy wife), and the kural speaks of a partner's character rather than her loss, but it vividly shows splendour made empty without the partner.

entries.source: Manusmriti 9.28 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Bühler text and an unusually precise match — both make the wife the sole condition of a complete life.
Among the closest parallels in the whole chapter; Tamil commentators have themselves cited this verse alongside the kural.
Verbatim and thematically strong on the positive half, but the Qur'anic verse has no counterpart to the kural's negative half.
Paraphrase of a famous passage (marked non-quote because English renderings differ widely); the Talmud pivots on the husband's worth rather than the wife's, an inversion worth noting.

entries.source: Saṁyutta Nikāya 1.54, Vatthu Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
entries.rationale: Verbatim; matches the kural's positive half strongly and, as a bonus, pairs wife and children exactly as Kural 60 does.

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 39 'Chaste Women', st. 3 (= st. 383), English translation in The Indian Antiquary
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text close in idiom to the Kural. It gives only the positive half of the couplet, and the translation is the Indian Antiquary one on wisdomlib.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable to strong fit on woman as indispensable to a man's life, though the Guru speaks of women in general, not of the wife's particular excellence (maanbu) that the Kural makes the deciding factor.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.182–185 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Loeb text; Homer's ideal is mutual and symmetrical, whereas the kural is framed around the wife's quality.

entries.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, prose 4 (c. 524 CE)
entries.rationale: Accurate paraphrase of a real passage; the argument is about consolation in ruin rather than a general maxim about wives.

entries.source: Empress Theodora counsels Justinian to stand firm in the Nika revolt
entries.rationale: A strong dramatisation of the first half of the kural; her exact words come to us only through Procopius.

entries.source: Valmiki, Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Sita in the Ashoka Vana)
entries.rationale: A well-founded archetypal match; the Ramayana also contains the agni-pariksha episode, which modern critics read as undercutting rather than confirming this ideal.
Strong on the inner-strength-over-outward-goods axis; 'meek and quiet' is a different virtue-profile from the Tamil thiNmai (firmness).
Verbatim excerpt of the relevant clause; readers should note the same verse contains disciplinary provisions that are heavily debated and are not paralleled in the Kural.

entries.source: Proverbs 31:10, 'Eshet Chayil' (Jewish Publication Society, 1917); recited in the Friday-night home liturgy
entries.rationale: Verbatim JPS text and a near-identical rhetorical question; note this verse is shared scripture with Christianity, so the distinctively Jewish element is its liturgical use.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.49, Paṭhamaidhalokika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
entries.rationale: Verbatim and a genuine match on unbreakable constancy, though framed as conduct toward the husband rather than as intrinsic strength.

entries.source: Vimalasūri, Paumacariya (Prakrit, c. 4th century CE), the fire-ordeal episode; summarised in 'Paumacariya (critical study)', wisdomlib.org
entries.rationale: The ordeal-turned-lake is confirmed from secondary summaries; I did not consult a primary translation. The miracle also appears in Hindu tellings, but the turn to Jain renunciation is distinctively Jain.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 274, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 9, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shares the value of steadfast fidelity as an inner quality, but it addresses men and does not call a faithful wife a treasure, which is the Kural's actual claim.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey, Books 2, 19 and 23 (the shroud, the recognition, the test of the bed)
entries.rationale: Very strong archetypal correspondence; Penelope's firmness is also strategic cunning (mētis), a dimension the kural does not name.

entries.source: Plutarch, Mulierum Virtutes (Bravery of Women), Moralia 242E–243A
entries.rationale: Genuine and relevant, but Plutarch is arguing about courage in public crises, not the marital constancy the kural means by karpu.

entries.source: Maria van Reigersberch frees Hugo Grotius from Loevestein Castle
entries.rationale: A strong picture of a wife's firmness and devotion as a priceless treasure, though karpu in the kural refers specifically to fidelity of mind rather than courage or ingenuity.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (the Savitri and Satyavan episode)
entries.rationale: Strong match on 'devotion commands the cosmos'; Savitri's power works through argument and vow rather than through worshipping her husband as a god.
The rain-at-a-word motif matches exactly, but Christianity has no analogue to the husband-as-sole-object-of-worship premise; scored low for that reason.

entries.source: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1159 (also Sunan Ibn Majah 1852), narrated by Abu Hurayra
entries.rationale: Widely attested wording, though English renderings vary slightly; note the hadith explicitly withholds the act of worship that the kural appears to grant.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23b (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Verbatim and an unusually exact motif-match on the rain; the Talmud grounds her power in charity to the poor rather than in devotion to her husband.
Deliberately scored low: Buddhism explicitly rejects husband-worship and treats spouses as ethical equals, so this is a best-available 'next-best' match only.

entries.source: Āvaśyaka-cūrṇi of Jinadāsa (story of Subhadrā); summarised in Jainpedia, 'Subhadrā'
entries.rationale: Confirmed from Jainpedia. Subhadrā's power comes from chastity and Jain faith, not from treating her husband as a god, so the theology of 'worshipping no god but her husband' does not carry over.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 787, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Saloks Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best and partly a contrast: Sikhism honours a wife's faithfulness and early-morning devotion but would not have her worship her husband in place of God, and it has no teaching that such a wife can command the rain.

entries.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XI.410–748 (the Ceyx and Alcyone episode)
entries.rationale: Genuine and apt motif (weather obeys a devoted wife); the transformation is a divine reward after death rather than power wielded in life.

entries.source: Plutarch, Conjugalia Praecepta (Advice to Bride and Groom) §19, Moralia 140D (trans. F. C. Babbitt, Loeb Classical Library)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Loeb text and the single closest parallel to this couplet found in any tradition surveyed; both are also open to the same modern critique.

entries.source: Kasturba Gandhi prepares to speak in her husband's place
entries.rationale: Next-best only: no historical event can show a person commanding the rain, and this couplet's literal claim is contested even among commentators; Kasturba illustrates only the authority that devotion can confer.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva §74; the ardhangini / sahadharmini formulations in classical dharma literature
entries.rationale: Sound paraphrase of a well-attested passage and concept; the Sanskrit terms are later crystallisations rather than words in the epic line itself.
Verbatim; covers guarding the husband's interests, the household, and tireless constancy — three of the kural's four terms.
Verbatim and a rich image for mutual guarding, but the Qur'anic clause is symmetrical where the kural assigns the duties to the wife.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 62b (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Verbatim, and a genuine parallel on guarding the spouse's honour — but the Talmud here addresses the husband's duty, mirroring rather than matching the kural.
Accurate summary of a well-known sutta; strictly symmetrical between spouses, which the kural is not.

entries.source: Jain Rāma narratives (Paumacariya; Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭi-śalākā-puruṣa-caritra, Book VII); summarised in Jainpedia, 'Añjanāsundarī'
entries.rationale: Confirmed from Jainpedia. Traditional details such as the length of the separation vary between versions and are left out, and the story stresses endurance more than active care of the household.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Saloks 126-127 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the form (a list of virtues that define the true wife) matches, but the Husband here is God and the love is spiritual, not marital, and the virtues differ from the Kural's self-guarding and care for the family name.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 24.196–198 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Loeb text; maps onto three of the kural's four clauses (guarding self, husband, reputation) with striking exactness.

entries.source: Musonius Rufus, Fragment XIII A, 'On the Chief End of Marriage' (trans. Cora E. Lutz, Yale Classical Studies X, 1947)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Lutz translation; Musonius applies the standard equally to both spouses, which is a real and significant difference from the kural.

entries.source: Ruth Williams Khama stands by Seretse Khama through exile
entries.rationale: Shows unwavering constancy and care for her husband, but the sources say little about the other duties the kural lists, such as guarding the household's good name.

entries.source: Manusmriti 9.12 (trans. Ganganath Jha, with Medhātithi's commentary, 1920)
entries.rationale: Verbatim and the single closest textual parallel in this chapter; both texts share the confinement/self-guarding antithesis exactly.
Verbatim and a strong match on inner-vs-outer guarding, though it is addressed to everyone rather than framed against the confinement of women.
Verbatim excerpt; the self-guarding framing matches well, though the passage prescribes outward norms that the kural does not.
Well-attested wording and a genuine self-mastery-over-fortification parallel, but it is a general ethical maxim with no reference to women or marriage.
Verbatim Buddharakkhita rendering and an exceptionally close structural match on self-protection as primary.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. Rājīmatī is a nun and Ariṣṭanemi's abandoned bride, not a wife in a household, but the self-guarding principle is a near-exact match.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 787, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 2, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the verse states the general principle (coerced goodness is worthless) but says nothing about women, seclusion or guarding; Sikh tradition's opposition to purdah fits the theme but could not be verified verbatim here.

entries.source: Apollodorus, The Library 2.4.1; Pindar, Pythian 12; Horace, Odes 3.16
entries.rationale: An apt and vivid illustration of the futility of confinement, though the myth turns on divine power rather than on the woman's own moral agency.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (1103a–b) and III.1 (1109b–1110a)
entries.rationale: Accurate summary of Aristotle's doctrine of the voluntary and of habituation; Aristotle is not discussing women or marriage, so the application is ours.

entries.source: Begum Rokeya publishes Sultana's Dream and founds a girls' school
entries.rationale: Captures the kural's rejection of enforced confinement well, though Rokeya argued for education and freedom rather than for karpu as such.

entries.source: Manusmriti 5.165 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Bühler text and an almost exact doctrinal match on heavenly reward for wifely devotion.
Verbatim; 'heirs together of the grace of life' matches the heavenly-glory theme well, though the verse addresses husbands and contains the much-debated 'weaker vessel' phrase.

entries.source: Hadith of the Prophet Muhammad, Musnad Ahmad 1661 and Ibn Hibban 4163; also Mishkat al-Masabih 3254 (graded hasan)
entries.rationale: Wording is the standard English rendering; note that this hadith's numbering varies across collections and it is not in Bukhari or Muslim.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the Davidson translation and a remarkably direct parallel, including the promise that women's reward exceeds men's.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.49, Paṭhamaidhalokika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
entries.rationale: Verbatim; the deva-realm reward for a virtuous wife is a direct match, though the sutta's causes include faith and wisdom alongside marital conduct.

entries.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra vv. 63–64, tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917, pp. 30–31
entries.rationale: Verified against the archive.org OCR (spelling slightly normalised from the OCR). Verse numbers follow the standard Sanskrit numbering because Champat Rai's edition is unnumbered. The reward comes from keeping a vow, not from honouring a husband, so the fit is partial.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, Pauri 37, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: Sita's name links to wifely faithfulness, but in the Japji these are spiritual heroes filled with God, not wives rewarded for honouring husbands, and Sikhism teaches no special heaven earned by wifely devotion.

entries.source: Euripides, Alcestis (438 BCE), esp. lines 435–475 and 1000–1005
entries.rationale: Strong archetypal match on posthumous honour for a devoted wife; Euripides is also widely read as ironising Admetus, which complicates the moral.
Genuine on the 'shared discipline yields shared heavenly reward' axis, but Plato's pairs are philosophical lovers, not spouses, and the context is pederastic erōs.

entries.source: Clara Schumann carries Robert Schumann's music to the world
entries.rationale: Partial fit: the glory the kural promises is in the world of the celestials, while Clara's fame is earthly and owed as much to her own artistry as to honouring her husband.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.56 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
entries.rationale: Widely quoted Bühler rendering; the causal arrow runs the opposite way (how women are honoured, rather than how they guard honour), so it is a mirror rather than a match.
Verbatim, and one of the sharpest matches in the chapter — both locate the payoff in public standing rather than private happiness.

entries.source: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3895 (also Sunan Ibn Majah 1977), narrated by 'A'isha
entries.rationale: Widely attested wording, but it measures the husband by his conduct toward his wife, whereas the kural measures him by hers — a reversal worth flagging.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a (Koren Noé / William Davidson Edition)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the Davidson translation; the Talmud places the obligation on the husband to honour her, where the kural places it on her to guard the name.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.63, Bhariya Sutta (the Buddha to Sujātā, in Anāthapiṇḍika's house)
entries.rationale: Accurate summary of a well-known sutta; it is directed at the wife's own destination more than at the husband's public bearing.

entries.source: Vimalasūri, Paumacariya, the exile-of-Sītā episode; summarised in 'Paumacariya (critical study)', wisdomlib.org
entries.rationale: Next-best match. The underlying assumption is shared, but here the wife is blameless, which reverses the Kural's case. Confirmed only from secondary summaries.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 730, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only and largely a contrast: no SGGS passage found makes a husband's honour depend on his wife's conduct, and Sikh teaching places responsibility for reputation on each individual.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 11.405–434 (the shade of Agamemnon to Odysseus)
entries.rationale: Very strong narrative match on public glory annulled by domestic dishonour; paraphrased rather than quoted because the relevant lines span a long speech.
A real and interesting parallel on bearing-as-index-of-honour, but Aristotle never connects it to a spouse; the link is interpretive.

entries.source: Julius Caesar divorces Pompeia after the Bona Dea scandal
entries.rationale: Closely tied to the kural's concern for the household's reputation and the husband's public standing, though Pompeia's own wrongdoing was never established.

entries.source: Rig Veda 10.85 (the Sūryā-vivāha / marriage hymn), esp. vv. 42–47 (trans. R. T. H. Griffith, 1896)
entries.rationale: Faithful summary of the hymn's blessings; paraphrased because the hymn's benedictions are distributed across many verses rather than stated in one line.
Verbatim and an exceptionally close match — the same two-term picture of domestic blessing in the same order.
Verbatim; pairs spouse and children as one blessing exactly as the kural does, though without the ornament/ornamented hierarchy.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 23b (Rav Huna on the Shabbat lamp)
entries.rationale: Accurate paraphrase of a well-known passage; 'lamp' is literal in the Talmud and metaphorical in the kural, so the correspondence is thematic.

entries.source: Sutta Nipāta 2.4, Maṅgala Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral)
entries.rationale: Verbatim, and the shared Indic term maṅgala makes this a genuine lexical as well as thematic parallel.

entries.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §91 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
entries.rationale: Verified on wisdomlib's Jacobi text. A strong image of a child as the household's ornament, but the passage praises the child's merit, not the wife's virtue, so it covers only half of the couplet.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 773, Raag Soohee, Chhant (Laavan), Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shares the sense of marriage as auspicious and dharmic, but does not single out the wife's excellence or call good children its ornament.
Honest low score: the marriage-as-blessing-on-the-house theme is a real match, but Baucis and Philemon are childless, so the kural's second half has no counterpart.

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.17.54 (trans. Walter Miller, Loeb Classical Library, 1913)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Loeb text; the sequence marriage → children → shared home mirrors the kural's blessing → ornament → household with real precision.

entries.source: The Curies: a shared Nobel Prize and a daughter who won her own
entries.rationale: A fitting image of an excellent wife and a jewel-like child, though the kural's mangalam is a broader domestic blessing than scientific achievement.

entries.source: Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10.5 (the doctrine of the three debts, ṛṇa-traya)
entries.rationale: Described as a doctrine rather than quoted, because English renderings of the Taittirīya passage vary widely; the conceptual match is strong and is the one Valluvar's own commentator applies here.
Verified verbatim against the KJV; both texts explicitly rank children as the supreme thing one receives.
Verified verbatim, but the Qur'an subordinates children to enduring deeds whereas the Kural makes them the highest gain outright — a real difference in ranking.
Standard KJV wording; a strong narrative match, though Abram's concern is dynastic inheritance rather than Valluvar's emphasis on the child's discernment.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.39, Puttasutta, vv. 506–507 (trans. Ānandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Ānandajoti Bhikkhu's verse translation; a close functional parallel, though framed as five practical reasons rather than a single superlative claim.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it is a prophecy about one particular child (the future Mahâvîra) rather than a general maxim, and the learning named is Vedic, so the fit is partial.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 328, Raag Gauri, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit stated in reverse: both make wisdom the measure of a child's worth, but Kabir means devotional wisdom of God, and his tone is condemnatory where the Kural's is celebratory.
Paraphrase of the myth; the match is on the desperate valuation of offspring, but the Greek story is about dynastic succession and says nothing about the child's wisdom.
Paraphrased rather than quoted because translations of this passage differ considerably; the argument is accurately represented but Aristotle is explaining the bond, not ranking goods.

entries.source: Aage Bohr follows his father Niels Bohr to a Nobel Prize in Physics
entries.rationale: A clear documented case of a learned child carrying on a parent's work, though the sources record the achievement rather than the father's own valuation of it.

entries.source: Manusmṛti 9.138 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, 1886)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Bühler's standard translation; a near one-to-one match on the mechanism of post-mortem deliverance through offspring.
Verified verbatim but a weak match: the direction of moral transfer is reversed, and Christianity has no doctrine of seven births for the Kural's central image to land on.

entries.source: Sahih Muslim 1631, Book of Wills (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com; the only gap is that Islam has one afterlife rather than seven births.
Rendered as a paraphrase of the principle because English translations of the Aramaic 'berā mezakkeh abbā' vary; the conceptual match, including the one-way direction of merit, is unusually precise.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.39, Puttasutta, v. 507 (trans. Ānandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the mechanism matches (offerings benefiting the departed) but Buddhism frames it as merit dedication, not as evil being prevented from touching the parent.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.8 and 14.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; included as an honest counterpoint, because Jain karma theory denies that a child's merit can protect a parent across births.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 310, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the idea of one person's virtue protecting the whole family matches, but the verse is not about children specifically, and Sikhism ties release to God's grace rather than to transferred merit across seven births.
Paraphrase of the episode; the good-children-protect-the-parent theme is present, but there is no rebirth framework and the sons' reward is death, which cuts against the Kural's tone.
Accurate paraphrase of Plato's argument, but he speaks of continuity and immortality of the line rather than of evil being warded off across seven births.

entries.source: Suor Maria Celeste takes on her father Galileo's penance
entries.rationale: Remarkably close to the commentarial reading of a child's merit relieving a parent, though the kural's promise about seven births is beyond what any event can show.
Paraphrased rather than quoted because English renderings of this dense passage differ sharply; the doctrinal match with the couplet's second line is very close.
Verified verbatim; covers the 'children are wealth' half well, but says the opposite of the Kural on inherited versus earned standing.
Verified verbatim; a strong match on the second line, though the Qur'anic verses are not about children specifically.
Verified verbatim; a precise match to the second half of the couplet, and notably in tension with Kural 62's transferable merit.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikāya 135, Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta (trans. Ñāṇamoli Thera)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Ñāṇamoli's translation; an unusually exact conceptual and lexical match to the couplet's second line.
Verified verbatim; it matches the first line (children as wealth) but not the second (children's wealth coming from their own deeds), and in the lecture the sentiment is a step toward renunciation.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar, Pauri 2, Rai Balwand and Satta Doom (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial and in tension with the first half of the Kural: it confirms that desert follows one's own deeds, but it shows sons who were not their father's true wealth.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.301–302 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Murray Loeb text; strong on self-earned standing, but the episode is about heroic reputation rather than a family's wealth.
Paraphrased rather than quoted since Carter's and Higginson's renderings differ; the corrective it offers to 'children are my wealth' is genuine but is Epictetus's own emphasis, not the Kural's.

entries.source: Andrew Carnegie publishes 'Wealth', the Gospel of Wealth
entries.rationale: Matches the kural's second line on wealth earned by one's own deeds well, but says little about children as the parent's own treasure.
Paraphrase of a well-attested narrative cycle rather than a quoted verse; the imagistic match — child, hands, food, parental delight — is remarkably close.
Verified verbatim and the child-plus-plain-food image is genuinely parallel, but the Gospel's point is miraculous provision, not parental affection.

entries.source: Sahih Muslim 1373b, Book of Pilgrimage (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com; a warm and specific food-and-children parallel, though about honouring a child rather than the parent's own pleasure.
Verified verbatim, but the link is structural (a meal organised around children) rather than the Kural's specific image of food touched by small hands.

entries.source: Ashokāvadāna, the gift of dust (Divyāvadāna, ch. 26)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a narrative from a post-canonical Sanskrit avadāna; thematically apt on the value of a child's touch on food, but the framework is merit-making, not domestic delight.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§104–107 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased from the verified Jacobi text. No Jain source found treats a child's touch on food as a delight; this is a next-best thematic neighbour only.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 478, Raag Asa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shares the theme of a parent's fond tolerance of a child's mess and mistakes, but it lacks the Kural's image of food and taste and is really a metaphor for God's grace.

entries.source: Homeric Hymn 2 (To Demeter), 235–237 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the shared vocabulary of ambrosia, a child, and feeding is striking, though the Greek hymn's logic is the mirror image of the Kural's.

entries.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus (trans. Cyril Bailey, 1926)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Bailey; a real parallel on plain food outranking luxury, but Epicurus has no interest in children and reaches the conclusion by a quite different route.

entries.source: Victor Hugo publishes The Art of Being a Grandfather
entries.rationale: Captures the delight in small children's ordinary acts, but concerns grandchildren and poetry rather than the specific image of a shared meal.

entries.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8 and the vātsalya tradition
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a broad tradition rather than a single verse; the sensory emphasis genuinely matches, but it is devotional rather than the Kural's domestic register.
Verified verbatim; a strong match on the touching of children, though the ear-pleasure half of the couplet has no counterpart here.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5997, Book of Good Manners (narrated by Abū Hurayrah)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com; an excellent match on touch, framed as mercy rather than as delight.
Verified verbatim; the tactile imagery matches closely, though it is deployed as a metaphor for divine comfort rather than as a claim about parenthood.
Included honestly as an inversion, not an echo — the renunciate strand of Buddhism directly contradicts this couplet, and there is no strong affirming parallel in the early canon.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§92–94 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; it is touch felt in the womb rather than the touch of a born child, and hearing (the kural's second half) is not addressed. The resolve at the end of §94 was used for Kural 41; this is a different sentence.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1266, Raag Malaar, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shares the bodily closeness of parent and child, but it does not speak of hearing the child, and the image serves as a metaphor for God's care rather than a statement about parental joy.

entries.source: Homer, Iliad 6.472–474 (trans. Ian Johnston, Vancouver Island University)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Johnston's published translation; one of the closest matches in the chapter for the couplet's tactile claim.

entries.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 3.894–896 (trans. William Ellery Leonard, 1916)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Leonard translation; an unusually precise philosophical parallel, with the caveat that Lucretius cites it in order to argue it should not be feared to lose.

entries.source: Kangaroo mother care is developed in Bogota
entries.rationale: A strong documented case of parent-child touch being valued, though the motive was medical survival rather than the parent's delight the kural describes.

entries.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.8–10.21 (the flute of Kṛṣṇa and Yaśodā's vātsalya)
entries.rationale: A genuine and pleasing image-level resonance, but the tradition never stages the comparison as a contest the way Valluvar does; scored low for that reason.
Verified verbatim; a real match on the surpassing value of children's voices, though framed as worship rather than as domestic sweetness.
Verified verbatim, but this is an articulate miracle, essentially the opposite of the endearing unintelligibility that the Tamil word maḻalai denotes.
Verified verbatim; the elevation of infant speech matches, but the psalm's frame is theological power, not the ear's pleasure.

entries.source: Vinaya, Mahāvagga I.54 (the ordination of Rāhula)
entries.rationale: Deliberately scored low and honestly: the early Buddhist canon has no praise of a child's babble, and this is the closest scene available rather than a true parallel.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §92 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: The quoted clause is verbatim from Jacobi, but the entry is marked as a paraphrased event because it frames a narrative. It has nothing on a child's speech, so it is a partial, next-best match.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 396, Raag Asa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: no SGGS passage was found comparing a child's lisping speech with music; this verse shares only the image of a trusting child speaking to a parent.
Paraphrase of the myth; the pipe-versus-lute framing is an unusually exact coincidence with the Kural's two instruments, but children play no part in the Greek story.
Paraphrased because translations of this passage diverge; the argument is faithfully represented but concerns social history rather than the comparison with music.

entries.source: Charles Darwin records his infant son's first expressions and sounds
entries.rationale: Shows a father deeply absorbed in his infant's early sounds and expressions, but the record is scientific rather than a comparison with music.
Described rather than quoted because the standard translations of 6.1.1 differ noticeably; the scene is an exceptionally close match for the couplet's claim about a father's duty.
Verified verbatim; strong on the father's formative duty, but the aim is religious upbringing rather than the Kural's public standing among scholars.
Verified verbatim against Sunnah.com, but honestly flagged: this hadith is graded weak (ḍaʿīf) by adh-Dhahabī and al-Albānī, and its emphasis is manners rather than learning.
Verified verbatim against the Sefaria text; an excellent match on the framing of paternal duty as formation, though it includes ritual obligations the Kural has no interest in.

entries.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (the six directions: parents)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested list whose English wording varies by translator; a strong structural match, though 'a profession' is narrower than the Kural's assembly of the learned.
Verified verbatim; the text says the son studied in his father's house but does not explicitly credit the father or mention a learned assembly, so the fit is partial.

Next-best only: it shares the priority of educating the young, but it is a Guru's work for a whole community rather than a father's duty to his own son, and Britannica treats the schools as tradition rather than documented history.

entries.source: Homer, Iliad 9.442–443 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1924)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Murray Loeb rendering; the reference to assemblies 'where men become preeminent' in the preceding lines makes this the chapter's closest Greek parallel.

entries.source: Plato, Protagoras 325c–d (trans. W. R. M. Lamb, Loeb Classical Library)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Perseus text; matches on the father's duty to form the child, though Protagoras is describing practice in order to win a debate about whether virtue is teachable.

entries.source: Philip II of Macedon engages Aristotle as tutor to Alexander
entries.rationale: A close illustration of a father investing in his son's education, though Alexander became famous as a conqueror rather than as a scholar.
Paraphrase of the framing narrative; the son-surpasses-father theme is unmistakable, though the Upaniṣad presents it through conflict rather than universal delight.
Verified verbatim; the widening of delight from parents to all who heard him matches the couplet's second line closely.
Verified verbatim; strong on a child's exceptional wisdom, though the Qur'an does not draw the comparison to the parents that the Kural makes central.
Verified verbatim; a real match on a child's wisdom gladdening the wider community, but the parental comparison is implicit rather than stated.

entries.source: Itivuttaka 74, Puttasutta, vv. 504–505 (trans. Ānandajoti Bhikkhu, Buddhist Wisdom Verses)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the Pali category atijāta — the child born superior to the parents — is as close a technical parallel to this couplet as the cross-tradition search produced.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.6–7 and 14.51–53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong narrative fit. Other verses of this lecture (14.24–28, 14.40) were used for Kurals 36 and 38.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Asa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shares the idea that wisdom is a public good, but it says nothing of children surpassing their parents, which is the heart of Kural 68.
Paraphrase of the hymn's narrative; the delight of a father in a child who outsmarts his elders matches well, though the Greek child's cleverness is thievish rather than learned.
Accurate paraphrase, but the boy is not Meno's child and Plato's interest is the theory of recollection, so the parental dimension of the couplet is absent.

entries.source: Leopold Mozart sets aside his own career to train Wolfgang
entries.rationale: An unusually exact fit: a child outshining an accomplished parent, with the benefit spreading far beyond the family.

entries.source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa (Kausalyā and Rāma)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a theme running through the epic rather than a single citable verse; thematically apt but diffuse, hence the modest score.
Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on both the mechanism (hearing a report) and the superlative claim, differing only in that the speaker is a spiritual father.
Verified verbatim but honestly weak: it is Zechariah, not the mother, who marvels, and the joy-at-hearing-praise structure of the Kural is not present.
Verified verbatim; an exceptionally close verbal and conceptual match, lacking only the Kural's explicit comparison with the hour of birth.

entries.source: Pali commentarial tradition on Sāriputta's death (Dhammapada Commentary; see also SN 47.13)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a post-canonical commentarial narrative rather than a canonical text, and the recognition comes by vision rather than by report; scored accordingly.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book I (Âdîshvaracharitra), ch. III, part 12, 'Marudevî's omniscience and death' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a close match, although the son is praised as a Jina rather than simply as a man of worth (cāṉṟōṉ).

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 496, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: both centre a mother's joy on her son's goodness, but this is a hope and prayer, not the joy of hearing others praise him, and the goodness meant is devotion to God.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 1.360 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb Classical Library, 1919)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Murray Loeb text; she hears him directly rather than hearing others praise him, which is the one gap.
Paraphrased since translations of the passage differ; the analysis of maternal love matches well, but Aristotle is not comparing that joy with the joy of childbirth.

entries.source: Einstein sends his ailing mother news that his theory has been confirmed
entries.rationale: The mother hearing of her son's vindication is well documented, though her own reaction is not recorded, so the joy itself is inferred.

entries.source: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla Kāṇḍa (the putrakāmeṣṭi of Daśaratha)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a famous episode rather than a quoted verse; the tapas-for-a-son framework it supplies is precisely the one the couplet's idiom presupposes.
Verified verbatim; the direction is reversed — the father praises the son rather than bystanders inferring the father's merit from the son.
Verified verbatim; a solid match on the son's duty of requital, but its content is quite different from the Kural's purely reputational answer.
Verified verbatim; close on the principle of requital through character, though it lacks the Kural's distinctive public-saying mechanism.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.34 (Book of the Twos, on repaying one's parents)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested discourse whose English wordings vary; a strong conceptual match, differing in that the Buddha's repayment acts directly on the parents rather than through public reputation.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahâvîra §§110–111 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: The hymn wording is verbatim from Jacobi, but the entry is a paraphrased event. The praise is for Mahâvîra himself, not for his father, so the fit is partial; the related vow of §94 was used for Kural 41.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 310, Raag Gauri, Gauri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong structural fit (a son's worth makes people bless his father), though the son here is the Guru himself, and there is no Kural-style talk of the father's penance.

entries.source: Homer, Iliad 6.476–481 (trans. Ian Johnston, Vancouver Island University)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Johnston's published translation; the closest parallel in the chapter — both verses make the father's reward a saying uttered by onlookers about the son.

entries.source: Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis), Book III, ch. 32 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (On Benefits/Book III, Stewart). Seneca frames this as a son's benefit to his father that brings the father lasting fame, which is a close match to the Kural; the specific 'what penance did his father do' exclamation is not in Seneca.

entries.source: Dorabji Tata completes his father Jamsetji's steel works
entries.rationale: A good case of a son's achievement bringing honour to his father's name, though the credit is shared with Dorabji's cousin Ratanji and many others.

entries.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 11.14.24, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; near-identical claim that love is betrayed by involuntary tears, though the object of love is God rather than a suffering friend.

entries.source: Gospel of John 11:35–36, King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; the onlookers' reaction is an almost word-for-word enactment of 'the tear proclaims the love.'

entries.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1303 (Book of Funerals), narrated by Anas ibn Mālik
entries.rationale: Wording verified against the standard sunnah.com English rendering; minor variation exists across translations of the same Arabic text.
Verified verbatim KJV; the narrative explicitly turns on the impossibility of holding love in.
Paraphrase of a well-attested episode; the match on 'tears reveal hidden love' is strong, but the sutta's own emphasis is on non-attachment rather than on love's visibility.
Verified verbatim; the image is a strong match, but the lecture uses it to show that human love cannot protect anyone, which is a different point from Valluvar's.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 94, Raag Maajh, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong match on tears as the visible sign of love, but the Gurbani love is devotional longing for God, while the Kural speaks of tears shed for a suffering loved one.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.93–95, trans. A. T. Murray (Loeb, 1919)
entries.rationale: Verified against the Perseus/Murray text; the concealment-and-detection structure matches closely, though Odysseus' tears are chiefly grief and longing rather than love for a suffering friend.

entries.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), Part I, Section I, Chapter I
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim opening sentence; strong on involuntariness of sympathy, weaker on the specific image of tears as public testimony.

entries.source: Jim Redmond helps his injured son Derek finish the Olympic 400 metres
entries.rationale: A very close dramatisation of love made visible by a loved one's suffering, though the kural's specific image is a tear rather than an action.

entries.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 6.10 — the story of Dadhīci
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested Purāṇic episode (also in the Ṛg Veda and Mahābhārata); the bone imagery makes it an unusually exact parallel.

entries.source: Gospel of John 15:13, King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; same logic of the loving person belonging to others, though framed as a single act rather than a settled disposition.

entries.source: Qurʾān 59:9 (Sūrat al-Ḥashr), The Clear Quran, trans. Dr. Mustafa Khattab
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on quran.com; the contrast of īthār with shuḥḥ (soul-selfishness) maps directly onto the couplet's two halves.
Verified against Sefaria's text; captures the self/other antithesis precisely, though it stops short of the Kural's 'even my bones' extremity.

entries.source: Sasa Jātaka (Jātaka no. 316), Pāli Jātaka collection
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known canonical tale; the total bodily self-gift matches the couplet closely.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book V (Shântinâthacaritra), ch. IV, part 7, 'Story of the dove and hawk' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a distinctly Jain version of the well-known self-sacrifice motif, and a close match.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 50, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Good parallel for the possessive half of the couplet; the verse does not itself picture the loving person giving even their bones to others, which is the Kural's second and more striking claim.
Accurate paraphrase of the play's premise; the contrast between the self-keeping parents and the self-giving wife is an unusually neat parallel.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, 1169a, trans. W. D. Ross
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in the Ross translation; strong philosophical parallel, though Aristotle grounds it in self-love rightly understood rather than in anbu as such.

entries.source: Maximilian Kolbe offers his life for a fellow prisoner at Auschwitz
entries.rationale: Almost a literal enactment of giving even one's bones to others, documented by the Auschwitz Memorial and the survivor himself.
Faithful paraphrase, but the Upaniṣad redirects love toward the Self while the Kural keeps it directed at other embodied beings — a real philosophical divergence.

entries.source: Epistle of James 2:26, King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; the analogical structure matches very closely, though James's subject is faith-and-works rather than love-and-life.

entries.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6011 (also Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2586), narrated by al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr
entries.rationale: Wording verified against standard English renderings of the hadith; shared body imagery, though applied to the community rather than the individual soul.

entries.source: Sifra, Kedoshim 4:12; cf. Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim 9:4
entries.rationale: The Akiva dictum is verified and famous; the match is thematic (love as organising principle) rather than sharing the Kural's soul-body imagery.

entries.source: Karaṇīya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipāta 1.8 / Khuddakapāṭha 9, trans. Amaravati Sangha
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Amaravati translation on Access to Insight; strong on love as a whole-life orientation, weaker on the specific soul-body claim.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim. The theme of oneness with other beings fits, but Jainism does not say the soul is embodied for the purpose of love: embodiment is caused by karmic bondage.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (So Purakh section of Rehras), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Close structural parallel on the purpose of embodiment; in Gurbani that purpose is union with God through the Name, whereas the Kural speaks of love (anbu) more broadly, including love between people.
Accurate retelling; the 'inseparable union' theme fits well, but the tale is about two people rather than about soul and body.

entries.source: Empedocles of Acragas, On Nature, fragments DK B17, B35 (5th century BCE)
entries.rationale: Accurate summary of the surviving fragments; the parallel is genuinely structural (love as what binds body to life) though Empedocles' Love is impersonal and physical.

entries.source: Viktor Frankl writes Man's Search for Meaning
entries.rationale: Frankl's documented conclusion closely matches the kural's teleological reading, but it is a reflection recorded in a book rather than a single public event.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gītā 4.3, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; sakhya-bhakti (friendship as a mode of love) is a good match, though the Gītā does not lay out love→eagerness→friendship as stages.

entries.source: Gospel of John 15:15, King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; sits in the immediate context of the 'love one another' commandment, so the love→friendship progression is explicit.

entries.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 13 (Book of Belief), narrated by Anas ibn Mālik
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against sunnah.com; excellent match on love generating other-directed desire, slightly less explicit about friendship as the outcome.
Verified verbatim KJV; the spontaneity and the love→friendship causation both match the couplet unusually well.

entries.source: Upaḍḍha Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya 45.2, trans. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Access to Insight translation; very strong on the supreme value of friendship, though the Buddha derives the path from friendship rather than friendship from love.
Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; maitrî corresponds to friendship, but the sutra is a list of contemplations, not Valluvar's causal chain from love to friendship.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on universal friendship flowing from inner transformation, but the hymn credits the holy congregation, not a stated chain from love through eagerness to friendship.

entries.source: The legend of Damon and Pythias, recounted in Cicero, De Officiis III.45 and Valerius Maximus, Memorable Doings and Sayings IV.7
entries.rationale: Composite retelling from several ancient sources with no single canonical text; the thematic match to 'friendship as supreme unsought excellence' is strong.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.1, 1155a, trans. W. D. Ross
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in the Ross translation; Aristotle also derives true philia from goodwill and affection, closely paralleling the couplet's sequence.

entries.source: Jesse Owens and Luz Long become friends at the Berlin Olympics
entries.rationale: A well-documented friendship that came unsought out of goodwill, though the sources do not trace the inner steps from affection to friendship the kural describes; the disputed advice story is deliberately left out.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gītā 12.13–14, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the distinction conferred is divine favour rather than worldly happiness, which is a real difference from the Kural's 'in this world'.
Verified verbatim KJV; excellent on love as an abiding state, though the promised good is union with God rather than worldly felicity.

entries.source: Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 1924, narrated by ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr
entries.rationale: Wording verified against sunnah.com's English rendering; mercy rather than love is the operative term, and the payoff is partly otherworldly.
Verified verbatim KJV; an unusually close match — both are wisdom-literature couplets locating this-worldly happiness in love.

entries.source: Mettānisaṁsa Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.16, trans. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu
