entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the sutta is explicitly a list of this-life benefits of loving-kindness, matching வையகத்து ('in this world') precisely.
Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a strong doctrinal parallel, although in Jainism even pleasant karma is ultimately a bond to be shed.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 5, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit with this-worldly peace as love's fruit; the love in the Japji is directed to God through praise, while the Kural's love is a general disposition toward others.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.182–185, trans. A. T. Murray (Loeb, 1919)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against the Perseus/Murray text; strong match, and notably both sit within a 'household life' ethical frame.
Verified verbatim across standard translations; an exceptionally close philosophical parallel to the couplet's this-worldly happiness claim.

entries.source: Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning marry and settle in Florence
entries.rationale: A good documented example of happiness and renown flowing from a loving life, though their fame as poets began before the marriage.

entries.source: Vālmīki, Rāmāyaṇa, Sundara Kāṇḍa (the burning of Laṅkā)
entries.rationale: Accurate paraphrase of a central episode; a strong illustration of love fuelling martial force, though the epic does not state the principle abstractly.

entries.source: Gospel of John 2:15, King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; a well-recognised instance of love expressing itself as force, though 'zeal' rather than 'love' is the text's own term.
Verified verbatim; an unusually direct scriptural statement that compassion for the oppressed is the ground of legitimate force.
Faithful paraphrase of the biblical narrative; the text does not name love as the motive explicitly, though kinship obligation is plainly the driver.

entries.source: Upāyakauśalya Sūtra (Skill-in-Means Sūtra), the tale of the sea-captain
entries.rationale: Honest low rating: Buddhism's mainstream commitment is to ahiṃsā, and this is a contested Mahāyāna edge case rather than a central teaching — the best available match, not a strong one.
Verified verbatim. Jainism's ahimsa conflicts with any endorsement of martial force, so this is a reinterpretation rather than agreement and is scored below 60.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek (salok 20), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: The Sikh fusion of love and courage (saint-soldier) is a genuine parallel, but the verse itself speaks of spiritual self-surrender; the martial link comes from the later Khalsa tradition, not the verse's own words.

entries.source: Homer, Iliad, Books XVIII–XXII (the wrath of Achilles after Patroclus' death)
entries.rationale: Accurate summary of the epic's central turn; one of the clearest illustrations in world literature of love as the engine of ferocity.

entries.source: Augustine of Hippo, Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Tractate VII.8 (c. 407 CE)
entries.rationale: The Latin 'dilige et quod vis fac' and its context are verified; the traditional English rendering is quoted here, and Augustine's surrounding argument matches the Kural's logic closely.

entries.source: Desmond Doss rescues wounded comrades on Okinawa
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of love fuelling courage in war, though Doss's bravery was protective rather than martial in the sense of fighting.

entries.source: Manusmṛti (Laws of Manu) 8.15, trans. Georg Bühler (Sacred Books of the East, 1886)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in the Bühler translation; a very close structural match, though Manu's trigger is violating dharma rather than specifically lacking love.

entries.source: Matthew 25:45 (in context of 25:41–46), King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; the fire imagery and the 'loveless by omission' charge both align closely with the couplet.
Verified verbatim; the sūra's target — piety without compassion — is precisely the loveless person that aram scorches.
Verified verbatim KJV; the coincidence of 'sun' plus 'righteousness' plus 'scorching the unworthy' makes this an unusually precise image match.
Standard Buddharakkhita wording; the automatic-consequence structure matches, but 'impure mind' is broader than 'lovelessness' and there is no scorching imagery.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.44 and 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; the idea that dharma itself punishes is a close fit, though the verses are aimed at lapsed monks rather than at lovelessness in general.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 67, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best match only: the verse shares the idea that love is indispensable, but lacks the Kural's vivid image of righteousness scorching the loveless like the sun scorching a boneless worm.
Accurate summary of the play; the 'moral order as active tormentor' parallel is real, though the Furies punish a specific crime rather than a general absence of love.
Accurate summary of the Republic's argument; strong on self-inflicted moral misery, though Plato emphasises disordered appetite rather than absence of love as such.

entries.source: Belgium takes the Congo Free State from King Leopold II
entries.rationale: A reasonable illustration of a cruel enterprise undone by moral pressure, though Leopold was paid for the colony and abuses did not end at once.
Faithful paraphrase of the passage; the withering-tree image matches closely, though the animating principle there is jīva/ātman rather than love.

entries.source: Gospel of John 15:6, King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; strong image match, and the passage's own conclusion (John 15:12) is a command to love.
Verified verbatim; the rooted/uprooted tree parallel is strong, though the Qurʾānic subject is the good word rather than love specifically.

entries.source: Jeremiah 17:6 (in context of 17:5–8), King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; the desert-and-dry-plant imagery is an exceptionally close match to the couplet's பாலை setting.
Verified wording in the Buddharakkhita translation; the 'appearance without substance' structure matches, though the missing quality is practice rather than love.
Verified verbatim; the image of hollow appearance matches well, but the emptiness here is a lack of discipline rather than a lack of love.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong match on the tree image of hollow outward flourishing; the hymn's lack is of virtue and the Name in general rather than of love specifically.
Accurate retelling; the pairing of lovelessness with withering-away makes it a strong, though mythologically rather than proverbially framed, parallel.

entries.source: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a, trans. Benjamin Jowett
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in the Jowett translation; strong on the claim that the unrelated life is not a human life, though Aristotle's term is political community rather than love.

entries.source: The world learns of Romania's state orphanages
entries.rationale: Strong scientific evidence that life without affection is a diminished semblance of life, though it concerns children deprived of love rather than people who withhold it.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gītā 3.6, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the outward-organs/inward-state contrast matches well, though the inner quality at stake is detachment rather than love.

entries.source: 1 Corinthians 13:3 (in context of 13:1–3), King James Version
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim KJV; one of the closest cross-tradition matches in the entire chapter — both texts even use the body as the thing rendered useless.

entries.source: Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2564c, narrated by Abū Hurayra
entries.rationale: Wording verified against sunnah.com; explicit body-versus-heart contrast makes it a very close match.
Verified verbatim KJV; near-identical outward/inward contrast, though 'heart' is broader than anbu specifically.
Wording verified against the Buddharakkhita translation; strong outward/inward contrast, though the inner quality is discipline rather than love.
Verified verbatim; the outer-versus-inner structure is close, but the inner quality named is equanimity or knowledge rather than love. Kural 30 drew on other verses of this lecture.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 58, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Good fit on outer versus inner, but the love meant is spiritual love for God expressed through the bride image, not the Kural's general love, and ornaments are not bodily organs.
Accurate retelling; a vivid illustration of outward perfection without inward life, but the tale's own theme is desire and divine favour rather than love as an inner organ.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII, ch. 1 (1155a) (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Ross). Strong structural parallel (what use are outward goods without inner affection), but Aristotle speaks of external goods and friendship, not bodily limbs and love as the body's inner organ.

entries.source: Harry Harlow presents The Nature of Love
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the experiment shows the primacy of love-like comfort over bodily provision, but the kural is about a person lacking love, not an infant deprived of it, and the research is now viewed as ethically troubling.

entries.source: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam) 2.3.24, trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the 'unloving heart is dead matter' image matches well, though the love in question is directed at God.
Verified verbatim KJV; both make love the literal dividing line between life and death rather than a mere virtue.

entries.source: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 52 (Book of Belief), narrated by al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr
entries.rationale: Wording verified against sunnah.com; very close anatomical logic, though the hadith's concern is soundness of the heart broadly rather than love specifically.
Verified verbatim KJV; the anatomical framing of moral transformation parallels the couplet closely.
Verified wording in the Buddharakkhita translation; the imagery matches strikingly, though the Buddhist point is impermanence rather than lovelessness.

Verified verbatim. The dismissive view of the body is shared, but the Jain reasoning (impermanence and impurity, the ashuchi contemplation) is different from Valluvar's point about love as what animates the body.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: a loveless body counted as dead; the only difference is that Farid's love (birha) is love and longing for God rather than love for people.
Honest moderate rating: an accurate account of Homer's underworld and an evocative parallel to 'a body that is not a life', but Homer is describing actual death, not moral lovelessness.

entries.source: Aristotle, De Anima II.1, 412b, trans. J. A. Smith
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in the Smith translation; an unusually precise philosophical analogue, with Aristotle's 'eye of a statue' matching the Kural's 'bones wrapped in skin'.

entries.source: Baba Amte founds Anandwan for people with leprosy
entries.rationale: A reasonable illustration of a life animated by love, though the kural's sharper point concerns the deadness of the loveless, which this event shows only by contrast.
The single most famous Indic formulation of guest-reverence; renders the Kural's premise almost word for word, though the Kural adds the economic argument that the Upanishad does not.
Verified verbatim; a direct command to households about guests, though it motivates by the guest's hidden identity rather than by the purpose of domestic labour.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6135, Book of Good Manners (Al-Adab)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; an exact functional parallel — household duty defined by the guest's claim.
Marked as paraphrase because English renderings of the mishnah vary; the substance — the wide-open house — is uncontested and maps very closely onto the Kural.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.41, Ādiya Sutta (Benefits to be Obtained from Wealth)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased from the sutta's structure; a genuine parallel on the purpose of household wealth, though guests are one item in a list rather than the sole purpose.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 297 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam page, including its typo 'doties'. The verse makes giving essential to householding, though it does not speak of guests as specifically as the Kural does.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, articles on langar and Sikh practice, and on Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on household life justified by hospitality; the langar is a communal institution of the congregation rather than the private household the Kural describes.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 14.57–58 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb)
entries.rationale: Verified against the Perseus/Loeb text; the closest Greek analogue to the Kural's claim that the household exists to serve whoever arrives.

entries.source: Immanuel Kant, Toward Perpetual Peace (1795), Third Definitive Article
entries.rationale: Paraphrased because English translations differ; a real thematic link, but Kant deliberately narrows hospitality to a juridical minimum, whereas Valluvar makes it the maximal purpose of domestic life.

entries.source: The Rule of Saint Benedict orders that guests be received as Christ
entries.rationale: A strong institutional parallel to the kural's claim, though a monastery is a religious community rather than the lay householder Valluvar addresses.
Verified against the Paramananda translation; the imagery of the guest kept outside is almost identical, though the Upanishad specifies a Brahmin guest where the Kural universalises.
Paraphrase of a narrative rather than a quotation; the situational match (feasting while someone waits outside) is very close, though the parable concerns a beggar rather than a guest.
Verified verbatim on the Quranic Arabic Corpus; a strong match on giving food one desires, but its recipients are the poor and captive rather than a guest at the door.
This is the standard and near-universal English rendering of the Aramaic formula; the liturgical placement before the meal makes the parallel unusually exact.
Verified wording; one of the closest cross-tradition parallels in the whole chapter — both texts stake the claim on an extreme case (the deathless medicine / the last mouthful).

entries.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 173 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 113 on wisdomlib.org
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Vijay K. Jain's translation as quoted on wisdomlib, not Ajit Prasada's canonical one. The Jain guest is specifically an ascetic, not any visitor, and the Kural's 'deathless medicine' hyperbole has no counterpart.

Good parallel on the moral priority of eating together; the Akbar episode is reported by Britannica as something 'said' by tradition, and the rule concerns communal equality rather than a host's private meal.
Paraphrase of a narrative; a vivid inverted parallel rather than a direct teaching, and the Cyclops' cannibalism far exceeds the ordinary selfishness the Kural addresses.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 19.10, quoting Epicurus
entries.rationale: Paraphrased rather than quoted since translations vary; the shared premise is real, but Epicurus is concerned with friendship and pleasure, not with an obligation to an unknown guest.

entries.source: The villagers of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon shelter refugees
entries.rationale: A powerful case of refusing to enjoy safety and food alone while strangers waited at the door, though the stakes were rescue rather than ordinary hospitality.

entries.source: Rig Veda 10.117.1 (trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
entries.rationale: Verified in Griffith's translation; a near one-to-one statement, though addressed to liberality in general rather than to guests specifically.
Verified verbatim; the narrative match to 'hospitality does not ruin the household' is very close, though the mechanism here is explicitly miraculous.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 5392, Book of Food and Meals
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a direct and practical parallel, though it speaks to a single extra guest rather than to a lifetime of daily hospitality.
Narrative paraphrase; the match on 'hospitality builds rather than wastes the house' is strong, but this is one extraordinary occasion rather than a daily practice.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.34, Sīha Sutta (To General Sīha)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the sutta's list; the shared point about present-life benefit is genuine, though the fruits named are social rather than material non-depletion.

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 10 'Liberality', st. 9 (= st. 99), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text, used because no canonical verse addresses the fear of being impoverished by giving this directly. Verified verbatim on the sacred-texts.com transcription of the Indian Antiquary translation.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on sharing that does not deplete; the hymn's inexhaustible treasure is spiritual (the Name), not the material provisions of a hospitable house.
Narrative paraphrase, but the specific detail of the inexhaustible vessel makes this an unusually precise match to the Kural's claim.
Paraphrase of a well-known doctrine; it explains the daily-repetition element well but says nothing about material non-depletion, which is the Kural's actual promise.

entries.source: Guru Amar Das makes the free kitchen central to Sikh life
entries.rationale: A close illustration of habitual daily hospitality that has never ruined its hosts, though it is a community institution rather than a single household.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.106 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Bühler's translation; names wealth as the first fruit of hospitality exactly as the Kural does, though without the image of the goddess dwelling in the house.
Verified verbatim; an excellent match on cheerfulness as the operative virtue, though it concerns almsgiving rather than hosting.
Verified verbatim; the gladness is conveyed by action rather than named as such, and the blessing that follows (a son) is not prosperity in the Kural's sense.
Verified wording; a striking parallel in linking hospitality to divine indwelling, though the Talmud ranks hospitality above the Divine Presence while the Kural has the deity move in as a reward.

entries.source: Anāthapiṇḍika narratives, Pali Canon (Vinaya Cullavagga VI; Aṅguttara Nikāya)
entries.rationale: A composite retelling drawn from several canonical passages rather than a single citable text; illustrative rather than doctrinal, and the causal claim the Kural makes is not asserted in the sources.

Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. Jainism has no prosperity goddess who rewards hosts as Śrī does in the Kural. The treasure is a sign of merit (puṇya), and the Kural's stress on the host's glad face is missing.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar), Satta and Balwand (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong match on gracious hospitality and abundance, without the Kural's goddess of prosperity; the verse praises Khivi's generosity rather than promising wealth as its reward.
Paraphrase; the shared image of an indwelling household goddess is genuine, but Hestia's presence is a cultic given rather than a reward earned by cheerful hosting.

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §64 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis II.44-89, Miller). Partial match: Cicero links hospitality to the host's benefit and influence, but he does not stress cheerfulness of countenance, and his benefit is social and political rather than prosperity as such.

entries.source: Gander takes in the passengers of 38 diverted airliners
entries.rationale: A good documented case of glad hospitality followed by honour and goodwill, though the reward was recognition rather than prosperity in the kural's sense.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verified in the Prabhupada translation; an exact conceptual match on eating the remnant, though the Gita's offering is to God and the Kural's is to the guest.
Verified verbatim; the sowing-and-reaping image is identical, though Paul keeps the proportion while the Kural pushes to the hyperbole of a field needing no seed at all.
Verified verbatim on the Quranic Arabic Corpus; one of the closest metaphorical parallels available, differing only in that the Qur'an quantifies the increase.
Verified verbatim, but the verse is genuinely ambiguous in Hebrew — some read it as commercial venture advice — so the hospitality reading is interpretive.
Paraphrase of the sutta's simile; the field-and-seed imagery matches strikingly, though the Buddhist text locates fertility in the recipient rather than in the donor's land.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. The field-and-seed image is a close match, but the Jain verse makes the guest the field, while the Kural suggests that the host's own field needs no sowing.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 24, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial fit: shares the agricultural image of deeds as the field, but says nothing of feeding guests first or eating what remains.
Narrative paraphrase; the hospitality-to-harvest link is unusually exact, though the hymn's emphasis falls on the Eleusinian Mysteries rather than on agricultural return.
A candidly weak match: Seneca's whole point is that one should *not* expect a return, whereas the Kural promises a spectacular one, so the traditions genuinely diverge here.

entries.source: The Choctaw Nation sends famine relief to Ireland
entries.rationale: Next-best only: a documented act of giving to others first from scarcity, but it was distant relief rather than feeding guests at home, and the kural's promise of an unsown harvest is not shown.
Narrative paraphrase of a well-attested episode; the sequential-guests structure and the heavenly recognition match the Kural remarkably closely.
Verified verbatim; the structural inversion — host becomes welcomed guest of heaven — is essentially identical to the Kural's.

entries.source: Qur'an 13:23 (Sahih International); the angels' greeting follows at 13:24
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim, but the reward here is for righteousness and patience generally rather than for hospitality specifically, so the link runs through the shared image rather than the shared cause.

entries.source: Ushpizin custom of Sukkot (Zohar, Emor 103b; widespread liturgical practice)
entries.rationale: A composite description of a living custom rather than a single citable verse; the thematic fit is strong but the direction of guesting is inverted relative to the Kural.
Verified in the Buddharakkhita translation; the welcome-on-arrival image is a very precise counterpart to the Kural's 'good guest to the heavenly ones.'

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 10 'Liberality', st. 1 (= st. 91), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text, verified verbatim on the sacred-texts.com transcription. It matches the heavenly reward but not the Kural's picture of a host who watches the road for guests or its wordplay of the host becoming a guest.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong structural parallel (service on earth answered by honour in the hereafter); seva is broader than hospitality and lacks the Kural's image of watching the road for the next guest.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 17.485–487 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb)
entries.rationale: Verified against the Perseus/Loeb text; the theoxeny motif directly connects earthly hospitality to divine visitors, though it motivates by fear rather than by hope of welcome.

Paraphrase of Derrida's central distinction; the match on 'waiting for the guest who has not yet arrived' is genuinely striking, though Derrida offers no heavenly reward and treats the ideal as an aporia rather than an achievable practice.

entries.source: The hospice of the Great St Bernard Pass is founded
entries.rationale: A strong image of hosts watching the road for coming guests, though the kural's reward of welcome among the heavenly can only be read in Bernard's later sainthood.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.70 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Bühler; the shared technical framing of hospitality as a sacrifice is exact, and almost certainly the background Valluvar is drawing on.
Verified verbatim; one of the strongest matches in the entire chapter — same proposition, same proportionality, same domain of hospitality.

entries.source: Jami` at-Tirmidhi 807 (graded Sahih), Book on Fasting
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; an excellent parallel, narrowed only by being specific to breaking a fast.
Verified wording via Sefaria; the 'no measure' formulation is a remarkably exact verbal parallel, though the Mishnah applies it to the obligation while the Kural applies it to the reward.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikāya 142, Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta (The Exposition of Offerings)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the sutta's scheme rather than a quotation, but the doctrinal identity with the Kural is as close as anything in this chapter.

entries.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. This is a near one-to-one match for the idea that the fruit is measured by the guest; the sutra adds manner, thing given and giver as further variables.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only, partly a contrast: the Kural grades the fruit of hospitality by the guest's merit, while Sikh teaching refuses to rank recipients and sees the same Light in all.
Narrative paraphrase; the proportionality-to-the-guest principle is genuinely present, but it operates through divine gratitude rather than as a stated general law.
Paraphrase of a well-known doctrine; the proportionality logic matches, but Aristotle is analysing the distribution of civic goods, not the spiritual fruit of hospitality.

entries.source: Lorenzo de' Medici takes the young Michelangelo into his household
entries.rationale: A reasonable illustration of a guest whose worth determined the yield, though this was patronage of a pupil as much as hospitality to a visitor.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.72 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Bühler; a strong match on the emptiness of the non-hospitable life, though Manu states it as present fact and the Kural as a future lament.
Verified verbatim; the situational and emotional match is very close, though the Kural's failure is specifically the omission of hospitality.
Verified verbatim on the Quranic Arabic Corpus; an excellent match on anxious hoarding, though the surah adds the element of contempt for others that the Kural does not.
Verified verbatim; a very close thematic match, differing only in that Qohelet does not name hospitality as the omitted alternative.
Verified in the Buddharakkhita translation; a good match on the fate of the non-giver, though it lacks the Kural's distinctive note of retrospective lament.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. It matches the too-late regret, but it speaks of good deeds in general rather than hospitality, and the regret comes in the next birth rather than in this life.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on the futility of hoarding, but the hymn does not set it against hospitality as the alternative the hoarder failed to choose.
Narrative paraphrase; captures the futility of hoarding vividly, but Midas's failing is greed for gold rather than neglect of guests.
Paraphrased because English renderings differ; the analysis of the lament is apt, but Epictetus prescribes detachment rather than the Kural's remedy of active hospitality.

entries.source: The fall of Heshen, the Qianlong emperor's favourite
entries.rationale: Next-best only: a documented case of hoarded wealth ending in total loss, but the sources tie his fall to corruption and politics, not to any failure of hospitality.

entries.source: Rig Veda 10.117.2–6 (trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
entries.rationale: Verified in Griffith's translation of the hymn; a close match on wealth-with-hardness, though the Vedic verse emphasises friendlessness rather than the Kural's charge of folly.
Verified verbatim; 'rich… and poor' in the same breath is an unusually exact verbal parallel to உடைமையுள் இன்மை, though the context is spiritual complacency rather than hospitality.
Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a direct parallel on the miser's wealth being destroyed, though framed as divine action rather than as inherent folly.

entries.source: 1 Samuel 25:25 (King James Version); narrative at 1 Samuel 25:2–38
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; one of the sharpest matches in the chapter — a rich man, a refusal of hospitality, and the explicit diagnosis of folly, exactly as in the Kural.
Paraphrase of the sutta's narrative and simile; the correspondence to 'poverty in the midst of wealth' is very close, and the Buddha likewise attributes it to want of understanding.

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār ch. 28 'Illiberality', st. 3 (= st. 273), English translation in The Indian Antiquary vol. II (1873)
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text, used because it matches the Kural's 'folly' framing almost exactly. Verified verbatim on the sacred-texts.com transcription; the recipient is specified as ascetics rather than guests in general.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Kabir (salok 192) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on the household that fails in hospitality being inwardly destitute; Kabir's guests are specifically the Holy, and he speaks of spiritual death rather than folly.
Narrative paraphrase; captures wealth collapsing into destitution powerfully, though Erysichthon's sin is sacrilege and his affliction a curse rather than simple inhospitality.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 2.6 (trans. Richard M. Gummere), quoting Epicurus
entries.rationale: Verified in the Gummere translation; the paradox of the rich-yet-poor is stated as directly as in the Kural, though Seneca locates the cause in craving rather than in failed hospitality.

entries.source: The voyage of the St. Louis
entries.rationale: A clear documented case of plenty refusing the guest, though it concerns national refugee policy rather than a household's hospitality.

entries.source: Manusmriti 3.101 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Bühler; a strong match on manner-as-substance, though Manu speaks of speech where the Kural speaks of the face.
Verified verbatim; an unusually precise match — the entire point of both verses is that the manner of hospitality is the hospitality.

entries.source: Sahih Muslim 2626, Book of Virtue and Good Manners
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; the shared focus on the face as the decisive element makes this among the closest matches in the chapter.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot (Mishnah, Tractate Avot) 1:15 (Sefaria Community Translation)
entries.rationale: Verified via Sefaria; 'receive every person with a pleasant countenance' is essentially a prose translation of this couplet's positive form.

entries.source: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.148, Sappurisadāna Sutta (A Person of Integrity's Gifts)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase, since English renderings of the five terms differ considerably; the doctrine that manner determines the value of the gift is a firm match.

entries.source: Amṛtacandra, Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya v. 168 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2012), as quoted in the explanatory note to Ratnakaraṇḍaka-śrāvakācāra v. 113 on wisdomlib.org; cf. Sarvārthasiddhi on Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib (Vijay K. Jain's translation, not Ajit Prasada's). It establishes that the manner of welcome comes first, but has nothing like the Kural's anicham-flower image of how quickly a cold look wounds.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 129) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Good fit on the fragility of the heart; Farid speaks of harsh words toward anyone, not specifically of a host's averted face toward a guest.
Narrative paraphrase; the emphasis on the instantaneous, unconditional welcome is a genuine parallel, though Homer shows the positive case rather than the Kural's negative one.

entries.source: Emmanuel Levinas, Totality and Infinity (1961), Section I and Section III
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of Levinas's central themes; the convergence on 'face' and 'welcome' as the foundation of ethics is remarkable, though Levinas is concerned with the guest's face while Valluvar is concerned with the host's.

entries.source: Marian Anderson is refused Constitution Hall and sings at the Lincoln Memorial
entries.rationale: Next-best only: a famous documented case of a guest turned away, but Anderson did not wither; she triumphed elsewhere, which partly cuts against the kural's image.

entries.source: Manusmriti 4.138 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 25)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Bühler's translation; the correspondence is close to one-to-one, including the explicit rejection of 'agreeable falsehood' (= padiru).
Verbatim KJV; the phrase 'truth in love' matches the Kural's two conditions precisely, though Paul's frame is ecclesial growth rather than general ethics.
Verbatim Sahih International wording, but the verse stresses uprightness of speech without the Kural's explicit note of tenderness.

entries.source: Psalms 55:21 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)
entries.rationale: Verbatim KJV; a strong thematic match but expressed as a portrait of deceit rather than a positive definition, and quoted here via a Christian translation of the Tanakh.

entries.source: Vācā Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.198 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Thanissaro's translation; the five factors subsume both of Valluvar's conditions and add timing.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 92 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam page. This is a close definitional match, though the Jain verse is addressed to monks and does not stress the Kural's warmth (eeram) as such.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 31, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on sweet speech flowing from inner realization; the verse does not separately name freedom from guile, and its bride image is spiritual, not romantic.

entries.source: Homer, Iliad 1.247–249 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb / Perseus)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Perseus; an exemplary figure rather than a stated principle, and Homer does not thematise guilelessness.

entries.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §18 (ninth rule) (tr. George Long)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book XI). Strong match on affection without guile; the Kural's further point that such words come from people who have grasped what is right is only implicit in Marcus's Stoic context.

entries.source: Vaclav Havel's first New Year's address as president
entries.rationale: A good example of guileless, well-meant speech from one who had seen the truth, though its content was sobering rather than sweet in the ordinary sense.
Paraphrase of a verified passage; it elevates the manner of giving but stops short of the Kural's explicit ranking of word above gift.
Verified verbatim in the KJV Apocrypha; one of the closest single-verse parallels to any Kural in this chapter.
Verified verbatim; the Qur'an's comparison is with flawed charity, slightly narrower than the Kural's comparison with wholehearted giving.
Paraphrase of a verified passage (wording varies by translation); the substantive match is nearly exact.
Accurate paraphrase of a canonical list, but Buddhism pairs the two rather than ranking speech above giving.
Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi's translation). The pairing of gift and speech is close, but the verse does not directly rank a kind word above a material gift, so this is a partial match.

entries.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 28, Pauri 15 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)
entries.rationale: Partial: pairs sweet speech with giving but does not rank the cheerful face and kind word above the gift; Bhai Gurdas is authoritative early exegesis, not scripture. Wording verified via the BaniDB database behind searchgurbani.
Faithful summary of the episode; the parallel is real but inferred from narrative rather than stated as a maxim.

entries.source: Seneca, De Beneficiis (On Benefits), Books I–II
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of Seneca's recurring argument rather than a single verified line; English renderings of the 'stony bread' image vary widely by translator.

entries.source: Princess Diana shakes hands with an AIDS patient
entries.rationale: A strong case of warmth of manner outweighing material help, though the gesture was a touch rather than kind words.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the standard As It Is rendering; elevates speech to austerity, matching the Kural's elevation of it to aram, though without the facial/visual elements.
Verbatim KJV; it describes the heart–face link the Kural assumes but does not make the moral claim that this constitutes virtue.
Verified against Sunnah.com; wording is the standard English rendering and the conceptual match is near-exact.
Verified against Sefaria; the match on the facial element is exact, though Shammai does not add the Kural's claim about the inner source of speech.
Buddharakkhita's wording, quoted with an ellipsis; addresses the interiority condition precisely but not the face or gaze.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 91 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It matches the Kural's demand that words come from within, but says nothing of the welcoming face and kind gaze, so it is a reasonable but partial fit.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: the verse praises God's sweet speech rather than defining human virtue, and it omits the Kural's welcoming face and kindly look.
Accurate summary, but Greek myth personifies social charm without making the Kural's moral identification of it with virtue.

entries.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book XI, §15 (tr. George Long)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book XI). Close on the face and eyes showing inner goodness; Marcus does not mention sweet speech, which is the Kural's third element.
Very close to the kural's picture of warm, heartfelt words as virtue in itself, documented by the Vatican's own transcript.

entries.source: Subhāṣita, attributed to Chāṇakya Nīti 16.13 (also collected in the Subhāṣita Ratna Bhāṇḍāgāra)
entries.rationale: Source attribution verified; rendered as paraphrase because English translations of this subhāṣita vary considerably and no single canonical version exists.
Verbatim KJV; the mechanism (royal favour) is narrower and more courtly than the Kural's universal 'toward anyone at all'.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 2989 (Book of Jihad, chapter on charity)
entries.rationale: Rendered as paraphrase because the phrase appears in several hadith collections with differing wording; the underlying teaching is well attested.

entries.source: Ben Sira / Ecclesiasticus 6:5 (King James Version, Apocrypha)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim including the KJV's 'fairspeaking'; promises abundance of friends rather than explicitly freedom from poverty.
Accurate summary of a canonical list; 'blessing' is broader and vaguer than the Kural's specific promise about poverty.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 86 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It matches the universal scope (yaarmaattum), but it concerns forgiveness and friendship rather than speech, and has no counterpart to the Kural's promise of freedom from want. Next-best only.

entries.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 12, Pauri 16 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on gentle speech yielding happiness, but lacks the Kural's stress on speaking kindly to everyone without exception and on escaping poverty; Bhai Gurdas is exegesis, not scripture.
Verified verbatim in Evelyn-White; the reward is prestige and authority rather than freedom from poverty, and the gift is divinely bestowed rather than earned.

entries.source: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom, §118 (trans. Joseph Jacobs, 1892)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in the Jacobs translation; Gracián's motive is frankly strategic, where Valluvar's is moral, so the tone diverges even though the prediction matches.

entries.source: Fred Rogers testifies to the US Senate for public television
entries.rationale: A strong case of kind speech averting material want, though the final appropriation was decided by a wider political process.
Verse and content verified; given as paraphrase because English translations vary widely and no standard version is canonical.
Verbatim KJV; the ornament named is meekness of spirit rather than speech specifically, but the humility half maps exactly.
Verified verbatim; the two qualities are joined exactly as in the Kural, though the ornament metaphor is absent.
Paraphrase, since English renderings of the term for 'yielding/suave' differ substantially; the pairing of humility and pleasantness is secure.
Paraphrase, as translations of these verses diverge; the target is religious pretension rather than social ornament, so the fit is partial.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 89 (cf. v. 88) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com, including its awkward English 'worthy of proud'. It matches humility and refraining from insult, but has no ornament metaphor and no explicit praise of sweet speech.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one pairing of humility and sweetness as the highest good; Gurbani calls them the essence of virtue rather than using the Kural's image of ornament.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 8.169–175 (trans. A. T. Murray, Loeb / Perseus)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Perseus; 'sweet modesty' (aidoi meilichiē) captures both of the Kural's terms, though framed as divine gift rather than cultivated virtue.

entries.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, Counsels and Maxims, ch. III 'Our Relation to Others', §36
entries.rationale: Quotation verified and located, but Schopenhauer's interest is instrumental (managing people) rather than the Kural's claim about what adorns a person.

entries.source: Gandhi attends the royal reception at Buckingham Palace in his dhoti
entries.rationale: A vivid documented example of humility worn as one's ornament, though it illustrates the humility half of the kural more than kind speech.
Accurate paraphrase, but the sutra concerns inner attitudes and mental purification rather than speech and its social effects.
Verbatim KJV; the deliberate selection of beneficial speech matches the Kural's naadi almost exactly.
Verbatim Sahih International; describes the transformation of enmity rather than a general increase of virtue, but the causal logic is the same.
Paraphrase of a verified passage; the frame is sanctification/desecration of the Name rather than a general account of virtue's increase.

entries.source: Cunda Kammāraputta Sutta, Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.176 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Thanissaro's translation; the canonical positive statement of kindly speech in the Pali Canon.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 94 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It agrees on putting the hearer's benefit first but partly diverges on pleasantness, and says nothing of evil waning and virtue growing, so it is next-best.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 78) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Good fit on goodness diminishing evil, but Farid speaks of good deeds in general, not specifically of carefully chosen, pleasant speech.

entries.source: Aeschylus, Eumenides 970 (cf. 885) (trans. H. W. Smyth, rev. Bannon and Nagy)
entries.rationale: Verified against the Center for Hellenic Studies text; a mythic dramatisation rather than a precept, but the transformation of evil by persuasion is exact.
Accurate summary of Plato's argument; his concern is the epistemology of rhetoric rather than the Kural's claim about virtue increasing in the world.

entries.source: Nelson Mandela appeals for calm after the killing of Chris Hani
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of deliberately chosen good words reducing harm, though the outcome also depended on many other actors.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the As It Is rendering; the alignment of benefit with pleasantness is close to one-to-one with the Kural.
Verbatim KJV; the 'salt' metaphor is usually read as usefulness or pointedness, which aligns well but is interpretively looser than the Kural's explicit payan.
Verbatim Sahih International; the command to say 'that which is best' is a strong match, though it does not address the speaker's own return.

entries.source: Proverbs 16:24 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)
entries.rationale: Verbatim KJV; the benefit accrues to the hearer only, where the Kural also tracks the speaker's gain, and this is a Christian translation of the Tanakh.

entries.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Thanissaro's translation; one of the most systematic treatments of the Kural's problem in any tradition.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 95 (cf. v. 96) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com. It is a strong match for the social goodwill the speaker earns, while the merit half of the Kural is only implied through v. 96.

entries.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 29, Pauri 4 (English translation as given on BaniDB / searchgurbani.com)
entries.rationale: Partial: shares speech-bound-to-character and its moral fruit, but not the Kural's twin reward of social goodwill; Bhai Gurdas is exegesis, not scripture.
Accurate summary, but the passage concerns poetic authority rather than the ethics of everyday speech, so the connection is thematic only.
Verified verbatim in the Roberts translation, quoted with an ellipsis; Aristotle's interest is persuasive efficacy where Valluvar's is moral merit.

entries.source: Ashoka's Rock Edict XII on restraint in speech
entries.rationale: A close parallel to the kural's claim that character-bound speech yields mutual benefit, though it is a documented teaching rather than an event showing the result.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.40 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the As It Is rendering; the two-world promise matches exactly, but the subject is good action generally rather than speech.
Verbatim KJV; the two-world accountability of speech matches, though the emphasis falls on judgment rather than on the happiness the Kural promises.
Verified against Sunnah.com; the hadith explicitly conditions speech on the Last Day, giving a tight match to the Kural's two-world frame.
Paraphrase, as translations of the formula differ; 'making peace between people' is a speech act, but the list is broader than speech alone.
Buddharakkhita's wording; the two-world formula is near-identical, though the referent is meritorious deeds generally rather than speech.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. The 'this world and the next' promise in 1.15 concerns self-mastery generally, not speech, so the link is a next-best combination.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong mirror-image fit covering both this world (reputation) and the next (the Lord's Court), though framed as a warning rather than as the Kural's positive promise.
Honest weak match: Greek myth has no ethic of speech extending into the afterlife, so this is the best available structural analogue only.
Accurate summary of the dialogue's closing argument; the concern is justice in oratory rather than kindness in ordinary speech.
A strong example of speech purged of meanness, though the kural's promise of joy in this life and the next cannot be shown by any event.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.4 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gītā As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from the As It Is rendering; classifies harshness as a vice but does not reproduce the Kural's argument from personal experience.
Verbatim KJV; one of the most direct parallels in the chapter, though framed as consequence rather than as a question about motive.
Verbatim Sahih International; the harsh/gentle contrast matches closely, in a leadership context rather than a general one.
Paraphrase of a verified passage; establishes the seriousness of harsh words but not the Kural's argument from experienced pleasure.
Buddharakkhita's wording; both the prohibition and the appeal to what the speaker himself will feel align closely.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com. It shares the appeal to experience, but it concerns a pupil and teacher and lacks the Kural's Golden-Rule reasoning from one's own pleasure to another's.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on the sweet/harsh contrast and the folly of harshness; it lacks the Kural's appeal to the speaker's own experience of being spoken to kindly.
Accurate summary; a cautionary figure rather than a stated principle, and Homer's treatment of Thersites carries class assumptions the Kural does not share.
Verified in Long's translation; addresses anger's cost generally rather than harsh speech specifically.

entries.source: The Seventeen-Article Constitution warns against anger
entries.rationale: Next-best only: a documented ancient text making a parallel argument from shared experience against anger, but it concerns resentment generally rather than harsh speech, and its authorship is debated.

entries.source: Manusmriti 2.161 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 25)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Bühler; a prohibition on harsh speech rather than the Kural's specific argument that the pleasant alternative is freely available.
Verbatim KJV; the fruit imagery and the subject (the tongue) match well, though James argues about consistency rather than about a freely available choice.
Verbatim Sahih International, quoted with an ellipsis; an unusually close match of both subject and imagery.

entries.source: Proverbs 25:11 (Hebrew Bible; King James Version rendering)
entries.rationale: Verbatim KJV; the shared fruit imagery is striking but Proverbs praises the good word without contrasting it against the available bad one, and this is a Christian rendering of the Tanakh.
Sutta identity and content verified; given as paraphrase because a published verbatim English rendering was not confirmed.

entries.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.14 with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org. It is a strong doctrinal match for condemning harsh speech, but has no counterpart to the ripe-and-unripe-fruit image or the point that kind words are always at hand.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 972, Raag Raamkalee, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Close on the fruit image and the folly of choosing badly, but Kabir's subject is spiritual delusion in general, not harsh versus pleasant speech.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 719–721 (trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Evelyn-White; gnomic wisdom rather than myth proper, and it praises restraint where the Kural praises sweetness.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.6, 1126b (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in the Ross translation; Aristotle analyses the vice structurally where Valluvar diagnoses it as simple bad judgment.
A strong illustration of choosing harsh words over available mild ones, though Bismarck's aim was deliberate provocation rather than careless harshness.

entries.source: Manusmriti 2.227 (G. Bühler trans., Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
entries.rationale: Strong match on the 'unrepayable debt' idea, but the benefactors are parents, not someone who helps without any prior tie, which is the Kural's specific point.
Close structural match (unearned benefit); the Christian frame is divine grace rather than human gratitude between equals, and the verse does not itself discuss repayment.

entries.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4811 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
entries.rationale: Establishes the duty of gratitude to human benefactors, but says nothing about the unrepayable size of unprompted help.
Good emotional match; however Boaz explains in 2:11 that he acts because of her loyalty to Naomi, so the kindness is not wholly 'unprompted'.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.32 (Kataññu Sutta, Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)
entries.rationale: Striking verbal parallel ('this great earth' cannot repay); the benefactors are parents rather than unrelated helpers, so the 'unprompted' element is absent.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. IV, part 7 'The story of Candanā' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib; a narrative illustration rather than a doctrinal statement, and the Kural's cosmic hyperbole (earth and heaven cannot repay) is only implied by her gift of the treasure.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 809, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on unearned benefaction and the debt of gratitude; the benefactor is God rather than a human helper, and the verse confesses ingratitude rather than stating the immeasurability of the gift.
Primarily a xenia (hospitality) scene; gratitude and repayment are present but the Kural's claim about the incalculable size of the debt is only implied.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.14, 1163b (W. D. Ross trans.)
entries.rationale: Explicit 'no equivalent return is possible' claim; restricted to gods and parents rather than unprompted helpers.

entries.source: Raoul Wallenberg protects the Jews of Budapest
entries.rationale: A very close fit for unearned, unrepayable help; the kural speaks from the recipient's side, while the documented record focuses on the giver.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 49-51 and 67-68 (sarga numbering varies by edition)
entries.rationale: Good narrative fit for timely help honoured beyond its practical result; the text does not state the 'worth more than the world' evaluation explicitly.
Matches the idea that small help in need carries immense value; framed from the giver's reward rather than the recipient's gratitude.
Strong match on small-but-timely help having outsized worth; here the one who 'thanks' is God rather than the recipient.

entries.source: Rashi on Exodus 7:19 (drawing on Midrash Tanchuma)
entries.rationale: Classic Jewish teaching on hakarat hatov for timely help; concerns an inanimate benefactor, so it is illustrative rather than a direct parallel.

entries.source: Jataka Nidanakatha (commentarial biography); Mahabodhi Temple Complex, Bodh Gaya
entries.rationale: Weak-to-moderate: the 'gratitude' interpretation comes from later tradition rather than the canonical suttas; used as the best available narrative parallel.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X, ch. IV, parts 6-7 'Vīra's special vow' and 'The story of Candanā' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Quote verified on wisdomlib; strong narrative fit on smallness and timing, but the story celebrates the giver's merit more than the recipient's gratitude, and it shares a narrative with the entry for 101.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: shares the stress on help at the critical moment, but the helper is the divine Name, not a human favour, and the verse does not speak of gratitude or of the help's small size.

entries.source: Aesop's Fables, The Ant and the Dove (Perry Index 235; G. F. Townsend trans.)
entries.rationale: Aesopic fable rather than myth proper, but a clean illustration of small help at the critical moment.
Seneca speaks mainly to the giver's promptness, whereas the Kural speaks to the recipient's valuation; the principle is shared.

entries.source: The little ships help evacuate Dunkirk
entries.rationale: Timeliness fits well, but IWM notes that most soldiers actually left from the harbour mole on large ships, so the small boats were only one part of the rescue.
Direct match on 'without expectation of return' (anupakarine); the Gita speaks from the giver's side, while the Kural speaks to the recipient's gratitude.
Strong match on disinterested giving; the verse even mentions the 'unthankful', but it is addressed to givers rather than recipients.
Very close match: explicit renunciation of any return, even of gratitude; again framed from the giver's side.
Clear conceptual match on disinterested kindness; the Kural's recipient-side 'weighing' is not addressed.
Mahayana metaphysical frame (non-attachment to signs) differs from the Kural's ethical frame, but the vastness image and non-calculating giving line up.

entries.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 19 'Greatness', st. 4 (= st. 184), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text, used because no canonical scripture found addresses this closely. It praises the unreckoning giver but says nothing of how the recipient should value the help, so the fit is partial.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on help given without calculating reward; the Kural's point about the recipient's appraisal (greater than the ocean) has no counterpart in the verse.

entries.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.618-724 (Roman retelling of a Phrygian legend)
entries.rationale: Good fit for disinterested giving; the source is a Latin poet's treatment of a Greek-world myth, and gratitude here flows from gods to humans.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.13, 1162b (W. D. Ross trans.)
entries.rationale: Near-direct conceptual parallel; Aristotle goes on to say the recipient should still repay if possible, which fits the chapter as a whole.

entries.source: CERN puts the World Wide Web in the public domain
entries.rationale: A strong example of help given without calculating returns, though it was an institutional decision partly aimed at maximising the web's spread rather than a purely personal act of kindness.
Captures the valuing of small gifts by their spirit; it is God receiving worship rather than a human recipient showing gratitude.
Excellent match on revaluing a small gift; the context is almsgiving to the Temple rather than gratitude for a favour received.
Shares the 'nothing is too small' principle, but concerns divine accounting of deeds rather than a recipient magnifying a favour.
Near one-to-one match: the grateful recipient magnifies the benefactor's effort while the ungrateful one minimises it.

entries.source: Dhammapada Commentary on verse 76 (Radha Thera story)
entries.rationale: Very close narrative match (tiny gift, huge grateful return); the source is the commentarial tradition, not the canonical verse itself.

entries.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 22 'The choice of friends', st. 6 (= st. 216), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Next-best match from a Tamil Jain text: it shares the palmyra image and links lasting friendship to remembering the past, but it lacks the millet-to-palm magnification of a small kindness.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1283, Raag Malaar, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: shares only the small-versus-immense image; the verse concerns the power of the Name, not the grateful person's magnifying of a small favour.

entries.source: Aesop's Fables, The Lion and the Mouse (Perry Index 150; G. F. Townsend trans.)
entries.rationale: Fable rather than myth; it shows small help proving great, but the lion is corrected by events rather than showing discerning gratitude from the start.
Strong conceptual match; Seneca locates value in intention, while the Kural stresses the recipient's discernment of the gift's fruit (பயன்).

entries.source: Gail Halvorsen, the Candy Bomber of Berlin
entries.rationale: Good fit for small favours magnified by grateful recipients, though the candy drops were part of a much larger relief effort.
Clear narrative match for requital measured by the recipient's nobility; the recipient here is divine, which heightens the point beyond ordinary ethics.
Shares the 'return exceeds the gift' image, but it is a promise about divine and social reciprocity, not about the recipient's character setting the measure.
Clear 'return with better' principle; applied to greetings, it is extended by commentators to all courtesies.
Good narrative illustration of generous requital; the verse itself does not state the principle, which is inferred from the story.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 2.31 (Kataññu Sutta, Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)
entries.rationale: Strong match on gratitude as a measure of the recipient's worth; it does not discuss the size of the requital.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of 35 qualities of the ideal śrāvaka, no. 28, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified on Sangave's jainworld page (a secondary rendering of Hemacandra's list); it establishes gratitude as a mark of good character but does not make the Kural's specific claim about measuring a favour by the recipient.

entries.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Amar Das' (paraphrase of traditional accounts)
entries.rationale: Next-best: a hagiographic tradition about devotion to the Guru rather than a teaching on gratitude's measure; Wikipedia used as last resort because the Britannica article checked does not narrate the service, and the details (years, water-fetching) are traditional.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 349-351 (H. G. Evelyn-White trans.)
entries.rationale: Archaic Greek didactic poetry rather than myth narrative; the principle of generous requital is a close fit, though its motive is partly prudential.

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis 1.48 (Walter Miller trans., Loeb 1913)
entries.rationale: Very close: explicit 'return more than received' plus the 'unsought kindness' of Kural 101; Cicero grounds it in duty rather than in the recipient's character as such.

entries.source: Andrew Carnegie repays Colonel Anderson's library
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's claim that a noble recipient repays far beyond the size of the original help.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Karna's reply to Krishna; K. M. Ganguli trans.)
entries.rationale: Very strong narrative match for loyalty to one who helped in adversity; complicated by the fact that Duryodhana is the epic's antagonist, so the loyalty is tragic.
Near-direct match: grateful remembrance of a friend who supported one in adversity.
Strong match on lasting loyalty; this hadith does not itself mention her support in adversity (that detail comes from other reports, e.g. in Musnad Ahmad).
Close verbal and conceptual match ('forsake not' friends, value of help in calamity).

entries.source: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (Narada Thera trans.)
entries.rationale: Describes what a good friend does rather than commanding the helped person not to forsake such a friend; the two are mirror images.

entries.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 22 'The choice of friends', st. 4 (= st. 214), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text; it matches the 'do not forget, do not forsake' structure but does not specifically name those who helped in adversity.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on the friend proven in the hour of trial; Gurbani's 'friends' here are ultimately the virtues and the holy who accompany the soul, and the verse does not command remembering or not abandoning them.

entries.source: Euripides, Heracles (c. 416 BCE), the Theseus episode
entries.rationale: Excellent match: gratitude for past rescue expressed as loyalty in the benefactor's own catastrophe.
Strong thematic match on adversity as the test of friendship; less focused on gratitude for help received.

entries.source: The Netherlands' yearly gift of tulips to Canada
entries.rationale: A close fit for loyalty to friends who helped in distress, expressed through a renewed national gift rather than a single personal friendship.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (Rama's farewell to Hanuman; chapter numbering varies by edition, commonly 7.40)
entries.rationale: Very close in spirit (unending debt to a rescuer); paraphrased because chapter numbering and wording differ across editions.
Matches ongoing grateful remembrance; the 'lifetimes' hyperbole and the specific image of wiping away sorrow are absent.
Captures lifelong remembrance of care; limited to parents rather than any friend who relieved one's distress.
Strong match: gratitude to a friend who saved one's life, extended beyond that friend's death to the next generation.
Good fit for remembered help during hardship; the sutta frames it as the choice of who could understand the teaching, with gratitude implicit.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX (Pārśvanāthacaritra), ch. III, part 9 'Attacks by Meghamālin' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: The quoted line and the episode were verified on wisdomlib; the framing narrative is my summary. It is a close fit, framed within Jain rebirth doctrine rather than a seven-birth count, and the same passage also supplies the entry for 110.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 462, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable-to-strong fit on lasting gratitude to a benefactor; the benefactor is the spiritual Guru, and the Sikh frame is not rebirth-based remembrance.
Close match on lifelong gratitude to a rescuer; the rebirth dimension of 'seven births' has no Homeric equivalent.
Strong match on deliberate lifelong remembrance of benefactors; not specific to those who relieved affliction.

entries.source: Turkey repays Japan for the Ertugrul rescue
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of gratitude remembered across generations; the event is national rather than personal, which suits the kural's hyperbole of seven births.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Hanuman's report to Sita; commonly sarga 113-116 depending on edition)
entries.rationale: Strong on forgiving injury; does not address remembering benefits, so it matches only half of the couplet.
Striking parallel on the same-day release of grievance; the gratitude half of the couplet is not addressed.
Clear match on forgiving injury; here the forgiver is the benefactor rather than the beneficiary, so the gratitude half is inverted.
Near-verbal match for not forgetting benefits; directed to God rather than human benefactors, and the forgetting-injury half comes from a different verse.
Strong match on releasing injury; does not address remembering benefits or the 'same day' immediacy.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; it is a canonical match for forgetting injuries, but it covers only half of the Kural's asymmetric 'remember good, forget harm'.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir 155 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: affirms forgiveness, but does not contain the Kural's asymmetry of remembering benefits while forgetting injuries.
Weak: Achilles lets go only after catastrophe and mainly to avenge Patroclus; it is a counter-example to 'same day' forgetting as much as an example.
Very close on the gravity of forgetting benefits; the forgiveness half of the Kural is not part of this passage.

entries.source: Pope John Paul II forgives the man who shot him
entries.rationale: A strong fit for releasing an injury immediately; the kural also pairs this with remembering benefits, which this event does not illustrate.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 2.1.11 (K. M. K. Murthy trans.)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match (Sanskrit: pleased by one kindness, does not remember even a hundred injuries); described as a trait of Rama rather than a general precept.
Moderate: the restoration rests on love and grace rather than explicitly on remembering Peter's past service.
Excellent structural match: a benefactor's later grave offence set aside by recalling his earlier service.
Remarkably close: rabbinic tradition reads this verse as hakarat hatov that survives later persecution.
Shares the aim of dissolving resentment, but offers non-hatred rather than the memory of a past benefit as the means.

entries.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 23 'The bearing with the faults of others', st. 5 (= st. 225), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text. The wisdomlib text has the typo 'consnmed', silently corrected here to 'consumed'. It is a good thematic fit, though the Nālaḍiyār grounds forbearance in friendship rather than explicitly in remembering a past benefit.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit as a mirror image of the Kural; it criticises ingratitude toward God rather than counselling us to forgive a benefactor's later harm.
Good illustration of past good cancelling present guilt; Medon's own offence is association rather than a grave personal injury.
Shares the goal of overcoming injury without retaliation; lacks the specific mechanism of recalling the injurer's earlier benefit.

entries.source: Akbar pardons his former regent Bairam Khan
entries.rationale: A good fit, though the sources record the pardon and its terms rather than Akbar's own reasons for showing mercy.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 4.34.12 (Desiraju Hanumanta Rao trans.)
entries.rationale: Near-identical structure: a list of expiable grave sins set against the inexpiable sin of kṛtaghnatā; the translator's 'treacherous' renders kṛtaghna ('one who destroys what was done for him').
Highlights ingratitude, but does not claim it is uniquely beyond forgiveness as the Kural does.
Strong on the gravity of ingratitude; addressed to gratitude toward God, and does not rank it as uniquely unforgivable.
Very close: returning evil for good brings inescapable consequences; lacks the explicit comparison with other sins.

entries.source: Jataka No. 72, Silavanaga Jataka (E. B. Cowell ed., vol. 1)
entries.rationale: Strong narrative match for the inescapable fate of the ingrate; a birth-story rather than a doctrinal statement.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book IX, ch. III, part 9 'Attacks by Meghamālin' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Both passages were verified verbatim on wisdomlib, and the 'no refuge' closely mirrors the Kural. In the Jain story, however, Meghamālin finds refuge by asking Pārśva's forgiveness, so the Kural's absolute verdict is softened. Same passage as 107.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1086, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on ingratitude as beyond rescue; Gurbani elsewhere also says God cherishes and forgives even the ungrateful (e.g. Ang 47), so this is not the whole Sikh picture.
Excellent match: Pindar explicitly draws the moral of repaying benefactors from Ixion's eternal punishment; paraphrased because the English wording could not be verified online.

entries.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 3.1.1.24
entries.rationale: Strong match on ranking; Hume invokes it as a test case for his theory that moral judgments rest on sentiment, not to argue its inexpiability.

entries.source: Brutus joins the conspiracy against Julius Caesar
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of ingratitude condemned without mercy, though Brutus's motives were political and Roman writers judged him in different ways.
Very close match: both name friend, neutral and enemy categories and require even-handedness. The Gita frames it as yogic equanimity rather than social justice.
Strong thematic match on partiality. James’s context is rich versus poor rather than friend, stranger and enemy.
Near one-to-one on the enemy case. The Qur’an adds a God-conscious framing (“nearer to righteousness”).
Core biblical statement of impartial judgment. Its categories are poor and mighty rather than friend and enemy.
Direct match on impartial judgment as the mark of the just. Less emphasis on the friend, stranger and enemy triad.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 19.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on impartiality toward friend and foe, though the Jain verse frames it as an ascetic's equanimity rather than social justice.

entries.source: SikhNet, 'The Story of Bhai Kanhaiya Singh' (paraphrase of the Sikh tradition)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on equal treatment of friend and foe; the account is well known in Sikh tradition but the source is a popular Sikh website and details vary between tellings.
Strong match on equal justice for insiders and outsiders. Hesiod’s framing is civic prosperity sent by Zeus.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Conceptual parallel on justice as other-directed. Aristotle does not list the friend, stranger and enemy groups.

entries.source: Henry Dunant and the women of Castiglione after Solferino
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of even-handed treatment of enemies, strangers and friends, applied to the care of the wounded.
Parallel on the indestructibility of the good person’s gains. The Gita speaks of spiritual progress, not material wealth or descendants.
Very close match: lasting wealth plus benefit to descendants. The text is shared with the Hebrew Bible.
Striking narrative parallel of a parent’s righteousness safeguarding the children’s inheritance. The virtue named is general righteousness rather than impartiality specifically.
Near one-to-one structure. The Psalm grounds it in fear of God rather than impartiality as such.

entries.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
entries.rationale: Good match on the durability of rightly gained wealth. It does not mention benefit to descendants.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of 35 qualities of the ideal śrāvaka, no. 1, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified on Sangave's jainworld page (a secondary rendering). It matches the just acquisition of wealth, but not the Kural's claim that such wealth endures as a support for descendants.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 375, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: shares the image of wealth that never decays, but concerns the Naam, not the material prosperity of the just, and says nothing of descendants.
Remarkably close: justice leads to prosperity and a better lot for descendants. Hesiod frames it through Zeus and oath-keeping.
Agrees on the long-run security of the just. Plato speaks of the soul’s good, not material wealth for descendants.

entries.source: Ernst Abbe creates the Carl Zeiss Foundation
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit for just wealth that endures for posterity, though the kural has a person's descendants in mind and the firm's long survival also owes much to other factors.
Clear condemnation of unjust gain. It does not state the Kural’s positive command to renounce such gain immediately.
Shares the logic of weighing gain against inner loss. Jesus is speaking of discipleship rather than impartiality specifically.
Very strong, since bribery is the classic breach of impartiality. It is framed as a prohibition rather than as renouncing gain already held.
Near-direct parallel. The Kural adds the urgency of giving it up “that very day.”
Close match on rejecting unjust success. The Dhammapada is phrased as a character description, not an instruction.

Verified on jainworld's Tattvārtha Sūtra page (not Tatia's translation). It fits thematically, but it concerns the vows in general rather than impartiality, and lacks the Kural's 'renounce it that very day'.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on renouncing unjust gain; the Kural's 'that very day' urgency and its concession that such gain may look beneficial are not in the verse.
