Strong thematic match, including the deceptive appeal of unjust gain. Hesiod stresses divine punishment rather than voluntary renunciation.
Shares the priority of virtue over gain. Socrates targets greed in general rather than injustice-derived gain specifically.

entries.source: Eugenio Monti lends his bolt to his rivals
entries.rationale: A strong fit for renouncing an unfair advantage immediately, though the advantage came from chance rather than from any wrong done by Monti.
Parallel on posthumous reputation as a verdict. The Gita’s context is martial duty, not impartiality.
Strong structural match (judge by outcomes). “Fruits” in Matthew means deeds during life rather than legacy after death.
Close fit to Parimelazhagar’s “offspring” reading. The hadith concerns ongoing reward rather than revealing worth.
Near one-to-one with the “legacy/reputation” interpretation of echcham.
Parallel on virtue’s lasting renown. It does not concern judging a person after death or offspring.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Next-best match only. The quote is verified, but Jain doctrine locates a person's results in their own karma, not in descendants or posthumous reputation, so the Kural's 'what remains' (echcham) has no direct Jain counterpart.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1094, Raag Maaroo, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: shares the idea that a life's worth appears in its effect on descendants, but the saving is spiritual and the verse does not speak of justice or of revealing it.
Good match on enduring fame versus infamy. The virtue praised is fidelity rather than impartiality.
Parallel on retrospective judgment. Solon judges happiness rather than justice.

entries.source: Justice Harlan's lone dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson
entries.rationale: A strong fit for the reputation reading of the kural; it does not illustrate the older reading about descendants.
Close match on equanimity amid gain and loss. The Gita’s application is duty in battle rather than fairness to others.
Good parallel on steadiness in fortune and misfortune. Paul speaks of contentment rather than fairness.
Strong match, including the idea that fortunes are ordained. The Qur’an does not tie this to impartiality.
Powerful match on integrity through loss. Job’s integrity is broader than impartiality.
Close match on unshakable equanimity. Praise and blame stand in for the Kural’s loss and gain.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 19.90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a strong fit on equanimity amid gain and loss, though the Jain verse stresses detachment rather than the Kural's fairness in judgment.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on equanimity in loss and gain; the Kural stresses unswerving fairness, while the verse stresses inner detachment.
Paraphrase, not a quotation. Weak-to-moderate: endurance rather than impartiality.
Strong structural parallel with Stoic ethics. Epictetus stresses acceptance more than fairness.

entries.source: Justice H. R. Khanna's dissent in ADM Jabalpur
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of steadfast impartiality in the face of foreseen personal loss.

entries.source: Manusmriti 8.15 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match; Bühler translates dharma as “justice” in this legal context.
General moral-consequence parallel. It is not specific to departing from impartiality.
Strong match on inner bias as the start of ruin. Addressed to a ruler-judge.
Good match on self-inflicted consequence. It lacks the Kural’s introspective “know this yourself” framing.

entries.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
entries.rationale: Very close: the four agati are the classical Buddhist list of partialities, and the result is decline.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim; a good fit on self-inflicted ruin, though the context is a lapsed monk rather than partiality. Jacobi notes that verses 38-53 may be a later addition.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on wrong intention leading to one's own harm; the Kural's self-diagnosis ('I am heading for ruin') and its focus on partiality are not explicit.
Good match on ruin following injustice. Punishment is external (Zeus) rather than self-recognized.
Strong conceptual parallel (injustice harms the agent). Plato’s argument is metaphysical rather than a practical warning.

entries.source: Former Prime Minister Tanaka and the Lockheed bribery scandal
entries.rationale: A reasonable but partial fit: the kural describes an inner warning sign, while the record shows only the outward consequences, which unfolded slowly over many years.
Narrative summary, not a quotation. Harishchandra’s virtue is truthfulness rather than impartiality.
Strong thematic match. Persecution is broader than poverty.
Good parallel on worth measured by righteousness. It does not mention poverty directly.
Near one-to-one match.
Moderate: it addresses birth and outward signs rather than poverty.

entries.source: Nālaḍiyār ch. 16 'The Good', st. 3 (= st. 153), English translation in The Indian Antiquary (wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: A Tamil Jain text, chosen because it addresses the just person's poverty directly; it describes the good person's steadiness rather than the world's verdict on them.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 992, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: affirms dignity in poverty but does not tie it to the poor person's fairness, and speaks of God's regard rather than the world's.
Summary, not a quotation. The virtue is piety and hospitality rather than impartiality. A Roman telling of a Greek-world myth.
Good parallel of poverty resulting from principled living. His principle is truth-seeking rather than impartiality.

entries.source: Sir Walter Scott chooses to repay his creditors
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit for honourable poverty; Scott's own risky business dealings helped cause the crash, so his fairness lay in the response rather than the cause.

Close in content; the Kural's ‘even inadvertently’ nuance is not present.
Strong match on speech as a mark of character.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches the prohibition on evil speech, but it is framed as a rule to keep rather than the Kural's claim that the virtuous become incapable of such speech.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Asa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: a command about truthful speech, not the Kural's point that habituated conduct makes evil speech impossible even in an unguarded moment.
Illustrates the danger of wrong speech rather than the ideal of never uttering it.
Paraphrase, because the text was not verified verbatim. A good match on disciplined speech.

entries.source: The Chofetz Chaim publishes his code on the laws of harmful speech
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the book teaches the discipline of speech the kural praises, but it is a work of instruction rather than an event showing that discipline under test.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 311 (Yaksha Prashna), tr. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on the learned-yet-ignorant paradox; Yudhishthira's standard is religious duty rather than social harmony.

Strong match on learning without practice being worthless.
Close: derech eretz is literally ‘the way of the land/world’, echoing the Kural's ‘harmony with the world’.
Very close match on learning without practice.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches the paradox of the learned fool, but the Kural's criterion of harmony with the world (social fit) differs from the Jain criterion of acting on doctrine.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on conduct over learning; the Kural's specific test of 'harmony with the world' is broader and more social than the salok.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.4, 1105b (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Very close match on theory without practice.

entries.source: Ignaz Semmelweis fails to win over his colleagues

entries.source: Parabhava Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.6 (trans. Narada Thera)

entries.source: Tattvārthasūtra 7.9, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi on unchastity (abrahma) (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The idea of lust as a failure of discernment is a close match, but the passage is about unchastity in general, not specifically about another man's wife (the following lines do mention 'other women').

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1348, Raag Prabhati, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit: both link coveting another's wife to a failure of real understanding, though the hymn targets religious hypocrisy rather than calling the desire folly in so many words.
Paraphrased narrative; strong on folly and its consequences, less on the specific claim about knowledge.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Thematic parallel on knowledge versus conduct; Aristotle does not mention adultery in this passage.

entries.source: Edward VIII abdicates to marry Wallis Simpson
entries.rationale: A reasonable but partial fit: Wallis Simpson was legally another's wife during the courtship, but Edward acted openly and sought marriage, and whether his choice was folly is a matter of opinion.
Narrative paraphrase; the 'standing at the door' detail makes this unusually close to the Kural's image.

entries.source: Proverbs 6:30-32 (KJV), part of the Christian Old Testament
entries.rationale: Very close: an explicit comparison among wrongdoers that names the adulterer the most senseless. Ellipsis marks omitted verse 31.
Strong match: explicit ranking plus the 'neighbour' detail. Ellipsis marks omitted intermediate question and answer.
Near one-to-one image match ('neighbour's door'). Ellipsis marks omitted words in verse 10.

entries.source: Parabhava Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.6 (trans. Narada Thera)
entries.rationale: Direct reference to others' wives in a list of downfalls; the Kural's superlative ('none more foolish') is not explicit.

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār 87 (ch. 9, 'The Not Desiring Other Men's Wives'), tr. G. U. Pope (1893); e-text at Project Madurai
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Pope's translation on projectmadurai.org. This is a Tamil Jain text rather than canonical scripture. It matches the folly theme well but has no equivalent of Valluvar's 'standing at the door' wordplay.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 155, Raag Gauri, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: shared condemnation of desiring another's wife, but no ranking of wrongdoers and no image of waiting at another's gate.
Narrative paraphrase; very close on 'lingering at another's house for his wife', though Penelope's marriage status was uncertain to the suitors.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.6 (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Strong on the categorical wrongness of adultery; no explicit ranking as 'most foolish'.

Very strong on the betrayal-of-trust element; the 'as good as dead' image is replaced by 'will not succeed'.
Close match on trust and betrayal; no 'death' imagery.
Thematic parallel on self-destruction; the verse does not mention adultery or trust.

entries.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.4.1.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

entries.source: Dasam Granth, Charitropakhyan (Charitar 21), verses 51-53 as numbered on BaniDB (attributed to Guru Gobind Singh; authorship contested)

Very close on the loss of trust and social 'death'; Epictetus's metaphor is a discarded tool rather than a corpse.

entries.source: Richard Wagner and Cosima von Bulow
entries.rationale: A strong fit for betrayal of a trusting friend's household, though Wagner and Cosima later married and the kural's verdict of moral death is the commentary's, not history's.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (narrative summary; trans. K. M. Ganguli)

entries.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1362, Phunhay Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Kakacūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 21 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey, Book XI (trans. Samuel Butler)

entries.source: Kakacūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 21 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. Its link between sharing and freedom from hunger is explicitly karmic across births, which the kural does not state.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the treasure here is primarily the spiritual wealth of the Name, read by analogy with the Sikh practice of sharing food (vand chhakna); the same verse is used elsewhere in this edition.

entries.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Section II (Ak. 4:423)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; Kant’s point is logical consistency of the maxim, not a practical promise that givers will not go hungry.

entries.source: Raiffeisen's bread association in the hunger winter
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: it shows sharing protecting a community from hunger, though it was an organised relief scheme rather than an individual's lifelong habit.
Paraphrase; parallel on the futility of possessiveness, but not specifically about the joy of giving.

Very close on hoarding and losing; lacks the Kural’s positive image of the joy of giving.
Close parallel on the joy of giving versus miserliness.

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 1 ('Unstable Wealth'), st. 10 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this Tamil Jain text closely matches the hoard-and-lose theme, though it does not mention the kural's 'joy of giving'.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 937, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on the futility of hoarding, but the verse does not speak of the joy of giving that the Kural says misers never know.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 357-360 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Strong match on the giver’s joy; Hesiod contrasts it with taking rather than with hoarding.
Strong on the disgrace of dying with hoarded wealth; Carnegie focuses on social duty rather than the personal joy of giving.

entries.source: Alexander empties the Persian treasury at Persepolis
entries.rationale: Next-best: it shows hoarded wealth being kept and then lost, but the sources do not document the Persian kings as misers or record anything about the joy of giving.

entries.source: Rig Veda 10.117.6 (tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match on eating alone as the worst condition.
Strong parallel: the unshared feast is condemned and the beggar ends up better off.
Parallel condemnation of not feeding the poor; no explicit comparison with begging.
Parallel on condemning refusal to share; not about food or a comparison with begging.
Near one-to-one: both single out eating without sharing as the failure of generosity.

entries.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 28 ('Illiberality'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text. It condemns unshared eating as the kural does but lacks the deliberately shocking comparison with begging.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir 192 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: Kabir condemns the house without service and devotion rather than solitary eating specifically; this salok also appears in an earlier chapter of this edition.
Paraphrase; a loose parallel on the misery of greed, not specifically about refusing to share food.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 19.10, quoting Epicurus (tr. R. M. Gummere)
entries.rationale: Strong on the wretchedness of eating alone; Epicurus’ concern is friendship, not charity to the needy.

entries.source: Spartan citizens share their meals in the common messes
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the messes show a society that rejected solitary eating, but they were compulsory and funded by helot labour, so they are not an act of generous sharing.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, story of King Shibi (Sivi)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; strong narrative illustration of valuing giving above life, framed as protection of a refugee rather than charity.
Loose structural parallel; Paul’s preference for death is about union with Christ, not the inability to give.
Shared theme of death and the inability to give, but reversed: the Qur’an’s person wants more life to give, the Kural’s giver prefers death to a life without giving.
Loose parallel; rabbinic tradition reads ‘tzedakah’ here as charity, but the verse does not say death is preferable to being unable to give.
Paraphrase; parallel on putting giving above self-preservation, not on preferring death to an inability to give.

entries.source: Samantabhadra, Ratnakaraṇḍa Śrāvakācāra 122 (cf. tr. Champat Rai Jain, 1917)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase only: the verse's content was checked through a secondary (Wikipedia) rendering, not against Champat Rai Jain's translation. The parallel is structural, and sallekhanā has nothing to do with being unable to give.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 239, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: both say a life without its proper purpose is not worth having, but Gurbani's measure is remembrance of God rather than the capacity to give, and it does not speak of preferring death.
Paraphrase; a self-sacrifice myth, only loosely related to the Kural’s claim about being unable to give.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.8 (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Good parallel on valuing noble self-giving above mere survival; not specifically about the inability to give charity.

entries.source: Julius Rosenwald's fund is required to spend itself out
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shows a life and fortune organised entirely around giving, but nothing documents the kural's claim that death is sweeter than being unable to give.
Strong on giving as the only lasting gain; the hymn speaks of friendship and comfort rather than fame or praise explicitly.
Matches giving-as-true-gain; lacks the Kural’s emphasis on praise/renown as the fruit of giving.
Strong on giving-as-multiplied-gain; the reward is divine rather than human praise.
Close on name-over-wealth; Proverbs does not here tie the good name specifically to generosity.
Close on giving as the one true gain; the payoff is happiness hereafter rather than renown in this world.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14–16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; both texts share the 'only true profit of life' framing, but the Jain gain is a heavenly rebirth through virtue, not renown or giving specifically.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466-467, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (pauri), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Roman retelling of a Greek-world myth; emphasises divine reward for hospitality more than human praise, but ends in lasting honour.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.1 (trans. W.D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Close on giving leading to esteem; Aristotle does not claim this is life’s only gain.

entries.source: Sir Thomas Bodley reopens Oxford's university library
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of giving that produced lasting renown, though the gift was to an institution rather than directly to the poor, as the classical commentary specifies.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 199 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Good on the wise exalting giving; the passage praises the gift itself rather than describing the giver’s social renown.

Very close: gift to the poor followed by lasting honour.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.34, Siha Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: generosity producing widely spoken reputation.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), ch. III, part 7 'The fast-breaking of Ṛṣabha' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (ellipses mark omissions). A strong narrative parallel, though the praise centres on a gift to a Jina rather than to ordinary suppliants.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 257, Raag Gauree, Bavan Akhri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: both tie praise to giving, but Sikh teaching assigns ultimate praise to God as the only Giver rather than to human benefactors.
Close on praise spreading across lands; the stated cause is righteousness in general, not giving specifically.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.3 (trans. W.D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Good on honour as conferred recognition; does not single out giving as its source.

entries.source: Maecenas becomes the patron of Virgil and Horace
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: the bardic praise described in the commentary settled on a patron so completely that his name became a byword.

Close: lasting honourable reputation is sought as a real good.
Very close on the survival of a righteous name.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.40 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 50, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial and partly contrasting: both start from the impermanence of the world, but Sikh teaching does not treat renown as the one thing that survives.

Honest contrast rather than parallel; included because Stoicism is the major philosophical challenge to valuing renown.

entries.source: James Prinsep deciphers the edicts of Ashoka
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: Ashoka's name survived through his recorded deeds, though it had in fact been largely forgotten until Prinsep's work, which complicates the claim of unbroken renown.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 198 (trans. K.M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: earthly fame from giving determines heavenly status.
Shared idea of heaven honouring earthly deeds of giving; no notion of fame or of heaven preferring humans over its own.
Parallel link between celestial and earthly regard; the order of cause and effect is inverted.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:13 (trans. Joshua Kulp; numbered 4:17 in some editions)
entries.rationale: Good on a good name outranking sacred status; no heavenly-realm imagery.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 7, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable as a direct engagement with world-wide renown, but the teaching runs against the Kural, relativising fame rather than exalting it.

Weak but real parallel; Socrates is speculative and speaks of conversing, not of heaven ranking humans above gods.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.2–3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.rationale: Good on renown tied to virtue; Aristotle does not say the unworthy would be better unborn.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis I.29 (trans. Walter Miller)

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh, Maajh ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Close; the Talmud states both halves, reward and its absence.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Ashtpadi 2, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match, including the context of transactions.

entries.source: Hwang Woo-suk's stem cell papers are found to be fabricated
entries.rationale: Shows fraud becoming a repeated pattern, but the kural's claim is about inner disposition, which can only be inferred from the record.
Weak-to-moderate: defines a thief by non-reciprocity, but does not state immediate ruin; chosen as the best available Hindu parallel.
Very close on immediate ruin from fraud; the narrative frames the lie as against the Holy Spirit.
Strong: persistent fraud in weights leading to destruction; collective rather than individual.
Close on self-destruction through deceitful gain.
Very close on this-worldly self-destruction through theft.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.3, with Jacobi's note citing Devendra's commentary (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
entries.rationale: Verse and note both checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The image of a thief destroyed in the very act fits very closely. The detail of the wall falling comes from the medieval commentary that Jacobi summarises, not from the verse itself.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 656, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on a life built on deception that ends in self-ruin. Kabir places the reckoning at the end of life, while the Kural stresses ruin in the act itself.
Moderate: an image of crafty deceit ending in futility; the punishment is eternal rather than immediate, and his deceits are not mainly commercial.
Strong conceptual parallel on pure injustice being self-defeating.

entries.source: The Mona Lisa thief is caught trying to sell it
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of ruin arriving in the act itself, though Peruggia received only a short prison sentence rather than being destroyed.
Strong on theft leading to the soul’s fall; the reward half appears in the surrounding verse 5.10.7.
Very close on exclusion from heaven for theft and extortion; Paul’s next verse (6:11) adds the possibility of cleansing.
Good on linking commercial fraud to ultimate fate; the reward of the honest comes later in the surah (83:22-28).

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Very close: honest dealing as the first criterion of heavenly judgement.
Good structural match on differing destinies; not specific to fraud.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The heaven-and-hell contrast fits, but the verse is about sin in general, not fraud, and in Jainism heaven is only a temporary birth short of liberation.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 684, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong match for the Kural's second half. Gurbani promises freedom from Death's messenger rather than a heaven of the gods, and it says nothing explicit about the defrauder's life failing him.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-227 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Good on justice rewarded by the gods; the reward is earthly prosperity rather than a heavenly world.
Parallel on security for the good after death; concerns goodness in general rather than honesty in dealings.

entries.source: Forger Han van Meegeren is convicted and dies weeks later
entries.rationale: Next-best only: his death came soon after his conviction, but the sources do not show that his fraud caused it, and the kural's second half about the honest is not illustrated.

Very close: truthfulness joined to ‘not causing distress’ (anudvega-karam). The Gita lists truth and harmlessness as twin requirements, while the Kural folds harmlessness into the definition of truth itself.
Shares the harm-free standard for speech, though Paul is talking about speech generally, not defining truthfulness. Ephesians 4:15 (‘speaking the truth in love’) is the closer thematic pairing.
Qawl sadid includes both accuracy and fairness; it does not explicitly define truth as harmlessness.
Truth and peace are coupled but not merged into one definition as in the Kural.

entries.source: Subhasita Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.3 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: harmlessness to others as the test of well-spoken, truthful speech.

entries.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.14, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near one-to-one match: both define truth by harmlessness rather than by correspondence to fact.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on speech that harms no one. Farid speaks of harshness, not of truthfulness as such, and he is a Bhagat whose verses are in the Granth, not a Guru.
A portrait of truthful, gentle character rather than a definition of truth; the pairing of truth with kindness is the real link.

entries.source: Kant, On a Supposed Right to Lie (1797)
entries.rationale: Deliberate contrast, not a parallel: Kant’s absolutism is the opposite pole from the Kural’s harm-based definition.

entries.source: Elisabeth Kubler-Ross talks honestly with dying patients
entries.rationale: A reasonable illustration of truth joined to harmlessness, though the kural's claim is a definition of truth itself, which the event only partly dramatises.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, Section 69 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Near-exact parallel, even in phrasing: ‘falsehood would become truth.’ Krishna’s list of permitted lies is narrower and more situational than the Kural’s general principle.
Christian interpreters differ: many (e.g., Augustine) praise Rahab’s faith and kindness but not the lie itself. The verse does not explicitly endorse falsehood.
Strong match; the Islamic exemption is limited to specific cases (reconciliation, and in other reports war and spouses), while the Kural states a general principle.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz tr.)
entries.rationale: Very close; the rabbinic exemption is tied specifically to peace (shalom), a subset of the Kural’s ‘faultless good.’

entries.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Partial contrast: shared benefit test, opposite conclusion on beneficial untruths (later Mahayana upaya teaching comes closer to the Kural).

entries.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.3.3.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, pp. 146-147)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a striking concrete case of the Kural's principle, though the text prefers silence first and does not state a general rule that beneficial lies are allowed.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A candid contrast, not a parallel: I found no SGGS passage that permits a beneficial falsehood, and this verse places falsehood squarely with sin.
Weak match: acknowledges truth-like falsehood but adds no moral test of benefit.
Good structural parallel (beneficial falsehood), but Plato’s version is political and elite-restricted, while the Kural’s is personal and universal.

entries.source: Doctors at Rome's Fatebenefratelli Hospital invent K Syndrome
entries.rationale: Very close to a dramatisation of the kural, since the lie harmed no innocent person and existed only to save lives; estimates of how many were saved vary between sources.
Close: the inner witness is the same; Manu’s context is courtroom testimony, while the Kural’s is universal.
Same image of a heart that condemns; John’s context is love and obedience in general, not lying specifically.
Strong psychological parallel: lying disturbs the inner self, truth calms it.
Shares the heart-truth link; the Psalm stresses reward, the Kural the inner punishment.

entries.source: Ambalatthika-rahulovada Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 61 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Close: both focus on deliberate lies and inner conscience; the Buddha frames it as shame that protects, the Kural as pain that punishes.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The inner-suffering theme fits well, but Jacobi notes that the Prakrit 'mosa' could also be read as 'stealing', and the verse belongs to a passage about greed for sense-objects.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 948, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on the lie harming the liar from within. Gurbani does not specify a lie told against one's own knowledge, and its image is poison rather than burning.
Same target (speech against one’s mind), but Achilles condemns the liar from outside rather than describing the liar’s inner torment.
Related but different: Plato’s ‘true lie’ is self-deception or ignorance, while the Kural’s liar knows the truth and is burned by that knowledge.

entries.source: Thomas More refuses to swear the oath his conscience rejected
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of refusing to lie against one's own knowledge, though it shows the precept being kept rather than the burning conscience of one who breaks it.
Illustrative story rather than a statement of principle; the match lies in its enduring place in popular memory.
Praise for inner guilelessness, but no claim about dwelling in the hearts of all people.
Good match through the root ṣ-d-q (truth): a lasting ‘truthful’ reputation. The verse is a prayer, not a general law.
Shares the idea of truth’s permanence but speaks of the words enduring, not the person living in others’ hearts.
Close in outcome (being loved by people); Buddharakkhita renders the truth element as ‘realized the truth’ rather than ‘speaks truth.’

entries.source: Mūlācāra 837 (Vaṭṭakera), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainworld.com, an English rendering I did not check against the Prakrit. It fits the 'dwelling in all hearts' idea well. A near-identical Saman Suttam rendering of the same idea is used for Kural 97.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: the verse matches the Kural's demand for truth in the heart but not its promise of being cherished by everyone.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 280-285 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Parallel reward structure (lasting standing), but Hesiod focuses on oaths and family fortune rather than inner honesty.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (paraphrase of W. D. Ross tr.)
entries.rationale: Matches the inner-character aspect; Aristotle does not promise the social reward the Kural names.

entries.source: Walter Cronkite is named the most trusted man in America
entries.rationale: A good fit for truthfulness winning a place in people's hearts, though some media historians question how rigorous the 1972 poll was.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 74 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Near-exact: truth weighed above sacrifice; the Kural names austerity and charity instead of the horse-sacrifice.
Truth over external ritual; ‘truth’ in John is broader (sincerity and divine reality), not truthful speech specifically.
Good match on truth over ritual form; the Qur’an includes charity within righteousness rather than ranking truth above it.
Strong: truth ‘in the inward parts’ matches ‘manaththodu,’ and the psalm explicitly ranks it above sacrifice.
Close: truth ranked over ascetic appearance; charity is not mentioned.

entries.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 843 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. It is a strong match on truth outranking austerity, but it does not mention charity (dānam). The verse is also used for Kural 128 in this edition.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong structural match: both rank austerity and charity below something inward. Japji's higher good is love of the Name, of which truthfulness is part but not the whole.
Weak, contrastive match: no Greek myth directly ranks truthfulness above sacrifice; this story shows ritual detached from truth.
Truthfulness equated with piety; Marcus does not explicitly rank it above austerity or charity.

entries.source: Martin Luther refuses to recant at the Diet of Worms
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the event shows truth from the heart over outward religion, though the comparison with austerity and gift-giving is only implicit.
Truth’s supremacy and its road to the highest good match well; the idea of ‘fame’ is not present.
Truth is foundational here, but the passage does not speak of fame or of truth generating all virtues.
Truthfulness is honoured, but listed alongside other virtues rather than as their source. (Bukhari 6094, under Kural 297, captures the generative claim.)
Truth is foundational, but shares the role with justice and peace; no reference to personal fame.
Truthfulness confers honour; it is one mark among many rather than the source of all virtue.

entries.source: Bhagavatī Ārādhanā 842 (Śivārya), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. It closely matches 'truth brings all virtues', but has nothing on the Kural's other claim about fame (pugazh).

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit on truth as the one source of all goodness. The Kural's theme of fame is absent, and Gurbani's sach also means the True Lord, not only truthful conduct.
Truth tied to reputation; the ‘all virtues’ claim is absent.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Strong on praise; Aristotle does not claim truthfulness generates the other virtues.

entries.source: Raja Harishchandra, the story of the truthful king, opens India's film industry
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the film is a real, documented event, but the truthful figure it celebrates is legendary, and some historians debate its claim to be the very first Indian feature.
Satya as a self-sufficient power; the sutra describes a yogic attainment, not a claim that other virtues are unnecessary.
‘Truth’ in John means divine revelation in Christ rather than truthful speech; the parallel is in truth’s sufficiency.
Very close: persistence in truth (‘keeps on telling the truth’) mirrors poyyaamai poyyaamai, and truth leads to all righteousness.
Stresses the seriousness of avoiding falsehood; says nothing about truth being sufficient on its own.
Strong: truth as the single keystone virtue, stated negatively.

entries.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, p. 33); cf. the Jainworld rendering of the same passage
entries.rationale: Jacobi's wording checked on sacred-texts.com, and the Jainworld wording checked separately. The passage puts truth above everything, but it does not say outright, as the Kural does, that other deeds become unnecessary. 'Truth' (sacca) here also carries the sense of doctrinal truth.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: both make truthfulness the single sufficient aim. Japji reaches it through obedience to Hukam rather than unfailing truthful speech, and it dismisses ritual rather than virtuous deeds.
Truthfulness in oaths as supreme; narrower (oaths only) and punitive rather than a claim of sufficiency.
Illustrates truth held as the single guiding commitment; not a doctrine that other virtues are optional.

entries.source: Solzhenitsyn publishes Live Not by Lies on the day of his arrest
entries.rationale: Very close to the kural's claim that unfailing non-lying is sufficient in itself, though Solzhenitsyn framed it politically rather than as a complete ethic.
Near-identical statement; Manu goes on to add further purifiers for soul and intellect.
Very close on inner vs. outer purity; the inner impurity named is greed and excess, with hypocrisy (a form of falsehood) the wider theme.
Inner purity is emphasised, but the verse contrasts it with wealth and offspring, not water or truth specifically. (Islam values both: wudu for the body, sincerity for the heart.)
Excellent structural match; ‘clean hands’ refers to deeds rather than washing with water.

entries.source: Vatthupama Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 7 (tr. Nyanaponika Thera)
entries.rationale: Near-exact: sacred-water bathing contrasted with inner purification by truthfulness and harmlessness.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The outer/inner purity contrast is exact, but the inner bath is named as the Law and celibacy; truthfulness appears only in the list of restraints at 12.41.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A near one-to-one match on truth as the cleanser of inner impurity. Gurbani's sach includes the True Lord dwelling within, a theistic sense the Kural does not state.
Strong inner/outer purity match; the inscription names holy thought rather than truthfulness specifically.
Inner/outer harmony is central; truthfulness is implied (no gap between inner and outer) rather than named.

entries.source: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: amnesty was a legal rather than moral cleansing, and the Commission has been criticised for its narrow scope.

Truth and light are closely linked; Madhavananda renders ‘asat/sat’ as evil/good (others translate unreal/real or falsehood/truth), and the Upanishad itself glosses the whole prayer as ‘make me immortal.’
Clear light/truth vs. darkness/lie pairing; the Kural speaks of the wise man’s inner lamp rather than fellowship with God.
Shared lamp imagery for inner guidance; the Qur’an’s lamp is divine light, not the human virtue of truthfulness.
Light and truth are paired as guides; they are God’s gifts rather than the person’s own truthfulness.
Shared inner-light image; the Buddhist light is wisdom/Dhamma broadly, not truthfulness specifically.

entries.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3 (Jainworld cites 3/3/66), English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'; cf. Ācārāṅga II.16.6 (tr. Jacobi, SBE 22)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. The light image is a free rendering: Jacobi's translation of the same passage has no lamp or light, and 'truth' there means doctrinal truth more than truthful speech.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong structural match: many outer lights against one true inner light. In Gurbani the true light is the Guru, whose word is truth, not truthfulness itself.
The light/truth link comes through Apollo’s identity (Phoebus, ‘bright’); the passage itself speaks of his truthful mind, not a lamp.

entries.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
entries.rationale: Vivid lamp parallel; the original seeks a real ‘man,’ and the ‘honest man’ reading is a later popular gloss.

entries.source: Nehru's broadcast after Gandhi's death: the light that shone was no ordinary light
entries.rationale: A strong illustration that uses the kural's own metaphor of truth as an undying light; transcripts of the extempore speech differ slightly in wording.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 74 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Near-identical claim of truth’s supremacy; the Mahabharata goes further in identifying Truth with God.
Truth is supreme, but here it is a divine person, not the human virtue of truthful speech.
Truthfulness singled out as what ultimately counts; not explicitly ranked above every other good.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 55a (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz tr.)
entries.rationale: Truth at the highest level of reality; a theological rather than purely ethical claim.

entries.source: Alavaka Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.10 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Very close in spirit; the Buddha names truth first among four supreme qualities rather than alone.

entries.source: Praśnavyākaraṇa Sūtra 2.2, English rendering as given on Jainworld, 'Jina Sutra – Quotations'
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. I did not check it against a scholarly translation of the Praśnavyākaraṇa, but as a supreme valuation of truth it matches the Kural very closely.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A near one-to-one match: both are first-person verdicts placing truth above everything. Guru Nanak adds a distinction between truth and truthful conduct that the Kural does not draw.

entries.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 356 (tr. R. C. Jebb, rev. Alex Sens)
entries.rationale: Truth’s supreme strength is dramatised; Teiresias speaks of prophetic truth, not truthfulness as a virtue.
Near-exact: truth ranked first among all goods for gods and humans.

entries.source: Truth Prevails becomes the motto on the Czechoslovak and Czech presidential flag
entries.rationale: Reasonable: the motto affirms the supremacy of truth, though it is a national symbol rather than a personal act of truthfulness.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Chaitraratha Parva, the Vasishtha–Vishvamitra episode)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic match (power plus restraint). Paraphrase of a narrative episode; details vary across retellings and the sons' deaths are attributed to the cursed king Kalmashapada acting at Vishvamitra's instigation.
Verbatim KJV. The verse is about non-retaliation with power in hand rather than anger as an emotion, but the structure matches the kural closely.

entries.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4777 (graded hasan by al-Albani)
entries.rationale: Verbatim from sunnah.com English; the condition 'when he is in a position to give vent to it' mirrors the kural almost exactly.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Verbatim. Shares the 'true strength is restraint' idea but lacks the kural's specific contrast between effective and ineffective anger.
Verbatim. Very close structural parallel between genuine restraint and mere appearance of control.

entries.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book I (Ādīśvaracaritra), ch. 5, part 11, 'The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near one-to-one illustration: the power to strike was real and fully present when Bāhubali held back.

entries.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Amar Das' (paraphrase of traditional accounts)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on restraint by one who could have retaliated. The source is Wikipedia, used as a last resort and summarising traditional Sikh accounts rather than contemporary records.

entries.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book III (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

entries.source: Grant offers generous terms to Lee's army at Appomattox
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of restraint exercised from a position of overwhelming power, though the sources describe Grant's generosity rather than any anger he had to suppress.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya-Samasya Parva, the tale of Kaushika, the devoted wife, and the Dharmavyadha)

Verbatim KJV. Addresses anger or threat toward subordinates; does not address the 'anger at the stronger' half.
Verbatim sunnah.com English. Excellent match for anger against the weak; implicit on anger against the strong.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 6b (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Sefaria English (bold markup removed). About domestic intimidation rooted in anger; fits the 'where anger is effective' half.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Verbatim. Also echoes 301: Vedehika's calm was only apparent while her anger had no occasion.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.54 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sahaskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book III (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

Verbatim sunnah.com English (punctuation lightly normalised). Universal prohibition matches 'toward anyone'.
Verbatim JPS 1917 via Sefaria. Strong match on letting go of resentment; no explicit claim that evils spring from anger.
Verbatim. Very close to maraththal (forgetting) as the cure.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a strong thematic fit, although it is addressed to monks facing verbal abuse rather than to everyone, and it does not state the Kural's claim that all evils spring from anger.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit on releasing resentment through forgiveness. Kabir does not say that all evils spring from anger, and the verse is a Bhagat's saying in the Granth, not a Guru's.

entries.source: Homer, Iliad, Book 1, opening lines (trans. Samuel Butler)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Butler. Strong on 'evils born of anger'; Homer does not prescribe forgetting it.

entries.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Stewart translation (Wikisource).

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 23.50–53 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The self-protection logic is a strong fit, but the passage speaks of all four passions rather than anger alone.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5 (trans. W. D. Ross)

entries.source: William Bligh is cast adrift after the mutiny on the Bounty

entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a vivid narrative parallel to anger rebounding on its owner. It is a 12th-century narrative source, not canonical scripture.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: both reject using anger as a means. Farid gives no image of self-injury and does not argue that anger rebounds on the angry person.

entries.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I.1 (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Stewart translation (Wikisource). Very close image and argument.

entries.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book VIII (Nemināthacaritra), ch. 10, part 3, 'Gajasukumāla' (tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a near-literal match to the Kural's fire image. Hemacandra describes Gajasukumāla's endurance in meditation rather than explicitly saying 'without anger'; the story is also told in the canonical Antakṛddaśā, which I did not check.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'How did Guru Arjan die?' (paraphrase); hot-plate details from Sikh tradition

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 17a (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)
entries.rationale: Verbatim Sefaria English (bold markup removed). About waiving grievances, closely related to not harbouring anger.
Verbatim. Reward framed as the absence of suffering rather than the attainment of desires.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29.67 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The fit is reasonable but partial: Jainism treats desires themselves as bondage, so the Kural's 'attaining all one desires' does not carry over directly.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A near one-to-one match: no anger in the mind, and everything is obtained. Farid adds returning good for evil, and the salok runs across the page break from Ang 1381 to 1382.

entries.source: Bjorn Borg, the Ice Man of tennis, wins five straight Wimbledon titles
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: Borg said he still felt anger inside and controlled its expression, whereas the kural asks that anger not arise even in thought; his teenage suspension is documented in his own recollection.

Verbatim KJV (abridged with ellipsis). Links anger and death; does not address the renunciant half.

Verbatim.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.56–58 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a strong fit for the Kural's second line. The first line, that the excessively angry are as good as dead, has no direct counterpart here.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on freedom from anger as the mark of spiritual attainment. Sikhism rejects world-renunciation, so it agrees with the Kural's inner point but not with its praise of ascetics, and the Kural's first half, that the angry are like the dead, is not matched.
Paraphrase. A mythic, civic transformation rather than individual renunciation; thematic match.
Verbatim Jowett (MIT Classics). A lived example rather than a doctrinal statement.

entries.source: Tolstoy makes Do not be angry the first commandment of his faith
entries.rationale: Next-best only: Tolstoy taught the renunciation of anger, but Britannica notes he did not succeed in living fully by his own teachings, and the kural's first line about the excessively angry being like the dead is not shown.

entries.source: Qur’an 4:29 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Good match on refusing wealth gained by harming others; framed as a legal prohibition rather than a character ideal.
Close on preferring righteousness over great wealth; ‘without right’ is broader than ‘by harming others.’
Very close: explicitly refuses wrongdoing even for wealth or kingdom.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a reasonable thematic fit; the Jain verse argues from consequences, whereas the Kural presents non-harm as a fixed principle (kol).

entries.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 43-44 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on refusing wealth gained through others' pain. The milk-and-blood detail is hagiography from the Janamsakhi tradition, which Macauliffe himself introduces with 'it is said'.

entries.source: Plato, Republic II, 359c–360d (the Ring of Gyges)
entries.rationale: The myth poses the Kural’s exact test (harm for great gain); Gyges himself fails it, so the parallel works by contrast.

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis III.21 (trans. Walter Miller, Loeb 1913)
entries.rationale: Very close: explicitly ranks not profiting from another’s loss above one’s own wealth.

entries.source: John Woolman refuses to write wills that bequeath enslaved people
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of refusing gain that depends on others' suffering, though the income Woolman gave up was modest rather than the great wealth the kural imagines; sources differ on his exact age in 1742.
Describes the non-hating, forgiving disposition but does not explicitly address retaliation against someone who has done harm.
Near one-to-one match: explicit prohibition of retaliating harm for harm.

entries.source: Qur’an 5:28 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Strong narrative parallel of refusing to retaliate against a hostile aggressor.
Direct prohibition of revenge; framed for ‘the children of thy people’ rather than universally.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Extreme and vivid form of the same non-retaliation principle; stresses inner non-anger more than outward non-harm.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.26–27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a close match for non-retaliation against deliberate injury, though it is framed as a rule for monks.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on refusing retaliation. The words are Sheikh Farid's, a Sufi saint whose verses are included in the Sikh scripture, not a Sikh Guru's.
Clear instance of declining revenge on an enemy; the harm refused is posthumous dishonour, not direct injury.
Near one-to-one match: explicit prohibition on returning evil for evil.

entries.source: Six-year-old Ruby Bridges prays for the crowds who jeered her
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of returning no harm for spite; the account of her prayers comes from Robert Coles, who knew her at the time.

Strong match: retaliation against unprovoked aggressors, with a warning that the harm rebounds.

entries.source: Qur’an 42:40 (trans. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
entries.rationale: Partial: the Qur’an permits equivalent retribution while preferring pardon; the Kural treats retaliation as self-harming without exception.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 671, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best match: the verse describes freedom from enmity in general and does not speak of unprovoked hatred or of the grief that retaliation brings, which are the Kural's specific points.

entries.source: Aeschylus, Agamemnon 1583–1602 (Aegisthus’ account of the feast of Thyestes)
entries.rationale: Strong illustration of retaliation rebounding on the avenger; Atreus had been wronged, though not wholly unprovoked in every version.

entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match of the negative Golden Rule.

entries.rationale: Very close: universal (‘any being in any state’) and extends to wishes.

entries.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.4.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid, Salok 129 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.rationale: Captures the consistency argument; speaks of blame rather than of experienced pain.

entries.source: Anna Sewell writes Black Beauty to win kindness for horses

entries.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section 113 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the same law of return, but without the Kural's striking compression of time into a single day.

entries.rationale: Captures immediacy and self-punishment; the penalty is inner degradation rather than outward misfortune.

entries.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.5.2.23–24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 386, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section CXV (K. M. Ganguli trans.)

entries.source: Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animal Food, Books 1–3
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the treatise’s overall argument; strong conceptual match, less aphoristic than the Kural.

Verified on quran.com; strong match for sharing, partial for the protection-of-life element.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)

Near one-to-one: same three members, same order, same claim that their ending is the end of suffering.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.9 and 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 185, 192)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The triad and the disease metaphor both match closely. The Buddhist slot uses the parallel 'three poisons', but this is a distinct Jain canonical source.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 693, Raag Dhanaasree, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one, including the image of erasing even the name; Gurbani's list is five thieves rather than the Kural's three, and the verse is a Bhagat's, not a Guru's.
Paraphrase; allegorical fit only. The myth itself is not about inner passions.
Paraphrase; strong match on knowledge dissolving passion. Spinoza has no triad and no rebirth.

entries.source: The World Health Assembly declares smallpox eradicated
entries.rationale: This is an analogy only: the event shows the principle of total eradication ending a disease, but has nothing to do with the inner faults the kural names.
Near-exact doctrinal match: desire as the direct cause of rebirth. Mundaka 3.2.1 in the same passage even uses the image of a ‘seed’.

Partial: identifies inner inclination (nafs/hawa) as the root of evil, but has no concept of rebirth.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:21 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
entries.rationale: Thematic match on desire as destructive root; the mechanism (rebirth) is absent.

entries.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)
entries.rationale: Essentially one-to-one: the Second Noble Truth names craving as the cause of ‘renewal of being’ (ponobbhavika).

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.6–7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close match: both make craving the generative cause of rebirth, though the Jain version runs it through delusion and karmic matter rather than using a seed image.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 152, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: Gurbani links moh and trishna to death and rebirth elsewhere, but no verified verse found calls desire the seed of birth, and this line speaks only of perishing.
Next-best match: desire as the primordial generative force, but Greek myth celebrates rather than condemns it and has no rebirth doctrine.

entries.source: Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, §§ 56-57, 68 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase, not a verbatim quote. Strong structural parallel, since Schopenhauer drew explicitly on Indian sources, but he gives a metaphysics of will rather than a literal rebirth doctrine.
The event shows craving multiplying itself in one lifetime, but the kural's claim about desire as the seed of repeated rebirth cannot be illustrated historically.
Strong narrative match: all lesser desires are rejected for the single desire for liberating knowledge.
Good match on redirecting desire; the object (heaven versus non-birth) differs.
Moderate: redirects preference toward the enduring, but lacks the paradox of ‘desiring desirelessness’.
Moderate: shares the ‘one desire only’ structure; the object differs.
Very close: the ‘yearning to be passion-free’ is fulfilled through destroying craving.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit: the 'desire for liberation that destroys greed' matches the kural's paradox. The same paragraph goes on to say such a soul will not be born more than three more times, which echoes piravaamai, freedom from birth.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 154, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on transcending desire from within; Gurbani frames it as the Guru's teaching for life in the world, not as a desire for non-birth.

entries.source: Prodicus’ ‘Choice of Heracles’, in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Next-best match: a choice between pleasures and a higher good, but there is no idea of liberation from birth.
Strong match on deliberate suppression of desire as the path; Stoic freedom is not framed as freedom from rebirth.

Strong: desirelessness as self-sufficient contentment; the Gita does not use the ‘wealth’ metaphor explicitly.
Strong match on contentment as true ‘gain’.
Near one-to-one: redefines wealth as the soul’s freedom from want.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
entries.rationale: Very close parallel; Avot speaks of contentment rather than complete desirelessness.
Near-verbatim thematic match (‘contentment the greatest wealth’).

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.16 and 9.58 (context 9.46–49) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Both verses checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit, since the episode literally sets renounced wealth against the happiness of being free from ties, here and hereafter. It is a narrative illustration rather than a one-line maxim.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on contentment as the true treasure; Guru Arjan locates the highest good in the Name rather than in desirelessness itself.
Illustrative narrative of contented poverty; the ‘greatest wealth’ claim is implied rather than stated.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 2.6 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one inversion of the Kural’s claim.

entries.source: Diocletian gives up the throne and retires to Split
entries.rationale: A documented renunciation of supreme power, but the sources do not establish that Diocletian acted from inner freedom from desire rather than age, illness or policy.
Strong on desire as the defilement of purity; the Kural’s second line (truth as the means) is less directly mirrored.
Close structural match (truth → purified soul); does not define purity specifically as desirelessness.
Moderate: inner purification of the soul; the link to truth is not explicit.
Good match: purity is linked both to not desiring ‘vanity’ and to truthfulness.
Strong structural match: truth (insight) → turning from craving → purification.

entries.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 9.6, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one for the first line (purity = freedom from craving). The Jain text does not reproduce the kural's second line, that this freedom comes from longing for truth, beyond listing truthfulness as a sister virtue.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on inner rather than ritual purity; Guru Nanak defines purity by God's presence in the mind, while the Kural defines it as the absence of craving born of longing for truth.
Philosophical myth rather than traditional mythology; parallel is thematic.
Paraphrase. Strong parallel on both halves of the couplet.

entries.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein gives away his inherited fortune
entries.rationale: The renunciation of wealth is documented, but the sources do not tie it directly to a longing for truth, and his teaching years were troubled.
Very close: exclusive claim (‘he alone’) tied to inner desirelessness.
Good match on inner renunciation as the defining mark; lacks the explicit contrast with merely outward renouncers.
Partial: inner detachment is implied, but the inner-versus-outer contrast is not stated.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
entries.rationale: Structural parallel (redefining a title by inner mastery); speaks of subduing, not eliminating, desire.
Very close: the failed outward renunciant who has not cut off craving.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one: both separate outward renunciation from inward freedom from desire, and both use the language of incomplete cutting. Jacobi notes that verses 38–53 may be a later addition to the lecture.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one; Guru Nanak uses the definition to reject outward asceticism in favour of inner freedom while living in the world.
Weak/next-best: Midas’ flaw is folly rather than lingering desire; used as the closest mythic image of incomplete renunciation.
Near one-to-one: freedom is defined exclusively by the absence of desire.

entries.source: Queen Christina abdicates but seeks other crowns
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of outward renunciation without inner renunciation, though her reasons for abdicating were mixed and partly religious.
Strong: desire as the enemy; the element of deception is implied (Gita 3.40 speaks of it deluding the embodied).

Good match on desire as a self-deceiving trap.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong thematic fit on desire as a deceiver. The kural's specific point that fearing desire is the virtue is implied by the verse, not stated in it.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 510, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on desire as a deceiver that ruins; the Kural speaks of desire itself, Guru Amar Das of Maya, the world's allure that feeds it.
Excellent narrative parallel for vigilant fear of deceptive desire.

entries.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Preface (trans. R. H. M. Elwes)
entries.rationale: Strong on desire misleading the self; Spinoza speaks of emotions generally and prescribes understanding rather than fear.

entries.source: John Wesley holds his spending fixed as his income rises
entries.rationale: Wesley's documented self-restraint fits the kural's vigilance well, though the exact yearly figures come from his own later accounts as relayed by historians.

entries.source: Katha Upanishad 2.3.14 (numbered II.6.14 in trans. Max Müller, SBE 15)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: total cessation of desire → immortality.
Strong: transient desire versus enduring deeds/life.

entries.source: Pirkei Avot 2:4 (trans. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
entries.rationale: Strong structural match on the ‘surrender your will, receive your will’ paradox.
Good: complete letting go → deathlessness; the ‘as one wishes’ element is absent.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.107 and 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Both verses checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on 'total cutting of desire leads to liberation'. The kural's specific idea that the right deeds then come 'as one wishes' has no exact Jain counterpart.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on total desirelessness bringing the highest good; the Sikh reward is God's indwelling and merger, not a promise of imperishable deeds.

entries.source: Vinoba Bhave receives the first Bhoodan land gift

Near one-to-one, including the ‘again and again’ recurrence.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.100 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one in structure and claim. The kural's image of sorrow coming 'one after another' (menmel) is reflected elsewhere in the lecture (32.33, 'a long succession of pains') rather than in this verse.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 138, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Paraphrase. Strong parallel on desire as the source of unending toil.

entries.source: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (trans. Ñanamoli Thera)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: the cessation of craving is the cessation of suffering (nirodha).

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit: desire as the root sorrow and dispassion as its end. The kural's stress on joy 'even here' (eendum) is only implicit in this verse.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 588, Raag Vadhans (Vadhans ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus 131 (trans. R. D. Hicks)
entries.rationale: Strong: joy as the absence of disturbance; Epicurus prunes vain desires rather than eliminating all desire.

entries.source: Thoreau's two years at Walden Pond

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278-279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Paraphrase. Strong philosophical parallel: effort and outcome are fated together.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Paraphrase and gloss; Heraclitus makes character the fate, whereas Valluvar makes fate shape character.

entries.source: Ramanujan writes to G. H. Hardy

Paraphrase. Strong structural match: separate causes for wealth and for wisdom.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.15 (cf. 33.2–4) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Paraphrase. Strong match on the observed split between good fortune and wisdom.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.15, Jacobi's footnote (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book II (Prose 1-2, 8)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase. A strong thematic match on the reversibility of fortune.

entries.source: William Perkin's failed quinine experiment produces mauve
entries.rationale: A clear documented reversal in which a failure became a source of wealth; only the opposite direction of the kural, good turning bad, is not shown.
Moderate: shares non-ownership of outcomes, but not the image of wealth leaving or returning.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.31 (cf. 13.10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (Ashtpadi 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on gifts that cannot be held against the Giver's will; Sukhmani's own aim is gratitude, and it does not cover the Kural's other half, that what is one's own cannot be thrown away.

entries.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.13, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one on possession without enjoyment. Where commentators read Valluvar's 'Apportioner' (vakuththaan) as God, Jainism disagrees: there is no ordainer, and the apportioning is done by the soul's own karma.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib, Pauri 25, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
