Very strong match; framed as a religious obligation.
Paraphrase. Strong match on equanimity in gain and loss.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong thematic fit on equanimity toward good and bad fortune. The Jain verse grounds it in conquering the passions rather than in the kural's argument that both come from the same fate.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on equanimity toward good and bad fortune; the hymn grounds it in God's presence rather than in the Kural's argument that both come from the same fate.
Paraphrase. A strong match on a single divine source of good and ill.
Paraphrase. Strong thematic kinship; more affirmative than Valluvar’s equanimity.

entries.source: Shackleton's men survive the loss of the Endurance
entries.rationale: Shackleton's composure in disaster is well documented in outline, but the sources record his actions more than his inner equanimity, so the fit is partly inferred.
Strong match: attempted avoidance is overridden by what is bound to happen.
Strong match: many human devices, one prevailing counsel.
Strong match on inescapability despite precautions; the example is death specifically.
Partial and contrastive: affirms that all is foreseen and also that choice is free.
Strong match on inescapability; the force is kamma, which Buddhism does not treat as fixed fate.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: both see the force as inescapable, but Jainism rejects fate as an independent power. Mahāvīra argued against the Ājīvika view that 'all things are unalterably fixed' (Saddālaputta episode of the Uvāsagadasāo, read in a jainworld.com retelling), and he held that karma can be destroyed by austerity.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1376, Salok Bhagat Kabir 219 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near match on human planning being overruled; Gurbani attributes this to a personal Lord's will (hukam) rather than to impersonal fate.
Narrative paraphrase. A near one-to-one match: the attempt to escape fulfils the fate.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 107.10-11 (quoting Cleanthes)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase. A strong match on the supremacy of fate over resistance.

entries.source: The royal family's flight to Varennes
entries.rationale: A vivid case of a planned escape being overtaken, though the failure is explained historically by delays and recognition rather than by fate.
Very close structural parallel; paraphrased because the Book 6 wording was not verified verbatim online.
Partial match — covers the ‘people’ element only, not the full six-part model.
Covers only the military/defence elements; no single Islamic text lists all six.
Narrative parallel covering most of the six elements; not a stated doctrine.
Similar ‘list of royal assets’ form; the specific items only partially overlap (jewel and queen treasures have no Kural equivalent).

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The royal imagery (army, power, insignia of kingship, the lion) matches closely, but the verse is a simile praising the learned monk, not a teaching on statecraft, so the fit is partial.

Strong thematic fit on building the structural strength of a polity; Guru Hargobind's forces served to defend a faith community, not a kingdom, and the Kural's six-part list is not reproduced item by item.
Mythic illustration of the army and alliance limbs only.

entries.source: Aristotle, Politics, Book VII, ch. 8 (1328b) (tr. Benjamin Jowett)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett, Book VII). Striking six-fold structure with overlaps (arms/army, revenue/resources); Aristotle's arts, religion and judiciary do not match the Kural's ministers, allies and forts, and there is no lion simile. The sixth item is summarised in the explanation, not quoted.

Next-best: the event recovers a text that sets out the same theory of the state's limbs, but it is a scholarly discovery rather than a ruler who actually possessed all six and stood like a lion among kings.
Strong match — nearly all four Kural virtues appear in the Gita’s list of royal-warrior traits.
Covers wisdom and strength; generosity is not named.
Clear match for wisdom and courage/strength; generosity and energy not addressed.
Matches only the first quality (fearlessness).
Overlaps on generosity and discipline; emphasis differs (non-anger, non-violence).

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.6.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi). Three of the kural's four qualities (courage, giving, wisdom) appear, but they describe the renunciant Mahavira, not a ruler, and Jain 'giving' here means protecting life rather than royal largesse.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Salok 16, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Covers fearlessness and wisdom but not generosity or energy, and it describes the spiritually wise person in general, not a king.
Paraphrase; covers courage only, with an implicit link to royal generosity/honour.
Paraphrased; a genuine list of ruler-qualities with substantial overlap.

entries.source: Elizabeth I addresses her troops at Tilbury
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the event shows courage and energy, but not the generosity and wisdom the kural also lists, and the kural stresses never lacking them rather than one display.
Very strong match on vigilance; learning and courage are addressed elsewhere in Book 1.
Matches the vigilance/diligence element only.
General teaching for all believers, not specific to rulers; translations vary so paraphrased.
Strong match for the learning element; vigilance and courage not addressed.

entries.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (tr. S. Dhammika)
entries.rationale: Strong match on vigilance and energy from an actual Buddhist ruler.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong match on unceasing alertness. However, the context is a monk's spiritual vigilance, and the kural's other two qualities (learning and resolve) are not addressed here.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 34, Siree Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: the vigilance meant is spiritual watchfulness against vice and maya, not a ruler's promptness, and learning and resolve, the Kural's other two qualities, are not covered.
Excellent match for vigilance (ironically delivered by a deceptive dream).
Matches learning; vigilance and resolve not addressed.

entries.source: Peter the Great works in foreign shipyards during the Grand Embassy
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the triad of vigilance, learning and resolve in a ruler, though Peter's reign also included harsh methods the kural would not endorse.
Matches the removal-of-wrong clause; the honour/valour element is not in this verse.
Strong match for justice and removal of wrong; courage not mentioned.
Strong on justice and self-restraint; courage/honour not explicit.
Close on righteousness and removing wrong; valour element absent.
Paraphrase; matches the righteousness element, not courage/honour.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The subject (a king's duty to put down wrong) is the same, but the Jain passage questions royal punishment rather than endorsing it, so this is a next-best contrast.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on righteousness joined with courage; the verse concerns the spiritual warrior in general rather than a king's duty to remove wrongdoing from the land, and other translators render 'deen' as the poor or helpless.
Mythic illustration of courageous removal of evil; honour theme implicit.
Paraphrased; strong conceptual match on joining courage to justice.

entries.source: King Haakon VII refuses to appoint Quisling
entries.rationale: A very close illustration of righteousness and courage held together under pressure, although the 'removing wrongdoing from the land' element was achieved only later with the Allies.
Paraphrase; very close in spirit to the collect-and-distribute cycle.
Parable about stewardship rather than kingship proper; covers two of four verbs.
Strong match for storing and guarding; Joseph is minister, not king.
Narrative match to the full cycle; administrator rather than monarch.
Paraphrase; strong match for creating and allocating wealth.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Jain scripture has no positive theory of royal public finance comparable to this kural. This is an honest contrast on the theme of the treasury, scored well below 60.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the earn-and-share ethic parallels producing and distributing wealth, but it is personal ethics, not public finance, and says nothing about collecting or safeguarding revenue.
Contrast rather than parallel; no close Greek-myth analogue for royal finance.
Paraphrase; authorship disputed (Aristotelian school); household rather than state.

entries.source: The Inca state's network of storehouses
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of the four-step cycle of public wealth, though it describes a long-running institution rather than a single dated event.
Near one-to-one match for accessibility; harsh speech not addressed here.
Spiritual rather than political kingship, but matches accessibility and gentleness.
Very strong match on accessibility of rulers.
Addressed to judges under Moses; matches accessibility, not speech.

entries.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict VI (tr. S. Dhammika)
entries.rationale: Strong match on accessibility.

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.6.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi). It matches only the 'not harsh in speech' half of the kural. The ease of approaching the king has no direct Jain parallel here.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: it matches the Kural's avoidance of harsh speech, but not its main point that the ruler be easy for his people to approach.
Paraphrase; accessibility matches, but Oedipus is later harsh in speech.

entries.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book I, §16 (tr. George Long)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Long, Book I); excerpts joined with ellipses from the long §16 portrait. Strong match on accessibility and absence of harshness; the Kural's result (the world praising his land) is not stated here.

entries.source: King Christian X's daily rides through occupied Copenhagen
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of a ruler being easily seen by his people, though the sources say little about his manner of speech, the kural's second condition.
Paraphrase of Rama’s described character; not a doctrinal statement.
Matches generosity; somewhat cynical tone, and kind speech not mentioned.
Strong match on kind speech producing loyalty; giving not mentioned in this verse.
Near-direct parallel, reinforced by the negative outcome of Rehoboam’s harshness.
Near one-to-one match on three elements; addressed to all, traditionally applied to rulers.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a weak, next-best fit. Jain scripture offers no close parallel to winning the world's consent through sweet words, gifts and protection, and the passage reverses the kural's roles.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 544, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the verse describes God, not a human ruler, and says nothing of kind speech or of the world following the ruler's word.
Strong on kind speech and consent; generosity absent.

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §48 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis II.44-89, Miller); the quote begins mid-sentence ('...and yet, it is not easy to say...'), with an editorial capital 'I'. Partial match: covers kind words winning affection, but not the Kural's pairing with generosity and protection of those who come to the ruler. The content of the royal letters is summarised from the surrounding passage.

entries.source: The Jam Sahib of Nawanagar shelters Polish refugee children
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of a ruler who gives, protects those who come to him and wins lasting affection, though the kural's political reward of the world following his word is only loosely matched.
Same image with an instructive difference in its grounds.
Ruler as God’s agent rather than as god; conditional on doing good.
Exaltation of the just ruler, but explicitly not deification.
Strong conceptual match, including the conditional nature of the title.
Honest partial match: same justice-based legitimacy, opposite view on divinity.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Jainism is non-theistic and has no 'king as god' idea, so this is a next-best parallel on a king who is revered above gods because of virtue.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1088, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: the shared idea is that legitimacy rests on worth, but Sikhism would not have people regard any ruler as God, and the line is often read inwardly as the throne of spiritual wisdom.
Near one-to-one: reverence as a god earned by just judgement.
Strong match; Aristotle speaks of outstanding virtue generally, not only justice.
A strong illustration of conditional deification earned by protection and order, though the deification was also an act of state policy and Augustus's rise involved civil war.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 37 (Vidura Niti), tr. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match, addressed to a king.
General wisdom teaching; not specific to kings.
Speaker’s perspective rather than the ruler’s; complementary match.
Narrative match; the short phrases are KJV wording but the entry summarises the episode.
Strong match; addressed to all, not specifically rulers.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The story fits a king accepting a harsh rebuke well, but its outcome is renunciation, not better governance.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar (Vaar Malaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: Gurbani here speaks the bitter word to power rather than praising a ruler who accepts it, so it illustrates the Kural's point only from the critic's side.
Paraphrase; strong thematic match.
Strong match from an actual ruler’s private reflections.

entries.source: Frederick Douglass confronts Abraham Lincoln about Black soldiers

Paraphrase; strong on care and protection, generosity implied.
Striking verbal match for the just sceptre; the other three qualities not listed.
Strong on care for subjects; generosity and compassion implicit.
Strong match on justice and the light metaphor.
Paraphrase; close match to all four elements.

entries.source: Jain tradition on Rishabhanatha (Adipurana and Svetambara accounts), as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Rishabhanatha'
entries.rationale: Paraphrased from Wikipedia as a last resort, because primary-text pages (Trishashti, Kalpa Sutra on wisdomlib) were unavailable this session. The fit with a caring, protective ruler is good, but the four specific virtues are not named one by one.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on benevolent, protective rule; the rule meant is God's, and commentators such as Sahib Singh read it inwardly as humility's reign in the heart, not as a human king's government.
Strong on just rule and people’s welfare.
Captures the ruler-for-subjects principle; not a list of the four virtues.

entries.source: King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet for his people
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of a ruler whose care for ordinary people became his lasting light, though the event centres on one achievement rather than all four qualities together.
Paraphrase of a famous passage. It pairs study with dharmic conduct, but it is a list of duties rather than a direct statement that conduct must match learning.

entries.source: Pravacanasara III.237 (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on living by what one knows; the verse speaks of Truth (God and the Name) rather than of learning as such, and does not address learning without flaw.

entries.source: General Greek mythology (Homeric Hymn 28 to Athena; Hesiod, Theogony 886–900 on Metis)
entries.rationale: Weak match. Greek myth has no clear story commanding people to live by their learning. Athena's joining of wisdom and craft is the closest available parallel.

entries.rationale: A very close fit for the second half of the kural, living by what one has learned; the first half, learning without flaw, is shown less directly.

Metaphorical match only. It shares the sight and illumination image but refers to scripture, not numeracy and literacy.
Verified via the Quran.com API. A strong match for 'letters'. Numbers are not mentioned.
Verified on Sefaria. It links numbers and letters to wisdom, but calls them 'desserts', which is less central than the Kural's 'eyes'.

entries.source: Mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. It praises learning in general. It does not name numbers and letters specifically.

entries.source: Jain tradition on Rishabhanatha, Brahmi and Sundari, as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Rishabhanatha'
entries.rationale: The content is a striking, distinctly Jain match on 'letters and numbers'. However, it is paraphrased from Wikipedia as a last resort, because a primary-text page (Trishashti or Adipurana) could not be checked this session.
Reasonable but partial: it concerns letters only, not numbers, and Britannica presents the schools as Sikh tradition ('Sikh lore') while stating the standardization of Gurmukhi as fact.

entries.source: Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 459–461 (trans. H. W. Smyth)

Paraphrase of a famous passage. Translations vary, so it is not given as a verbatim quote. The 'letters plus mathematics as the means of sight' theme is a strong match.

entries.source: Al-Khwarizmi writes on the Hindu art of reckoning
entries.rationale: A strong example of number as a way of seeing the world, but it shows only one of the kural's two eyes, number, and not letters.
Paraphrase of a well-known Sanskrit verse. Verse numbering varies by recension. The provocative 'the unlearned lack their true human faculty' theme is a strong match.
Standard KJV text. The 'eyes that do not see' theme is a close match, though the Gospel is about spiritual receptivity rather than education.

Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. The same 'harsh image for the unlearned' strategy, with an ox image instead of eye imagery.

entries.source: Pravacanasara III.234 (cf. III.233) (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Upadhye's translation on jainworld.com (verse 234). This is a near one-to-one use of the image of learning as the true eye, though the verse lacks the kural's harsh 'sores' contrast.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong structural parallel; for Guru Angad true sight comes from closeness to the Lord rather than from learning, and the verse is gentler toward the physically blind than the Kural's image.

entries.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus (esp. the Tiresias scene, lines 300–462, and the self-blinding)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased summary of the plot. The sight-versus-insight theme is a strong match.
Paraphrase. Plato's 'eye of the soul' image directly parallels the Kural's 'eyes of the learned'.

entries.source: Louis Braille devises a reading system for the blind
entries.rationale: Matches the traditional commentary that a learned person without sight still has eyes, though the kural's harsh image of the unlearned is not illustrated.
