Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. The 'lingering fragrance' is a good parallel to the lingering longing, though the hadith is about good companions in general rather than scholars.
Verified on Sefaria. It shows the elevated quality of learned conversation. The longing-at-parting element is absent.

entries.source: Mangala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. A general parallel about the blessing of learned company.

entries.source: Pravacanasara III.263 (Kundakunda, tr. A.N. Upadhye; jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainworld.com (verse 263). This is a next-best fit: it prescribes honour for the learned, but it is a monastic etiquette rule, not a description of the delight and longing their company creates.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 520, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the friends meant are the Guru's devotees rather than scholars, and the verse does not mention the longing to meet again after parting.
Paraphrase of the 'intermezzo' in Book 11. A strong match for joyful meeting and reluctance to part.
Paraphrase. A vivid match for the enchanting effect of a learned person's company, though Alcibiades' feelings are also ambivalent.
Captures the joy of meeting a learned person, but the crowds were drawn partly by fame, and the longing after parting is not documented in the sources used.
Wording confirmed via vedabase.io and other search results. Humble approach to a teacher is the direct theme.
Standard KJV text. It shares the teachable-versus-proud ranking, without the rich-and-poor image.
Verified via the Quran.com API. A clear narrative example of humble discipleship.
Verified on Sefaria. Together the two passages closely match both lines of the Kural.
Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. The wealth imagery for the teacher is a notable parallel.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on humble eagerness before the teacher, but it lacks the kural's poor-before-the-rich image and its condemnation of those who refuse to learn.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 353, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on humility before the teacher; in Sikhism the Guru is the spiritual guide to God rather than a teacher of learning in general, and the verse does not condemn those who will not learn.
Paraphrase. The 'shy student urged to approach the elder' scene closely matches the Kural's theme.
Paraphrase. It shares the humility-as-the-basis-of-wisdom theme but has no teacher-student image.

entries.source: Frederick Douglass trades bread for reading lessons
entries.rationale: A vivid picture of eager, unashamed learning; the kural's image is of humility before an established teacher, which differs somewhat from Douglass's improvised lessons.
Paraphrase of the Bhrigu narrative. Knowledge deepening with effort is a good parallel, but there is no water or well image.
Wording confirmed against multiple KJV sources. It shares the wellspring image, though not the 'proportional to digging' logic.
Verified via the Quran.com API. The inexhaustibility theme matches well. The 'more you dig, the more flows' logic is implicit rather than stated.
Verified on Sefaria. A spring image for a learned mind, closely matching the Kural.
Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. The proportional-growth logic matches well. The practice named is meditation, not learning.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The doctrinal match is strong, since both describe knowledge emerging in proportion to study, but the Jain verse has no well image.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1255, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: seeking that bears fruit is the shared idea, but Gurbani gives no matching image of growth in proportion to depth, and its search is for God, not for learning.
Paraphrase. It shares the spring-of-knowledge image, but inspiration comes as a gift rather than from effort.

entries.source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism, Part II, lines 215–218 (1711)
entries.rationale: Wording confirmed against Poetry Foundation and other editions. Depth-of-learning plus spring imagery is a close parallel.
Illustrates understanding growing in proportion to sustained study, though the kural speaks of learning in general rather than a single problem.

entries.source: Sanskrit subhashita (traditionally included in Chanakya Niti collections; attribution varies)
entries.rationale: The widely cited Sanskrit wording is given with a translation, so it is marked as a paraphrase. Attribution and verse numbering differ between collections. A very close thematic match.
Wording confirmed against multiple KJV sources. A strong narrative parallel for learning being honoured abroad. The 'until death' element is absent.
Verified via the Quran.com API. A good narrative parallel. (The popular saying 'seek knowledge even unto China' was avoided because hadith scholars widely regard it as weak.)
Verified on Sefaria. A strong match for the urgency of learning. The 'every land is his' element is absent.
Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. A partial match: it values wisdom over length of life but does not mention being at home everywhere.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a partial, next-best fit. The 'any village or town' idea matches, but the verse is about the monk's conduct and preaching, not about learning making every place one's own.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the universal belonging is the shared idea, but in the hymn it comes from the company of the holy (sadh sangat), not from learning.
Paraphrase of the proem, since translations vary. A good match for 'learning makes every land familiar'.

entries.source: Plato, Laches 188b (Solon); Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.63 (Diogenes)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of two well-attested sayings. Combined, they closely match both lines of the Kural.

entries.source: Al-Idrisi makes his home at the court of Roger II of Sicily
entries.rationale: A close fit for the kural's first half, learning as portable citizenship, while its second half about learning until death is shown only implicitly.
Wording confirmed via vedabase.io search results. Carry-over of spiritual attainment across births directly parallels the Kural.
Standard KJV text. A moderate match: wisdom's lasting value beyond death, in a different eschatological frame.
Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. A strong match for learning outlasting death, though in an afterlife frame rather than rebirth.
Verified on Sefaria. It matches learning as a companion beyond death. Its frame is the world to come rather than seven births.
Paraphrase of the traditional narrative. Its focus is spiritual perfections broadly rather than learning specifically.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a near one-to-one parallel on learning protecting the soul across many births. The Jain framing aims at final release, not only at protection in future lives.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (Ashtpadi 2), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: both speak of a support that lasts beyond this life, but for Guru Arjan it is the Name, not learning, and he does not speak of seven births.
Paraphrase. A philosophical myth rather than traditional mythology, but a good rebirth-and-wisdom parallel.
Paraphrase. Plato's theory of recollection strikingly parallels the Kural's cross-life view of learning.

entries.source: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine teaches doctors for six centuries
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the kural speaks of learning protecting its owner across future births, while this shows learning benefiting later generations, which matches only the secular reading.
Paraphrase built around the Sanskrit phrase. A moderate match: the wise delight in the world's good, but without the cycle of learning more.
Standard KJV text. A partial match on sharing one's light; the self-reinforcing love of learning is missing.
Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. A strong match for learning-to-share.
Verified on Sefaria. The learn-teach-learn more cycle closely matches the Kural.
Verified verbatim on Access to Insight. Joy and gift in knowledge are both present, so this is a strong match.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on learning that serves both self and others, although the kural's emphasis on growing delight is not explicit.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on learning that benefits the world; Guru Nanak stresses service to others rather than the learner's growing delight in learning.
Paraphrase. A good match for learning as shared delight; the learner's growing desire for more is not explicit.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 6.4
entries.rationale: Close paraphrase of the Gummere translation. It is not presented verbatim because the exact wording could not be fully confirmed. A very close thematic match.
Shows learning shared for the world's joy, but the kural's inner cycle of deepening love for learning is Tagore's own experience, which the sources do not document directly.

entries.source: Traditional Sanskrit subhashita on vidyā-dhana (widely cited; exact textual origin uncertain)
entries.rationale: Widely cited Sanskrit wording with a translation, marked as a paraphrase because translations vary and the original anthology source is uncertain. A near-identical theme.
Standard KJV text. It directly ranks wisdom above wealth; the 'imperishable' point is implicit.

entries.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 3641 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Sunnah.com. It directly contrasts knowledge with money as the true inheritance.
Paraphrase of the midrash, confirmed via Sefaria and Chabad.org retellings. A near-exact thematic match.

Paraphrase. A strong structural match for imperishable versus perishable wealth, but its 'treasure' is merit rather than learning. The source page could not be fetched during this session because of a rate limit.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Good thematic fit (inexhaustible riches, no equal), but it is a simile, not an explicit claim that learning alone is true wealth.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on an inexhaustible, ever-growing wealth; the treasure is the Name and devotion, not learning, and the line does not dismiss other possessions as the Kural does.
Weak to moderate match. It is a cautionary tale about the emptiness of material wealth, with no counterpart about learning.

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 9.18–19
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of Seneca's anecdote (the saying is often rendered 'omnia mea mecum sunt'). A close parallel.

entries.source: China's universities carry their learning to Kunming in wartime
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of learning outlasting material loss, though the kural's contrast with all other wealth is shown only by implication.
Paraphrase. Shares the idea that lack of scriptural grounding leaves one without footing, but the Gita’s focus is spiritual doubt, not public speaking in an assembly.
Close thematic match (unlearned would-be teachers speaking with confidence); lacks the Kural’s dice-board image.
Strong on the principle (do not act/speak without knowledge); broader than the Kural’s specific setting of a learned assembly.
Partial match: Proverbs targets hasty speech before hearing, the Kural targets speech without study. Both locate folly in ungrounded speaking.
Paraphrase. MN 22 concerns wrongly grasped learning used for debate; the Kural concerns lack of learning altogether. Related but not identical.

entries.source: Naladiyar, ch. 32 'Experience in (conducting of) assemblies', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Close fit: both describe an unlearned man exposing himself in an assembly of the learned. This is a Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: both reject empty debating, but the Kural prizes mastery of texts, while in the same salok (as Sant Singh Khalsa renders it) Gurbani says wisdom does not come from reading textbooks.
Weak, analogical match: about presuming skill in general, not about speaking in a learned assembly. Best available myth.
Paraphrase. Strong conceptual parallel (speaking without knowledge); Plato’s setting is persuasion of crowds rather than a learned assembly.

entries.source: Bishop Wilberforce argues against Darwin at the 1860 Oxford meeting
entries.rationale: A strong picture of speaking to a learned assembly without mastery of the texts, but Wilberforce was a learned man in other fields (a first-class mathematician and Fellow of the Royal Society), and the verdict that he lacked mastery comes from his opponents.
Paraphrase. Shared theme of attachment to eloquent words without depth; the Gita addresses ritualists, not public speakers.
Very close: craving self-expression without understanding. The Kural adds the simile of futile desire.
Good match on speaking/arguing without knowledge; the Qur’an’s subject is theological dispute specifically.
Captures the fool’s excess of words; does not carry the Kural’s idea of a desire doomed by a missing prerequisite.
Strong on speech ≠ wisdom; the Kural focuses on the futility of the desire itself.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The verse links ignorance and loose talk but has no equivalent of the Kural's striking simile, so the fit is partial.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the shared theme is speech without substance, but Guru Nanak contrasts words with conduct rather than with learning, and the Kural's harsh simile has no Gurbani counterpart.
Paraphrase. Parallel of craving recognition without mastery; context is music and divine rivalry, not speech.
Paraphrase of a different Apology passage (the poets). Shared theme of eloquence without knowledge.

entries.source: Florence Foster Jenkins sings at Carnegie Hall
entries.rationale: A vivid case of craving an audience without the needed basis, but it concerns singing rather than learned speech, and Jenkins and her audiences seem to have enjoyed the performances, so the futility the kural stresses is only partly shown.

entries.source: Bhartrhari, Nitishataka, verse 7 (numbering varies by edition)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the Sanskrit; the final phrase is transliterated directly. Near one-to-one match in content and setting.
Near one-to-one match; the Kural adds the specific setting of being ‘before the learned’.
Quote is an excerpt of the final clause of a longer hadith. General ethic of speech; not specific to the unlearned before scholars.
Paraphrase (translations vary: ‘a fence for wisdom is silence’). Akiva’s maxim is general; the Kural applies it to the unlearned.
Strong on acknowledging ignorance; silence is implied rather than stated.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one on keeping quiet before the wise. The Jain verse is addressed to a monk-pupil rather than to the unlearned in general.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: Gurbani values restraint in speech, but this line addresses everyone and is not about the unlearned keeping silent before scholars.

entries.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 8.10
entries.rationale: Paraphrase. Greek legendary tradition (Pythagorean lore) rather than myth proper; strong on silence of the unlearned before the learned.

entries.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, proposition 7 (tr. C. K. Ogden)
entries.rationale: Weak match: Wittgenstein’s limit is what language can express, not what an individual has learned. Included as the best-known philosophical maxim on principled silence.

entries.source: George Washington stays almost silent at the Constitutional Convention
entries.rationale: Washington was self-taught and widely read rather than truly unlearned, and his silence also followed from his role as presiding officer, so the event fits the kural's point only in part.
Paraphrase. Indirect: the Gita affirms learning from the realized rather than explicitly rejecting the insights of the unlearned.
Good match on wisdom being unreliable in a fool’s mouth; Proverbs stresses the fool’s misuse, the Kural the listener’s refusal.
Partial: the Qur’an’s unreliable source is morally untrustworthy (fasiq), not unlearned, and it counsels verification rather than rejection.
Contrast rather than parallel. Included honestly because no close Jewish parallel was found; it frames the tension the Kural resolves the other way.
Indirect: the verse is about the fool’s failure to understand, which grounds (but does not state) the Kural’s point about the wise not accepting his insight.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong on rejecting cleverness without real knowledge. However, the Jain verse is about salvation, not about how the learned judge someone, so the fit is thematic.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib (pauri 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: both distrust mere cleverness, but Guru Nanak contrasts it with surrender to God's hukam, not with formal learning.
Contrast/complication rather than parallel; Cassandra is inspired, not unlearned. Best available myth on truth disregarded because of its source.
Paraphrase. Very strong conceptual parallel (unreliability of untethered correct opinion).

entries.source: The Royal Society tests Leeuwenhoek's reports of tiny animals
entries.rationale: The Society's caution matches the kural closely, but the outcome also shows that the untrained man's insight was correct, which softens the kural's dismissive tone.
Paraphrase. Strong on self-deceived pseudo-learning; the Upanishad does not specify exposure through conversation.
Strong on false self-estimation; lacks the Kural’s scene of exposure before the learned.
Close on arguing without knowledge being exposed; the Qur’anic context is a specific dispute about Abraham.
Paraphrase. Close setting (conduct in learned conversation); framed as a behavioral contrast rather than a prediction of collapse.
Strong on false self-estimation; the Kural adds the moment of public exposure.

entries.source: Jain narrative tradition of Indrabhuti Gautama's conversion, as retold in 'Gautamswami' (jainworld.com Jain stories)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased from a Jain educational retelling, not primary scripture. Indrabhuti was a great scholar, not an unlearned man, so the story matches only the 'pride melts before the truly learned' part of the kural.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: both describe pride shrinking in good company, but Guru Arjan treats this as a blessing that cures haumai, not as the humiliation of an unlearned man.
Paraphrase. Good narrative parallel of ignorance exposed by speaking out among the skilled.
Strong on seeming-versus-real wisdom; Plato’s immediate target is reliance on writing.

entries.source: A royal commission tests Mesmer's animal magnetism
entries.rationale: Mesmer held a medical degree, so he was 'unlearned' only in that his theory had no scientific basis, and his exposure came through a formal inquiry rather than conversation.

entries.source: Hitopadesha, Prastavika (Introduction), verse on the unlearned son
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; verse numbering varies by edition. Strong on ‘present but useless’; the image is a blind eye, not barren land.
Good image of fruitless existence; the parable is about repentance rather than learning.
Mostly paraphrase with one verbatim phrase in quotation marks. Very close image (barren land ↔ one who does not take in knowledge).
Striking verbal parallel (salt land), but Jeremiah’s subject is the one who trusts in man rather than God, not the unlearned.
Paraphrase. Very close image; but the Buddha still teaches the ‘salty field’ out of compassion, so the moral emphasis differs.

entries.source: Naladiyar, ch. 34 'Ignorance', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Both use the image of a fruitless, lifeless thing for the unlearned, though the images differ (stone versus salt land). This is a Tamil Jain text.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1275, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit: the same image of barren saline soil, though for Guru Nanak what is missing is the Guru's guidance rather than book-learning.
Paraphrase. Archaic Greek wisdom poetry rather than myth; close in judgment (‘unprofitable’).

entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 82.3 (tr. R. M. Gummere)
entries.rationale: Strong match on life without learning as mere existence; Seneca speaks of leisure specifically.

entries.source: Japan's Education System Order aims for no illiterate household
entries.rationale: A policy rather than a dramatic event; it reflects the kural's high valuation of learning but does not itself show unlearned lives as barren.
Paraphrase of the Sanskrit. Near one-to-one match; the image is a scentless flower rather than a clay doll.
Shares the outer-beauty/inner-emptiness structure; Jesus’s target is moral hypocrisy, not lack of intellect.
Strong image match; the Qur’anic subject is the hypocrites’ lack of faith and understanding, not learning as such.
Close structural match (beauty minus discernment); Proverbs speaks of a woman, the Kural of anyone.
Paraphrase. Shared image of a painted figure; the Buddhist point is impermanence of the body, not lack of learning.

entries.source: Naladiyar, ch. 27 'Riches without goodness', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Partial fit: both contrast outer adornment with inner emptiness, but the Naladiyar's point concerns undeserved prosperity rather than physical beauty. This is a Tamil Jain text.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on fine appearance without substance; in the salok the missing quality is sweetness and humility rather than learning.

entries.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Fox and the Mask’ (Perry 27)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; wording varies across translations. Greek fable tradition rather than myth proper. Near-exact image match.
Paraphrase. Good match on priority of mind over looks; Charmides turns out to be promising, unlike the Kural’s subject.
Next-best only: the Turk is a machine, so it illustrates the kural's image of an empty decorated figure metaphorically rather than showing an unlearned person.
Paraphrase; verse numbering varies. Indirect: states the ideal sequence rather than the harm of wealth without learning.
The ‘fool’ here lacks spiritual wisdom rather than learning; no comparison with the poverty of the good.
Strong on wealth being unsafe with the ‘weak-minded’ (sufaha); lacks the comparison with virtuous poverty.
Close structure (good poor vs. fool); the fool’s wealth is implied (cf. Prov 28:6), not stated.
Very close; lacks only the explicit comparison with the poverty of the good.

entries.source: Naladiyar, ch. 27 'Riches without goodness', stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org, including the stray comma in the source. Same pairing as the kural, but the stanza explains it by karma instead of judging which state is worse. This is a Tamil Jain text.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 745, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: it supports the half of the Kural about the good poor, but says nothing about wealth held by the unlearned.
Paraphrase. Strong image of wealth harming the unwise; no contrast with the virtuous poor.
Paraphrase. Very strong conceptual match.
Next-best only: this is national financial mismanagement involving advisers and fraud rather than an unlearned individual, and the kural's comparison with the poverty of the good is not illustrated.
Paraphrase. Strong on birth yielding to merit; the Upanishad’s criterion is truthfulness, leading to learning.
Close match; Ecclesiastes contrasts wealth/office rather than birth, and is shared Hebrew Bible text.
Excerpt of the verse. Affirms elevation by knowledge; does not explicitly compare it with birth (cf. 49:13).
Paraphrase. Near one-to-one match in structure and meaning.
Strong on rejecting birth-based worth; the Buddha’s criterion is truth and righteousness rather than learning.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.1, 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on worth over birth. The Jain text values penance and self-control rather than book-learning as such, so the parallel is close but not exact.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1127, Raag Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near match: both rank knowledge above birth, though the Kural ranks within a caste order while Sikh teaching rejects caste altogether, and the knowledge it values is knowledge of God.
Paraphrase. Greek popular legend rather than myth; Aesop’s wisdom is native wit rather than formal learning.
Paraphrase. Plato’s criterion is natural capacity (then trained), close to but not identical with learning.

entries.source: B. R. Ambedkar rises through learning to chair the drafting of India's Constitution
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's claim that learning outweighs birth, though Ambedkar went further than the kural by fighting to abolish birth-based hierarchy altogether.
Paraphrase of the Sanskrit. Near one-to-one match; Bhartrhari adds music and art to literature.
Shares the animal comparison for the ignorant; Jude’s subject is moral corruption of false teachers.
Strong match on animal analogy for those without understanding; Qur’anic context is spiritual heedlessness.

entries.source: Psalm 49:20 (Hebrew Bible; KJV wording; Ps 49:21 in Hebrew numbering)
entries.rationale: Close; ‘understanding’ in the psalm is spiritual insight into mortality rather than book learning.
Close; the Dhammapada’s ‘little learning’ (appassuta) matches the Kural’s lack of study.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.5–6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The man-versus-beast comparison is shared, but the Jain verse is about turning from virtue and discipline rather than lacking learning as such.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on the human-versus-beast contrast; Guru Arjan bases it on conduct and spiritual blindness rather than lack of study.
Paraphrase. Allegorical reading (moly as knowledge/reason is an ancient interpretation, not Homer’s explicit claim).

entries.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 5.19 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one structural match; wording of the reply varies slightly between translations (‘from the dead’ / ‘to the dead’).

entries.source: King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet for ordinary people
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shows the high value placed on learning, but Sejong's compassionate project sought to lift the unlettered rather than to rank them below others as the kural's harsh comparison does.
Paraphrase of a well-known dialogue; the contrast of wealth vs. hearing-as-path-to-knowledge is a very close structural match.
Strong match: listening to a teacher ranked above all other occupation and as an inalienable possession.
Values knowledge supremely but does not specify hearing or compare it with wealth explicitly.
Shared primacy of hearing, but the Shema is about covenantal faith rather than ‘wealth’; the comparison is thematic.
Very close conceptual match — ‘treasure of hearing’ is nearly identical in wording and intent.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 3.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The identification of 'instruction in the Law' with hearing follows the lecture's own verses 8-11 ('having heard the Law'). This is a strong fit, though the Jain text lists hearing as one of four treasures rather than the single foremost one.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 10), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit: the Suniai pauris make listening the source of spiritual riches, but the listening meant is to the Name and the Guru's word, not to learned people in general.
Values counsel heard over material/military resources; the ‘wealth’ framing is implicit rather than stated.

entries.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De auditu (On Listening to Lectures) 1–2
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; strong match on the primacy of hearing, though Plutarch does not use the metaphor of wealth.

entries.source: Charlemagne learns by listening at his court
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of learning by hearing, though Einhard was an admiring biographer and Charlemagne also learned to read, so his knowledge did not come by ear alone.
Narrative paraphrase; exceptionally close match to the ear-food over stomach-food priority.
Very close: word as food, bodily food secondary; the Kural specifies hearing, Jesus the divine word.
Paraphrase; the ‘food caravan’ detail comes from tafsir tradition rather than the verse itself.
Strong match — hearing explicitly treated as nourishment more vital than bread.
Shares the food/taste metaphor and the ranking, but does not mention hearing specifically.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 26.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The ordering of study before food matches well, but this is a monastic timetable rather than a saying about hearing as such.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Mundavani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: both treat wisdom as nourishment, but the Mundavani does not rank it against bodily food or tell anyone to eat less.
Pairs hearing with food, but Homer treats them as complementary pleasures rather than ranking hearing first.
Paraphrase; very close metaphor, though Plato stresses caution about what one hears rather than prioritising it over eating.

entries.source: Marie Sklodowska studies in Paris on a meagre diet
entries.rationale: A good match for putting learning before food, but her frugality was driven partly by poverty, and much of her learning came from reading and laboratory work rather than from hearing alone.
Paraphrase; close on status elevation of the hearer, but the Gita promises heavenly worlds rather than equality with gods on earth.
Shares ‘blessed hearers’ theme; lacks the food/oblation imagery and equality with gods.
Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; close on celestial company for listeners/learners.
Paraphrase of aggadic passage; strong structural match (hearers likened to angels).
Honours hearing highly but does not equate hearers with gods; best available Buddhist parallel.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close on comparing the learned with gods. In Jainism, however, gods are embodied beings still in samsara and are not fed by sacrificial oblations, so the kural's sacrificial image has no Jain counterpart.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 9), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on listening raising people to the rank of gods, though for the Guru the deities are lesser beings within God's order, not objects of worship.
Weak-to-moderate: gods delight in hearing, but no claim that human listeners equal gods.
Historical parallel on institutionalised listening; the ‘equal to gods’ element is only indirect.

entries.source: UNESCO recognises the oral tradition of Vedic chanting
entries.rationale: Captures the kural's linking of hearing with sacrifice and sanctity, but it is the recognition of a tradition rather than an event showing hearers raised to the status of the gods.
Paraphrase; nearly the same argument as the Kural — hearing substitutes for learning and supports in the gravest distress.
Strong match on both elements: lack of study and support in a crisis through hearing.
Paraphrase; matches the unlearned-hearer theme but not the ‘support in adversity’ element.
Good match on unlearned listener; ‘support in adversity’ is implicit in Samuel’s later role.
Narrative paraphrase from the commentarial tradition; strong fit on support in distress.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Trisastisalakapurusacaritra, Parva X, ch. 11, 'Story of Rauhineya' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased. A search confirmed that wisdomlib.org's Johnson translation has this section (Parva X, ch. XI), but the page returned a server error, so the details were checked against several Jain retellings. Very close fit to listening as a support in adversity.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 11), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit: both make listening open to those without other resources; Japji speaks of finding the path rather than of support in misfortune.
Moderate: the hearing-as-support element fits; Odysseus is not ‘unlearned’ in the Kural’s sense.
Good match on oral over written learning; the ‘support in adversity’ element is absent.

entries.source: Bookbinder's apprentice Michael Faraday attends Humphry Davy's lectures
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural, though Faraday also educated himself by reading the books he bound.
Standard rendering paraphrased (translations vary); close image of dangerous path plus guidance of the wise.
Close on stability through heard words; image is foundation rather than staff.
Similar support metaphor; the source is revelation rather than virtuous human speakers.
Very close image (not slipping); the Psalm’s source is divine law rather than the speech of the virtuous.
Close on the value of heeding the virtuous; image differs (guide to treasure vs staff).

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 248 (Samyagjnanasutra) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word (including the source's spelling 'scriptureal') on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam text. The image differs (needle and thread versus walking staff), but the function, received teaching that keeps one safe, is the same.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 727, Raag Tilang, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the walking-stick image matches, but Namdev's support is God's Name, not the counsel of virtuous people.
Moderate: shared idea of timely advice preventing a fall; Hermes is a god rather than a ‘virtuous person’.
Paraphrase; stresses the example rather than the speech of the virtuous, but the protective function matches.

entries.source: Augustine listens to the sermons of Ambrose in Milan
entries.rationale: A close fit, though Augustine was also moved by Neoplatonist writings and by friends, so Ambrose's words were one support among several.

entries.source: Rig Veda 1.89.8; peace invocation of the Mundaka and Prashna Upanishads
entries.rationale: Translations vary, so marked as paraphrase; very close match on hearing good things.
Close on both selectivity and proportional reward for hearing.
Strong thematic match; lacks the ‘however little’ emphasis.
Paraphrase; close on gathering good from all quarters; less explicit about hearing.
Very close — explicitly about hearing a little that is good.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 245 (Samyagjnanasutra); the Prakrit is from the Dasavaikalika Sutra 4 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam text. Strong on hearing as the root of good, but the verse lacks the kural's stress on how even a little hearing is enough. The Dasavaikalika origin is the standard attribution and was not checked separately.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 6), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near match on how much even a little good hearing yields; the teaching meant is specifically the Guru's.
Inverse illustration — about what not to hear rather than the value of a little good hearing.
Paraphrase; concerns reading as well as hearing, but the ‘small portion, large benefit’ logic matches.

entries.source: Booker T. Washington overhears talk of Hampton Institute in a coal mine
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of how even a little good hearing can lead to greatness, though it rests largely on Washington's own autobiography.
Paraphrase; matches the method (careful hearing and inquiry) but not the claim about not speaking foolishly when mistaken.
Close on stored inner resources shaping speech; lacks the ‘even when mistaken’ nuance.
Paraphrase; concerns guarding speech but not the role of accumulated hearing.
Paraphrase; strong match on the disciplined speech of those trained in hearing.
Paraphrase; matches ‘careful examination of what is heard’, less the claim about speech.

entries.source: Saman Suttam v. 246 (Samyagjnanasutra) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam text. Reasonable but partial fit: it speaks of steadiness in conduct, not of avoiding foolish speech after a mistake.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 11), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it shares the idea of depth gained through listening, but says nothing about guarding against foolish speech after a mistake.
Moderate; Nestor exemplifies wise speech from long experience, though his advice here is ignored.
Paraphrase (standard Ross wording closely followed); concerns experience broadly rather than hearing specifically.

entries.source: Kepler refuses to ignore an eight-minute error in the orbit of Mars
entries.rationale: Fits the kural's point that thorough examination keeps errors from becoming folly, but Kepler's learning came from study and observation rather than the hearing this chapter praises.
Paraphrase; close on hearing-without-understanding.
Near one-to-one match on the core paradox.
Close match on functional deafness of unreceptive ears.
Very close match.
Strong match on exposure without reception.

entries.source: Naladiyar, ch. 33 'Defective knowledge', stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Close fit on hearing without taking anything in. This is a Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 922, Raag Raamkalee, Anand Sahib (pauri 37), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near match on the true purpose of the ear; the Truth meant is God's Name, not instruction in general.
Good illustration, though the failure is caused by a curse rather than lack of instruction.
Paraphrase of the fragment (translations vary); a near one-to-one match.
Illustrates hearing without truly hearing, but the kural concerns a lifelong failure to be shaped by instruction, and responsibility for the disaster was shared and complex.
Paraphrase; pairs learning with gentle speech but does not state the causal claim explicitly.
Close match on hearing preceding restrained speech.
Matches humble speech arising from wise instruction; the ‘refined hearing’ element is implicit.
Good match on hearing and restrained speech.
Paraphrase; close on learned humility in speech.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.10–13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com; the ellipses mark omitted items from the list. A good thematic fit, but the verse lists virtues and does not say that learning produces courteous speech.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on humble speech as a mark of worth, but Guru Nanak does not trace humility to listening.
Moderate illustration; not a direct statement of the principle.

entries.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.23
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a widely cited anecdote; close in spirit.

entries.source: Gandhi spends a year listening before taking part in Indian politics
entries.rationale: A clear case of deliberate listening shaping restrained speech, though Gandhi was already experienced and widely respected, so the year refined rather than created his humility.
Paraphrase of a well-known subhashita; strong match, though it names dharma rather than hearing.
Close on appetite-driven life; lacks the ear/hearing contrast.
Near one-to-one: unhearing ears and comparison with animals.
Strong on the beast comparison; hearing is not mentioned explicitly.
Very close: the ‘little-heard’ person likened to an animal living only for the body.

entries.source: Naladiyar, ch. 33 'Defective knowledge', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The closing question is nearly identical to the kural's, but the Naladiyar's target is people who ignore mortality, not people who prefer the palate to the ear. This is a Tamil Jain text.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on rejecting the palate's pleasures for higher nourishment, but the shabad is about the Name, not hearing, and it has no beast image.
Strong imagery match (tasteless ears made bestial); the context is music rather than wisdom.
Paraphrase; strong match on appetite-bound life as bestial.

entries.source: Crassus rejects advice before the Battle of Carrhae
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the kural condemns a whole life lived without cultivating the ear, while this is a single refusal of advice reported mainly by Plutarch.
Protection-by-understanding matches well. The Gita's context is spiritual liberation from fear, not the Kural's worldly and political ruin. The fortress image is absent.
Strong match on wisdom that enemies cannot overcome. In Luke the wisdom is divinely given for the moment, whereas the Kural means a cultivated personal faculty.
Narrative illustration, not a direct statement. The 'protection from ruin' half matches; the 'fortress enemies cannot breach' half is only implied.
Very close in theme: wisdom as the real city-defence, better than weapons. Paraphrased rather than quoted.
Remarkably close: both texts pair a fortress with a weapon, and both locate them in the mind and wisdom.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (diacritic asterisks removed). The fortress-plus-weapon pairing matches the Kural's karuvi/aran image very closely, though Nami's 'fortress' is faith and self-control rather than discernment (arivu) as such.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 574, Raag Vadhans, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on wisdom as a weapon; Gurbani's enemy is spiritual death and the vices rather than worldly ruin, and the fortress image is absent.
Illustrates wisdom as a weapon against destruction. Odysseus's metis is craftier and more trickster-like than Valluvar's ethical arivu, and the 'inner fortress' image is missing.
Very close image (inner citadel). The Stoic emphasis is on freedom from passion, while the Kural emphasises discernment. Quote abridged from the Long translation.
A vivid picture of wisdom as weapon and defence, but the kural's fortress is an inner one that cannot be taken, whereas Syracuse eventually fell.
Very close structure: restrain the wandering senses and mind, and choose the good over the merely pleasant. Paraphrased because translations vary.
Same two-part movement away from evil and toward good. Paul does not name the wandering mind or present this as the definition of wisdom.
Good match on restraining inclination. The Qur'an grounds this in fear of God, not in 'wisdom' as such.
Close in substance (mastering impulse), but Avot calls this 'might' rather than 'wisdom'. Paraphrased.
Near match: a wise person governing a fickle mind. The 'away from evil, toward good' direction is implicit.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one: knowledge restrains the wandering mind and keeps it on the right path, matching both the restraining and the redirecting halves of the Kural.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1022, Raag Maaroo (Solhe), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on wisdom restraining the wandering mind; the Kural also stresses steering the mind toward the good, which this line leaves implicit.

entries.source: Prodicus, 'The Choice of Heracles', as retold in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
entries.rationale: Good illustration of choosing the good over the pleasant. It is a single decisive choice rather than the ongoing steering of the mind the Kural describes.
Structural parallel is strong. Plato's tripartite soul is more elaborate than Valluvar's simple mind/wisdom pairing.

entries.source: Ignatius of Loyola learns to read the movements of his mind
entries.rationale: A close illustration of wisdom governing the wandering mind, framed in Ignatius's specifically Christian terms.
Matches the 'from anyone' half but not the critical 'discern the true substance' half. The popular rendering differs from literal translations (e.g. Griffith), so it is paraphrased.
Very close in method (test everything). It does not make the 'regardless of who speaks' point explicit.
Strong match on listening critically and following the best. The source-independence point is implicit.
Near match on source-independence of wisdom. Avot emphasises humility in learning; the Kural emphasises critical discernment. Paraphrased.
Very close parallel on independence from speaker authority. Paraphrased from the Thanissaro translation.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Good thematic fit, but the verse is about discerning the Law (dharma) behind differing rules, not a general maxim about weighing every speaker's claims. Jain anekantavada would also fit this Kural but is not quoted here.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 711, Raag Todee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: both value the power to discern truth, but Gurbani presents it as the Guru's gift and does not address weighing claims regardless of who speaks.
A negative example rather than a direct teaching. In the myth the disbelief is imposed by a divine curse, not by the listeners' own failure of judgment alone.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.6, 1096a (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Strong match on truth over persons. Aristotle's context is a philosophical disagreement with a revered teacher, which narrows the Kural's general principle.

entries.source: Ibn al-Haytham tests the authorities on light and vision
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's call to judge claims on their merits rather than by the authority of the speaker.
Partial match. It addresses the ethics of pleasing, beneficial speech but not clarity of explanation, and it omits the listening half entirely.
Good on speaking aptly to each listener. The subtle-listening half is only implied.
Matches the effective-speech half and explicitly names wisdom. The subtle-listening half is absent.
Good two-way match covering both listening and speaking. Avot emphasises etiquette and order more than the Kural's clarity and subtle perception. Paraphrased.
Matches the effective-explanation half. It lacks the explicit instruction to perceive subtle meaning in others' words.

Paraphrase of an episode read in full on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the lecture models clear speech and subtle understanding without stating them as a teaching on communication. Jacobi's own note says Gautama 'at once understands the true meaning of the similes.'

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: both judge speech, but Guru Nanak's standard is honour and truth, not clarity, and the Kural's second half on subtle listening is missing.
Illustrates persuasive, audience-fit speech but not subtle listening. Nestor's advice is also sometimes ignored.
Strong conceptual parallel covering both audience-fit speech and insight into others. Plato is theorising an art of rhetoric, while the Kural gives a trait of character.

entries.source: Kennedy answers Khrushchev's first letter in the Cuban Missile Crisis
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of skilled two-way communication, though the outcome also depended on a private concession and on Khrushchev's own choices.
Strong match to the equanimity reading. It misses the traditional commentary's specific focus on constancy in friendship with the great.
Good match to the friendship-constancy reading. It does not link this to 'wisdom' or to choosing eminent friends.
Matches the equanimity reading well but not the friendship reading.
Close match to the constancy-in-friendship reading. Paraphrased; numbering varies between 5:16 and 5:19 in some editions.
Very close to the traditional friendship reading. Paraphrased from Narada Thera's translation.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong match for the first half (befriending the worthy); the Kural's second half, steadiness in friendship without blooming and closing, has no direct counterpart here.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on steady friendship; Guru Nanak speaks of the companions who stand by the soul at the divine reckoning, read by some commentators as one's good deeds.
Illustrates steadfast friendship. It is not framed as 'wisdom', and the 'befriending the great' element is absent.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.3, 1156b (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Very close to the traditional reading (befriend the good; the friendship stays constant). Quote abridged from the Ross translation.

entries.source: The friendship of Goethe and Schiller
entries.rationale: A fine example of a lasting friendship between worthy men, though here each was the great one for the other rather than one person befriending the eminent.
Close in advising the wise to act in harmony with society. The Gita's aim is to avoid confusing the unenlightened, a more pedagogical motive than the Kural's.
Strong match on adaptive conduct. Paul's goal is evangelistic, while the Kural's is general social wisdom.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, no. 127 (saying of Ali)
entries.rationale: Matches the adaptive principle but is limited to speech. It is a Companion's saying, not a prophetic one. Paraphrased; translations vary.
Very close parallel ('do not deviate from custom'). Paraphrased.
Striking match, including the 'wise of the world' nuance. It concerns agreement in statements rather than conduct generally. Paraphrased.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, ch. 1 (the mārgānusārī qualities of the householder); paraphrased
entries.rationale: Next-best match. The list item on following approved social customs was confirmed only from a search summary of a jainworld.com page that would not load, so it is paraphrased and no verse number is given. Canonical scripture has no clear maxim on conforming to the world, and monastic texts stress renouncing it.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: both endorse engaged life in the world, but the Kural speaks of conforming to the worthy, while Guru Nanak speaks of service and honour before God.
Adaptability matches. Odysseus's flexibility is often strategic deception, which is more cunning than the Kural's harmonious conduct.

entries.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part 3
entries.rationale: Close parallel: conform to the customs of the most sensible. Paraphrased.

entries.source: Matteo Ricci adopts the ways of Chinese scholars
entries.rationale: A close illustration of adapting one's conduct to the settled ways of the worthy, though Ricci's ultimate aim was missionary.
Captures foresight of consequences indirectly. The Gita is classifying kinds of happiness, not directly defining wisdom as foresight.
Good match on foresight of outcomes. It is used as an analogy for counting the cost of discipleship.
Close in contrasting forward-looking wisdom with folly. The foresight is eschatological, not worldly. The hadith's chain is graded hasan by Tirmidhi but weak by some scholars. Paraphrased.
Near-verbatim conceptual parallel. Paraphrased from the Hebrew; English renderings vary.
Good match on foresight. The sutta is a meditation practice, not a definition of wisdom. Paraphrased from the Thanissaro translation.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Partial fit: the foresight here is specifically awareness of death and the urgency of spiritual effort, not the general practical judgment of consequences meant in the Porutpal context.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on timely foresight; in Gurbani it is mindfulness of God and duty rather than worldly prediction of consequences.
Near-perfect mythic embodiment of the Kural's foresight/folly opposition.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6.5, 1140a (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Strong on practical wisdom generally. Foresight is implied in deliberation rather than named as the defining trait. Quote abridged.

entries.source: Themistocles persuades Athens to build a fleet from its silver
entries.rationale: A strong example of foresight, though the stated purpose was the war with Aegina, so how clearly Themistocles foresaw the Persian threat is partly a judgement of later historians.
Near-exact conceptual match, since both place knowing what to fear within buddhi/arivu.
Strong structural match on calibrating fear. The object of right fear is divine judgment, whereas the Kural's is general.
Close link between knowledge and right fear. The object is specifically God, not dangers in general.
Near-perfect match of the wise/fool contrast on fear.
Near-verbatim conceptual parallel.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the verse teaches pervasive caution and does not contrast fearing the right things with the wrong ones as the Kural's chiasmus does, and the danger in view is spiritual (karmic bondage), not worldly.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 151, Raag Gauree Gwaarayree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: both treat rightly placed fear as wisdom, but the Kural means prudent fear of harmful acts, while Gurbani's bhau is reverent awe of God that frees one from other fears.
Clear narrative illustration of fearless folly. Daedalus embodies the wise fear only implicitly.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 3.7, 1115b (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Very close parallel. Aristotle frames it as courage while Valluvar frames it as wisdom, but the calibration of fear is identical.

entries.source: John Snow has the Broad Street pump handle removed
entries.rationale: A good fit for well-placed fear, though the removal came after the outbreak had peaked and the popular story has been simplified over time.
Very close narrative embodiment. The Panchatantra is a niti-shastra (practical wisdom) text, in the same genre as Porutpal.
Strong match on advance preparation making one unshakable. In the parable the 'foundation' is obedience to Jesus's words.
Matches the forward-looking preparation. The Qur'an's 'tomorrow' is primarily eschatological rather than worldly calamity.
Near-exact parallel.
Good match on advance guarding and its protection. The context is spiritual opportunity rather than worldly calamity.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.4.1, I.3.4.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit in structure. Jacobi's footnote explains the 'danger' as heaping up karma, so the protection meant is spiritual rather than against worldly calamity.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 819, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: the result (calamity cannot touch one) matches, but the protection comes from God's refuge, not from the person's own foresight.
Close narrative match of foresight plus precaution.
Very close. Seneca emphasises psychological preparation, the Kural both practical and mental. Paraphrased.

entries.source: Amundsen's carefully prepared journey to the South Pole
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of foresight turned into protection, though the false start shows that even careful planners can misjudge conditions.
Matches the supremacy of knowledge. The Gita's jnana is spiritual knowledge, while the Kural's arivu is practical wisdom. The 'fool has nothing' half is absent.
Strong narrative match. In the story riches are added as a divine reward rather than flowing from wisdom itself.
Close. The Qur'an says 'much good' rather than 'everything', and does not state the 'fool has nothing' converse.
Near-verbatim parallel of both halves. Paraphrased from the Aramaic; renderings vary.
Captures the supremacy of wisdom over quantity of life. It speaks of years rather than possessions.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.3.4.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the Acaranga speaks of the unity of true knowledge (an epistemological and soteriological claim), while the Kural says wisdom is worth more than every other possession.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit for the Kural's negative half; the positive claim that the wise possess everything is not stated, and the wisdom meant is the Guru's.
Symbolic parallel: sovereignty secured by internalising wisdom. The myth is also about preventing a successor, so the match is partial.
Very close philosophical parallel to both halves. Paraphrased from the Jowett translation.

entries.source: Japan's Charter Oath pledges to seek knowledge throughout the world
entries.rationale: Next-best only: it concerns a state's pursuit of knowledge rather than personal wisdom, and the Meiji reforms also had military and political aims.
Strong overlap on the triad of faults; the Gita frames it theologically (envy of God), the Kural politically (dignity of prosperity).
Two of the three faults match (lust, pride); anger is absent and the focus is world-renunciation rather than dignified prosperity.
Matches only the anger element (plus generosity, which anticipates Kurals 432 and 437); arrogance and lust are not named here.
Strong structural parallel (triad of ruinous faults); envy replaces anger.
Close match on faults; the goal differs (liberation versus honourable worldly success).

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit: pride, anger and craving appear in both lists. The Jain verse adds delusion, and its aim is liberation rather than a ruler's honoured prosperity.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 932, Raag Raamkalee (Dakhanee Oankaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on two of the Kural's three faults (lust and anger); arrogance is not named in this line, and the Guru speaks of spiritual ruin rather than a ruler's honour.
Illustrates only the arrogance element, by counter-example; anger and lust are not in view.
Conceptual parallel; Plato’s framework is psychological theory rather than a list of faults, and arrogance is not separately treated.

entries.source: Louis IX hears his subjects' cases himself at Vincennes
entries.rationale: Shows a ruler honoured for restraint and fairness, but the sources document his justice and piety more than the specific absence of all three faults the kural names.
Matches the false-pride element only; avarice and unworthy joy are not in this verse, and the Gita is not addressed to rulers specifically.
Close on leadership framing, avarice and improper pleasure (wine); false pride is covered only indirectly (1 Tim 3:6 warns against being ‘lifted up with pride’).
Strong match on all three faults in one figure; Qarun is a wealthy man of influence rather than a king.
Strong structural match (rules for the ruler’s character); the Torah targets accumulation rather than miserly refusal to give.

entries.source: Dasa-rājadhamma, Jātaka commentary (e.g. Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka, J 534)
entries.rationale: Good thematic match as the virtue side of the Kural’s vices; paraphrased list, not a verbatim quote, and the exact Jātaka location is given as a commonly cited example.

Checked word for word on jainworld.com's Saman Suttam (Samyamasutra) page. Reasonable but partial: it covers avarice and pride but not the Kural's third fault (unworthy delight), and it is not addressed to rulers.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Matches only the pride element of the Kural's triad; avarice and unseemly delight are not addressed, and the Gurbani point is spiritual rather than political.
Legendary history rather than myth; matches pride and unworthy delight, but Croesus is famous for lavish giving, not avarice.
Paraphrase. Plato’s remedy is structural (no property), while the Kural targets the ruler’s inner vice; pride and unworthy joy are not addressed.

entries.source: King Farouk of Egypt is forced to abdicate
entries.rationale: A clear case of unworthy pleasures harming a ruler; the sources stress extravagance more than avarice, so the kural's triad is matched only in part.
Matches the fear-of-disgrace motive; the Gita does not make the small-fault-as-large-fault comparison.
Strong match on the significance of small faults; the shame motive is not explicit.
Near one-to-one match of the magnification image; note this portion is Ibn Mas‘ud’s own saying within the narration.
Close in principle; the Mishnah speaks of commandments to keep rather than faults to avoid.
Strong match on refusing to minimise small faults; the Dhammapada argues by accumulation, the Kural by perception and shame.

Checked word for word on jainworld.com's Saman Suttam (Samyamasutra) page. Near one-to-one on magnifying small faults, though the Kural's motive is shame before blame, while the Jain verse rests on the danger of growth.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1364, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on magnifying one's own faults; Kabir's line is about humility before God and others, without the Kural's explicit dread of public disgrace.
Matches the role of shame as a guardian against wrong; there is no small-versus-large fault imagery.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.9 (tr. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Defines the Kural’s motive (fear of disgrace) precisely, but Aristotle does not praise magnifying small faults and treats shame as below full virtue.

entries.source: Hugh Dalton resigns over a budget leak
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's scale contrast between a tiny fault and a huge response, though sources note political pressure as well as conscience behind the resignation.
Strong match on the inner-enemy idea; the Gita names one specific fault rather than fault in general.
Strong imagery match (fault as hostile predator to be mastered); shared by Jewish and Christian readers.
Good match on the inner source of fault; the Quran stresses reliance on divine mercy, the Kural on self-guarding.
Close on the inner enemy and the need for ongoing protection; the Talmud’s remedy is specifically Torah study.
Very close parallel; the Kural adds the practical command to make guarding one’s chief aim.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on fault as the true enemy; the Kural's added advice to guard against fault as one's chief aim (or treasure) is implied here, not stated.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A close parallel: both treat inner faults as the real enemy; the Kural frames this as political prudence, Gurbani as the struggle against haumai and the five vices.
Paraphrase. Agamemnon partly shifts blame onto Atē, which is almost the opposite of the Kural’s call for self-responsibility.
Implicit parallel only; Socrates states the corollary (outside harm is powerless) rather than naming fault as the enemy.

entries.source: Sakichi Toyoda builds looms that stop themselves at the first fault
entries.rationale: A precise mechanical picture of treating faults as the real enemy, though it concerns manufacturing defects rather than the moral faults of a ruler.

entries.source: Panchatantra, Book I (fable of the three fish)
entries.rationale: Very close on foresight versus delay; the danger in the fable is external rather than a personal fault.
Near-direct parallel on foresight; the Kural’s fire-and-straw image stresses the speed of ruin.
Matches forethought and self-examination; the ‘tomorrow’ here is primarily the Hereafter rather than worldly ruin.
Strong match on foresight regarding one’s own conduct; no image of sudden ruin.
Good match on constant pre-emptive guarding; the ruin envisaged is rebirth in hell rather than a worldly collapse.

Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit in imagery and in the logic of prevention, though the Jain verse is about the senses and diet specifically, while the Kural speaks of faults in general.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 63, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: The straw-in-fire image matches closely, but Gurbani's cause of ruin is forgetting the Naam rather than failing to foresee faults, so the parallel is partial.
Excellent match on foresight versus hindsight; the harm is cosmic rather than a personal fault.

entries.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger) I.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
entries.rationale: Very close on pre-emptive guarding; Seneca discusses anger specifically, the Kural faults in general.

entries.source: The Chernobyl reactor explodes during a safety test
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of the cost of failing to prevent faults in advance, though the kural speaks of a person's life and character rather than an institution's safety system.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section LXXIV (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match, including the royal addressee and the small/large contrast (compare also Kural 433).
Near-exact parallel; the Kural applies it specifically to a ruler.
Very close match; this is a saying of the Companion Abu Hurayra, not attributed to the Prophet in this narration.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 107b (also Bava Batra 60b)
entries.rationale: Near-exact match on sequence and on the legitimacy of the judge.
Very close; Dhp 50 (‘let one see one’s own acts, done and undone’) gives the positive instruction.
Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: it puts self-correction first but does not speak of then judging others' faults, which is the Kural's second step.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on looking at one's own faults before others'; Farid advises refraining from judging others at all, while the Kural permits judging once one's own faults are gone.

entries.source: Phaedrus, Fables IV.10 (tr. H. T. Riley; Aesopic, Perry 266)
entries.rationale: Very close; a fable of the Aesopic tradition in Latin verse rather than myth proper.

entries.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger) III.36 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
entries.rationale: Strong on self-examination; Seneca does not state the second step (then judging others).

entries.source: Pope John Paul II's Day of Pardon
entries.rationale: Shows self-scrutiny placed before judgement of others, but it was an act of confession for an institution's past rather than a ruler's personal programme of reform.

entries.source: Bhartṛhari, Nītiśataka (verse on the three fates of wealth, c. 43 in common editions)
entries.rationale: Very close in logic; paraphrased because the exact English translation used was not verified, and verse numbering varies by edition.
Strong match on hoarded wealth perishing; James adds divine judgement.

entries.source: Quran 9:34 (Sahih International, latter part of verse)
entries.rationale: Good match on the fault; the consequence is punishment in the Hereafter rather than the wealth itself perishing.
Very close parallel on kept wealth perishing uselessly.

entries.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.19, Aputtaka Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match on the fate of a miser’s wealth.

entries.source: Acaranga Sutra I.2.1.4 and I.2.3.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close fit. The Jain remedy, however, is non-possession (aparigraha) rather than the Kural's right use of wealth through giving and enjoyment.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1252, Raag Saarang, Bhagat Namdev (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one on hoarded wealth coming to nothing; Namdev's remedy is the Saadh Sangat and remembrance of God rather than the Kural's giving and enjoyment, though Sikh teaching also enjoins vand chhakna (sharing).
Illustrates useless wealth and greed; Midas is greedy rather than stingy, and his wealth is not lost.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.5 (tr. W. D. Ross)
