entries.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased. Same idea of self-inflicted loss through carelessness, but it is about time, not fame.
Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a single lapse of attention, not a lack of ability, destroyed a man's good name.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: A nīti authority naming faults of heedlessness as barriers to success; it does not speak of fame or make the Kural's appeal to consensus.
Matches the universal scope and the demand for vigilance; it says nothing about fame.
A strong condemnation of heedlessness; the Kural's specific point about fame and scholarly consensus is not present.

entries.source: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, Mesillat Yesharim, chs. 1-2 (on Zehirut); Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 20b
entries.rationale: Paraphrased summary. Watchfulness is foundational in both, but Luzzatto's goal is holiness, not fame.
Very close: a general verdict that heedlessness is never praised.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse stresses heedfulness because life is fleeting, not because of fame or the agreement of all treatises.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 17, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the fate of the forgetful is shared, but Gurbani speaks of standing before God, not fame, and does not appeal to the agreement of all treatises.
A classic image of pleasure-induced forgetfulness; the link to fame has to be inferred.

entries.source: Pierre Hadot, Philosophy as a Way of Life, ed. Arnold I. Davidson (Blackwell, 1995), essay ‘Spiritual Exercises’
entries.rationale: A secondary-source summary. Good support for the broad consensus on attention, but it doesn't discuss fame.

entries.source: Henri Becquerel develops the plates he had put away
entries.rationale: Illustrates the kural from the positive side, attentiveness bringing fame, rather than showing heedlessness losing it; the kural's appeal to the agreement of all treatises has no direct parallel.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Both put the inner state before outer circumstance, but the Gita doesn't mention fortresses or heedlessness directly.
Close match on a protected house lost through failure to watch.
Strong match on outward strength failing because of an inner state of complacency.
A good narrative match: a prosperous, secure city destroyed through complacency.
An inner island of heedfulness set against outer defences; a close conceptual fit.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one on outward goods being useless to the careless; the fortress simile is replaced by the image of a lamp going out.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1104, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the futility of fortresses is shared, but Kabir's point is death and transience, not fear or heedlessness.
An excellent illustration of advantages made useless by a lapse in vigilance.

entries.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 20 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased. Shares the insight that fortresses are useless without the right inner condition, though for Machiavelli that condition is popular goodwill, not vigilance.

entries.source: The Dutch raid on the Medway
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of a great advantage made useless by unreadiness; the sources describe the fleet as laid up rather than spelling out the decisions behind it.

entries.source: Panchatantra, Book I (Mitrabheda), the fable of the three fish
entries.rationale: A near-perfect narrative parallel to guarding before trouble arrives; retold in prose.
A very close match on failing to prepare and regretting too late.
Strong match on regret that comes too late after negligence.
Close match on readiness before an unannounced crisis; the parable adds the image of the unprepared fools.
Very close, including the guarded city and the later grief of those who were negligent.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (the bracketed phrase is Jacobi's). Strong fit on regret for neglect, though the trouble in question is death, not an enemy.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on foresight versus regret after the blow; the forethought Gurbani means is remembrance of God rather than military vigilance.
An almost allegorical match: forgetting a warning, then understanding too late.

entries.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 24 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased. A strong political parallel on failure to prepare in calm times.
Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a known, guardable danger neglected until it could only be mourned.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 8.7 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Both ask for remembrance at all times; the Gita's object is devotional, the Kural's practical.
A direct call to continual vigilance; it doesn't state that nothing else is equal to it.
Close match on constant remembrance as the opposite of heedlessness.
A very close match: lifelong, diligent guarding against forgetfulness.

entries.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.17 (Appamada Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
entries.rationale: An exceptionally close match: heedfulness declared to be the unequalled good, and addressed to a king.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). Near one-to-one on vigilance toward all and at all times.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 21, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on unbroken attention at every moment; the object is God rather than the affairs of state.
A cautionary illustration of constant vigilance and its one fatal lapse, not a statement of its supreme value.
Paraphrased. A strong conceptual match on continuous, unfailing attention.

entries.source: Walsingham's watchfulness uncovers the Babington Plot
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of sustained vigilance in government, though Walsingham's methods included manipulation that the kural does not address.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.35 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Both move from ‘difficult’ to ‘possible’ through a disciplined mind; the Gita's object is mastering the mind itself.
Watchfulness is presented as the remedy for weakness, but the verse is less confident than the Kural about what vigilance can achieve.
Matches on persistent effort overcoming obstacles; the specific instrument of unforgetfulness is not named.
Paraphrased from memory of a well-known passage. Same confidence that diligent effort succeeds, without the Kural's emphasis on memory.
A close match on heedfulness overcoming all obstacles, great and small.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse concerns liberation rather than worldly tasks, and the mind is not explicitly called a tool.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 263, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Good fit on remembrance accomplishing tasks, though Gurbani credits remembrance of God and divine grace rather than human vigilance as the instrument.
An apt image of a tool that secures vigilance against lapse; the idea of an ‘impossible’ task is implied, not stated.
Matches the attentive, careful doing; the promise that nothing is impossible is not stated.

entries.source: Amundsen sails the Gjoa through the Northwest Passage
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of careful, persistent effort accomplishing a task long considered beyond reach.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Shares the call to do one's prescribed duties; the Kural's stress on forgetting them and the seven births are not present.
An exceptionally close match, even treating neglect of known duty as forgetfulness.
Matches on the loss that comes from neglecting good opportunities; it doesn't name specific praised deeds.

entries.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:17, trans. Joshua Kulp
entries.rationale: Clear agreement that deeds, not knowledge, are primary.
Matches the gap between praising and doing; it lacks the Kural's warning about consequences in later births.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong on consequences across births; the Kural's 'things the wise have praised' are kingly duties, whereas here they are religious duties.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1106, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: the warning against neglect is shared, but Kabir's essential duty is naam simran, not the royal duties of statecraft Parimelazhagar has in mind.
Homer himself raises forgetting as a possible cause of the neglected duty; a strong match.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Close match on the failure to do what is known to be good.

entries.source: Takaki Kanehiro's navy diet defeats beriberi
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of neglecting proven good practice; Takaki's own explanation (lack of protein) was later shown to be incomplete, though his remedy worked.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sections 11-17 (the story of Nahusha), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: A classic Indian example of elation leading to heedless ruin, the kind of story the Kural asks rulers to recall.
Nearly identical logic: remembering the fallen as a check on self-confidence.
A strong match of exultation leading to ruin, and the story is presented as a lesson for others.
A close match on the moment of strength becoming the moment of fall.
A strong parallel of success leading to ruin, used explicitly as a warning example.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). Close fit: a powerful king ruined by heedless indulgence.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable: both use the memory of fallen rulers to check elation, but Guru Nanak's lesson is mortality and the vanity of power rather than heedlessness as such.
An excellent illustration of exhilaration leading to forgetting a warning; not itself a teaching about remembering.

entries.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2
entries.rationale: Paraphrased. The same use of fallen examples to check confidence in prosperity.

entries.source: Scipio Aemilianus foresees Rome's own fall at Carthage
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's advice to recall the fallen in the moment of success; the kural stresses heedlessness as the cause of ruin, which Scipio's remark leaves implicit.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sambhava Parva), Drona's test of the Kuru princes, trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: A vivid narrative match for single-minded, unforgetting focus on one's aim.
A close match on unwavering focus on the aim; Paul's goal is spiritual rather than worldly.
Links attainment to what is intended, but the hadith is about the moral worth of deeds, not about achieving goals through sustained attention.
The same pattern of constant focus leading to steadfastness; the object here is God rather than a chosen goal.

entries.source: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta) §3.63, trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story
entries.rationale: The quoted words are the §3.63 exhortation; the final-words connection is noted in prose. Strong match on heedfulness as the means to the goal.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com ('&c.' abbreviates the refrain in the original). It is an exhortation to persevere rather than a statement that steady thought makes success easy.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 262, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: sustained attention is shared, but the Kural's object is any chosen aim while Gurbani's is God and the fruit is inner peace.
A clear negative illustration of losing a sure goal through distraction.

entries.source: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 11 ‘Attention’
entries.rationale: Shares the primacy of sustained attention; James is describing how experience is formed, not a recipe for success.

entries.source: Howard Carter's last season in the Valley of the Kings
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of sustained focus on a goal; the role of luck and of Carnarvon's funding means it is not purely a matter of steady thought.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section LXIX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)

An almost exact match on refusing favouritism in judgment; the investigative steps of the Kural are not in view.
Near one-to-one match on impartial hearing; the Kural adds consultation with the learned before sentencing.
An exceptionally close structural parallel: investigation followed by impartial judgment defines the just man.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse diagnoses the failure the Kural guards against, but Nami speaks as a renouncer who is doubtful about royal punishment altogether rather than as someone setting out a judicial procedure.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1240, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on justice as the king's defining duty; the salok does not describe the Kural's procedure of impartial inquiry and consultation.
Good thematic parallel on impartial judgment, but it concerns judgment of the dead, not a king’s earthly court.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.4, 1132a (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Close on the judge as embodied impartial justice; Aristotle is analysing corrective justice, not giving a procedure.

entries.source: The Supreme Court orders President Nixon to hand over the Watergate tapes

Shares the idea that people depend on the king for security, but lacks the rain comparison and the stress on justice.

Captures the people’s dependence on the ruler’s care; the rain image and the focus on justice are absent.
Same dependence of the people on just rule, without the Kural’s cosmic rain comparison.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 2, part 8 ‘Coronation as king’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 708, Raag Jaithsree (Jaithsree ki Vaar), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the rain-dependence image matches, but Gurbani applies it to devotion to God rather than to subjects and their ruler.
Nearly verbal overlap on the people looking to the just judge-king; the rain comparison is missing.

entries.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 4 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Clemency, Book I). Strong match on the people's total dependence on the ruler; Seneca's image is breath and mind rather than rain, and his stress is on the ruler's direction rather than specifically on just rule.

entries.source: Hammurabi sets up his law code on a public stela
entries.rationale: Shows subjects being invited to look to royal justice; the kural's comparison with all life depending on rain is broader than any single act can show.

entries.rationale: Close: royal power is the support of faith and justice; Maimonides speaks of purpose rather than of foundation.
Good fit on the protective role; the sutta places the Dhamma above the king rather than resting on him.

Good fit on temporal power sustaining religion, though in Sikhism miri is subordinate to and derived from piri, not the source of scripture as Parimelazhagar's Vedic reading implies.

Shares the ‘justice as foundation’ idea but does not mention scriptures or sages.

Close on the embrace of the people; it lacks the second half, the world’s answering loyalty.

A very close match to the Kural’s mutual embrace between ruler and ruled.
A near-exact conditional parallel: serve the people and their lasting loyalty follows.

entries.source: Ashoka, Kalinga Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)
entries.rationale: Strong on the ruler’s embrace; the people’s answering devotion is implied, not stated.

entries.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Ṛṣabha §211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It is a strong example of benevolent kingship, but the text does not state the Kural's reciprocal image of the world clinging to the king's feet.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable: the ideal of gentle rule matches, but many commentators read halemi raj as the inner reign of humility under God rather than an earthly kingdom.

entries.source: Seneca, Of Clemency (De Clementia), Book I, ch. 3 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on Wikisource (Stewart, Of Clemency, Book I); the ellipsis omits a clause about the ruler's daily care for his subjects' safety. Close match on the reciprocity of a caring ruler and devoted subjects.

entries.source: Thailand honours King Chulalongkorn, the Great Beloved King
entries.rationale: A close and almost literal fit to the image of the world clinging to the feet of a king who embraced his people.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section LXIX (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Very close: the same section explicitly ties seasonable rain and crops to the king’s just rule.
Shared link between righteous rule and fertility; in Isaiah the fruitfulness follows an outpouring of the spirit, not the king alone.
Parallel on moral order bringing sky-and-earth blessing; it concerns the community’s faith, not the ruler’s justice.
Very close in the pairing of seasonal rain and harvest; the condition is the nation’s obedience, not the king’s rule.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.70, Adhammika Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
entries.rationale: Near-perfect match: the king’s righteousness leads causally to rain and ripe crops.

entries.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 105, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: Gurbani makes no causal link between a ruler's justice and rainfall; only the rain-as-blessing image is shared.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225–233 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Very close: straight justice by rulers is tied directly to the fertility of the land.

entries.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus (The Economist), ch. IV, 8 (tr. H. G. Dakyns)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim in Dakyns' translation on Project Gutenberg (eBook #1173). Partial match: the link between good government and abundant harvests is explicit, but it works through policy and oversight, with no cosmic or seasonal element.

entries.source: Todar Mal's revenue settlement under Akbar
entries.rationale: No ruler can bring rain, so this is a next-best example of lawful rule bound up with agriculture rather than a demonstration of the kural's claim that just rule brings good seasons.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Section 14 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: A very close match on victory flowing from righteousness rather than force; this maxim is famous in Sanskrit as yato dharmas tato jayaḥ.
Matches the denial of military power; the psalm points to God’s care rather than to the king’s justice.

entries.source: Ibn Taymiyya, as cited from Majmu‘ al-Fatawa and his writings on public order (hisba)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit, but it is a medieval jurist’s maxim known through secondary citation, not scripture, and is paraphrased here.
Shares the rejection of might, but credits divine spirit rather than just rule; a looser parallel.

entries.source: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII (trans. S. Dhammika)
entries.rationale: Close match of righteousness over arms as the true source of victory.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 5, part 11 ‘The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase. The chapter's contents were confirmed this session only through a search excerpt of the wisdomlib text. The story rejects the spear as the Kural does, but it puts restraint and renunciation in the sceptre's place, not just rule.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1088, Raag Maaroo (Maaroo ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: both set righteousness above force, but Guru Nanak speaks of spiritual sovereignty and does not discuss military victory.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 276–280 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Shares justice-over-force, but concerns human life in general rather than a king’s victory.

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book II, §23 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))

entries.source: James II's army melts away in the Glorious Revolution
entries.rationale: A strong, near-literal illustration: military force failed a ruler whose people judged his rule unjust.

Close: justice given by the king becomes the guarantee of his own throne.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda (the story of Nriga, told by Rama)

entries.source: Ashoka, Kalinga Rock Edict I (trans. S. Dhammika)
entries.rationale: Matches the condemnation of neglected justice; addressed to officials, and the king’s self-ruin is not in view.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 145, Raag Maajh (Majh ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Plutarch, Life of Demetrius, ch. 42 (tr. Bernadotte Perrin)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (Perrin, Loeb 1920); inner double quotation marks rendered as single quotes. entries.source: The Wanli Emperor withdraws from government

Close on the legitimacy of government restraint; it does not mention the ruler’s duty to guard from outside.

entries.source: Ashoka, Pillar Edict IV (trans. S. Dhammika)

entries.rationale: Next-best only: the destructiveness of anger is shared, but the verse has nothing on failing to consult counsellors, which is half of the Kural's point.

Paraphrase of a very apt anecdote; the loss is moral and reputational rather than financial.

entries.source: Ibrahim Lodi alienates his nobles and loses the Delhi Sultanate

entries.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section LVII (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Matches the chapter-level reading of the couplet (loyalty as defence) more than its literal fortification sense.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.20-22 (cf. 9.18) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Cicero, De Officiis 2.24–25 (trans. W. Miller, Loeb)
entries.rationale: Captures the reversal of fear onto the ruler; Cicero does not discuss wartime defences.

entries.source: France enters the Franco-German War unprepared and the Second Empire falls
entries.rationale: A strong fit for swift ruin through lack of preparation; the chapter's link between unpreparedness and earlier rule by dread is not part of this example.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1288, Raag Malaar (Malaar ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.rationale: Matches the burden image only; the Cypria blames humanity in general, not tyrants and their agents.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 1 (description of Rama’s qualities); tradition of Rama-rajya
entries.rationale: Thematic parallel on the gracious king; the Ramayana does not state that the world exists because of this quality.

entries.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Vijay K. Jain's translation on wisdomlib. Pujyapada's gloss also notes that beings cause each other pain, so the sutra describes mutual dependence as much as kindness.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Raag Maajh (Baarah Maahaa), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Close in political context; Seneca speaks of clemency toward offenders, a narrower sense than kannottam.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.9; cf. 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
entries.rationale: Verse 4.9 checked word for word on sacred-texts.com, and 4.6 is paraphrased from the same page. Two of the Kural's four vices (procrastination, sleep) are covered; forgetfulness and the boat image are not.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 726, Raag Tilang, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable: heedlessness and sleep match two of the Kural's four failings, but the Kural analyses worldly ruin and Gurbani's sleep is spiritual unawareness.

entries.source: Seneca, De Brevitate Vitae 9 (trans. J. W. Basore)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased; strong on procrastination but does not address the other three vices.

entries.source: The Swiss watch industry is overtaken by the quartz watch
entries.rationale: A reasonable illustration of procrastination and complacency leading toward ruin; the kural's other two vices, sloth and oversleeping, are not part of this story, and recession also played a role.
Near one-to-one, and also addressed to kings; the only difference is phrasing.
Near one-to-one: great resources entrusted to the lazy produce nothing.
Strong principle match; the verse’s primary context is moral accountability before God.

entries.source: Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta (trans. Nārada Thera)
entries.rationale: Very close in substance; paraphrased because the passage was not re-fetched.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Sikhism: Guru Angad” (W. H. McLeod) (paraphrase)

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8, 1098b-1099a (trans. W. D. Ross)

entries.source: Commodus inherits the Roman Empire from Marcus Aurelius
entries.rationale: A strong fit for squandered inheritance through neglect of duty, though Commodus was energetic in his own pursuits rather than idle in the ordinary sense.

entries.source: Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva 133-136 (Vidulā-putra-anuśāsana), trans. K. M. Ganguli

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.16; cf. 27.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a narrative example of the scorn the lazy earn, close to the Kural, though set among monks rather than in society at large.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Paraphrased; a self-rebuke rather than reproach from others.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 600, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

entries.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 14 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased; very close in substance, though Machiavelli focuses on military neglect.

entries.source: Aesop, Hercules and the Waggoner (trans. G. F. Townsend)
entries.rationale: A Greek fable featuring a mythic figure; strong on self-help but has no family dimension.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1, 1103a-b (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased; supplies the theory behind the Kural’s remedy rather than a direct parallel.

entries.source: The idle young Charles Darwin becomes a dedicated naturalist
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of turning from idleness to effort and redeeming a family's hopes; the young Darwin's pastimes were energetic sport rather than inactivity.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra VI.8 (Mahāpadmacakricaritra), vv. 148-203 (tr. Helen M. Johnson, vol. IV, pp. 99-102); also Vividhatīrthakalpa (Hastināpura-kalpa)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase. entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib (Pauri 28), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: both promise the world to the one who masters himself, but the Kural's reward is a king's dominion, framed by a Vaishnava allusion Sikhism does not share, while Guru Nanak's is inner victory.
Loose thematic parallel; Heracles’ reward is divinity, and his labours were imposed rather than chosen.

entries.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased; close in claim (industry wins all), though addressed to ordinary people rather than kings.

entries.source: Alexander the Great's campaigns from Macedonia to India

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, pauri 15), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Shares the refusal to call a hard task impossible, but in Gurbani the victory comes through devotion to the Guru rather than through the person's own exertion, which is the Kural's point.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 286-292 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)

Very close in thought; paraphrased because the English wording was not checked against a live text.

entries.source: Diderot carries the Encyclopedie through to completion after it is banned

Vivid reversal story, though achieved by cunning and violence rather than the Kural’s simple refusal to be grieved.
Explains the mechanism behind the Kural’s claim, but lacks its striking image of trouble itself being defeated.

entries.source: Karoly Takacs wins Olympic gold shooting with his other hand
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's reversal, in which the misfortune rather than the man ends up defeated.
Shares steadfast labour despite setbacks; the Gita stresses detachment from results, the Kural sheer perseverance.
Shared agricultural image of unwavering forward effort; Jesus’ subject is discipleship, not adversity as such.
Captures relentless toil toward an end, but says nothing of trouble being defeated; a next-best match.
Good on persistent labour; lacks the Kural’s specific claim that persistence defeats trouble.
Near-identical animal-in-mire image; the Buddhist ‘bog’ is moral defilement rather than worldly obstacle.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (quoted with omissions marked). The bull appears only as one simile in a list; the Kural's picture of hauling through mire is not present, so the match is partial.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji Sahib (pauri 16), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the shared image is the patient bull bearing a heavy load, but Guru Nanak uses it to explain dharma and cosmic order, not personal endurance of hardship, and he goes on to question the literal myth.
Good image of brute perseverance through a blocked road, though Apollonius credits divine guidance too.
Shared bovine emblem of strength under pressure; Epictetus’ bull confronts a foe rather than hauling through ruts.

entries.source: The Overland Telegraph is pushed through Australia's wet season
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of persistence through repeated physical obstacles; sources differ slightly on how many months late the northern section was.
Excellent match for successive heaped troubles; the story’s explicit virtue is truthfulness more than cheerfulness.
Near one-to-one match on multiplied troubles that fail to destroy; Paul attributes his resilience to God’s power.
Strong on multiple trials and steadfastness; the Qur’an adds surrender to God, which the Kural does not mention.
Very close on heaped calamities; later chapters show Job in anguish, so the unbroken calm is only true of the prologue.
Good image of steadiness under repeated assault; the verse names praise and blame rather than calamity in general.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2, closing verse (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked on sacred-texts.com; Jacobi writes 'Kâ*s*yapa' (i.e. Mahavira), normalised here to Kâśyapa. Strong thematic fit; it does not explicitly mention troubles coming in succession.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Zafarnamah', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on unbroken spirit under successive calamities; the events are well attested, the Zafarnamah is preserved in the Dasam Granth, whose compilation is debated among Sikhs, and the Guru's inner state is described from Sikh tradition.
Strong match on successive imposed trials; Heracles triumphs by strength more than by the inner calm the Kural praises.
Close in spirit; Seneca stresses misfortune as a test, the Kural misfortune’s own defeat.

entries.source: Humayun loses his empire and regains Delhi years later
entries.rationale: A clear case of unbroken persistence through stacked misfortunes, though the sources document his actions rather than his inner state.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.71 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
entries.rationale: Close: absence of proprietorship leads to peace; the Gita frames it as a spiritual discipline rather than a worldly safeguard.
Strong on joy without possessions; Paul’s paradox is rooted in spiritual riches, not in prior non-attachment to wealth.
Near one-to-one match linking lack of exultation in gain with lack of despair in loss.
Shared ideal of contentment; the Mishnah does not address the moment of loss directly.
Captures freedom from grief through non-possession; the Kural addresses lay wealth, the Dhammapada monastic renunciation.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one on non-possessiveness preventing grief at loss; Nami has fully renounced, whereas the Kural speaks of not clinging.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 5), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one: both trace grief at loss to possessive clinging; Guru Arjan's ground for letting go is that everything belongs to God, a theistic reason the Kural does not give.
Good picture of contented non-attachment; the story concerns hospitality more than the experience of losing wealth.
Very close: both trace grief in loss to possessiveness in gain.

entries.source: Chuck Feeney gives away his fortune and lives modestly
entries.rationale: Next-best only: Feeney shows the detachment the kural praises, but he gave his wealth away rather than losing it, so the couplet's scene of misfortune is not directly shown.
Near one-to-one match on the body as the natural seat of pain that must not agitate the mind.
Strong body/inner-self distinction under suffering; Paul’s renewal is a work of grace.
Matches the premise of inevitable hardship; the verse does not itself draw the conclusion about calm.
Matches the premise closely; Eliphaz is later rebuked in the book, and he does not draw the Kural’s lesson of calm.
Near-identical teaching: bodily pain accepted, mental agitation over it declined.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on the body as the natural seat of pain; the Jain aim is renunciation of the body, which goes further than the Kural's calm acceptance.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on suffering as universal to embodied life; Farid speaks of the whole world rather than of the body as a target, and draws the lesson of humility rather than of composure.
Good on the inevitability of suffering; Homer’s tone is tragic resignation rather than the Kural’s serene refusal of agitation.
Near one-to-one match on the body as the site of harm and the mind as free of it.

entries.source: Matisse turns to paper cut-outs after major surgery
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of not letting bodily affliction become a calamity of the spirit, though the sources describe his work rather than his inner attitude to pain.
Near one-to-one match (sukheṣu vigata-spṛhaḥ / iṉpam viḻaiyāṉ; duḥkheṣv anudvigna / tuṉpam uṟutal ilaṉ).
Strong on expecting trouble and staying cheerful; the peace offered is found ‘in me’, a Christological ground absent from the Kural.
Affirms that hardship is to be expected; it does not address renouncing pleasure.
Close on accepting hardship; the Mishnah’s motive is devotion to God rather than protection from suffering.
Very close causal teaching; the Buddhist target is attachment to the dear, slightly broader than the Kural’s craving for pleasure.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close in both halves; it does not state the Kural's explicit idea that hardship is natural.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 469, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on not craving pleasure and accepting hardship; Guru Nanak's reason is spiritual (pleasure dulls the longing for God), whereas the Kural's is practical freedom from misery.
Strong narrative match; Odysseus is driven by longing for home rather than a principled rejection of pleasure.
Close on hardship as natural and bearable; Marcus does not mention renouncing pleasure.

entries.source: The Zen poet Ryokan chooses a life of poverty in a mountain hut
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of renouncing pleasure and accepting hardship as natural, though the details of his inner life come largely from his own poems.
Near one-to-one match of the paired attitudes to pleasure and pain.
Close on equanimity across fortune; Paul ties it to strength from Christ in the next verse.
Strong on balanced responses to joy and sorrow; the hadith frames them as gratitude and patience toward God.
Good on holding both conditions in view; Koheleth allows joy in prosperity where the Kural counsels restraint.
Near one-to-one match on equanimity in both joy and sorrow.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong parallel of equanimity across pleasure and pain; the Kural's cause-and-effect link (restraint in joy prevents collapse in sorrow) is implied, not stated.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong fit on evenness in pleasure and pain; the Kural states it as cause and effect (no revelling, so no sinking), while the salok describes a single settled state, and it adds equal regard for friend and foe.
A negative exemplum rather than a direct statement; her fall also punishes impiety toward the gods.

entries.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II
entries.rationale: Close argument; Boethius ultimately points beyond fortune to the highest good in God.

entries.source: Su Shi remains cheerful through exile to Huangzhou and Hainan
entries.rationale: Sources strongly document his calm in adversity; his restraint during prosperity, the couplet's other half, is less directly documented.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.37 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
entries.rationale: Close on counting initial pain as true pleasure; the Gita’s reward is self-realization rather than esteem from enemies.
Near one-to-one on taking pleasure in distress; Paul’s reward is Christ’s strength, not the admiration of foes.
Grounds the revaluation of pain; says nothing about winning honour or enemies’ esteem.
Strong on hardship reinterpreted as good and on esteem from former foes; Joseph credits God’s plan rather than his own attitude.
Shares the theme of honour won through self-mastery, but does not speak of taking pain as pleasure.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §117 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Good on equanimity in hardship; the Kural's specific reward, admiration even from enemies, is not in this passage and is only implied by Mahavira's later honour.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit on treating pain as one treats pleasure; the Kural's promised reward, a distinction admired even by enemies, has no counterpart in this devotional verse.
Good match of hardship embraced leading to glory; the enemies’ esteem in the Kural has no direct counterpart.
Close on the revaluation of hardship; Nietzsche says nothing about esteem from enemies.

entries.source: Abdelkader, after defeat and captivity, wins the esteem of Europe
entries.rationale: A reasonable illustration of distinction admired by former foes, but the sources document his conduct rather than his attitude to hardship, and the praise came for his rescue work more than his endurance.
Very close structural parallel from the classical Indian statecraft tradition; Kautilya adds contingency planning and completion.
Jesus uses this as a parable about the cost of discipleship, but the picture of careful royal counsel fits the Kural well.
Joseph acts here as a royal adviser giving a plan of means, time and method; a strong narrative match.
Matches only the timing element; Kohelet is reflecting on life in general, not on statecraft.

entries.source: Dhammaññu Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 7.64 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Shares the emphasis on timing, but it is monastic practice, not affairs of state.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). Abhayakumara is the classic wise minister of Jain narrative; the passage shows choosing the means, but not the Kural's full list (time, method).

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Zafarnamah', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Next-best: Sikh scripture has no doctrine of the minister; this text concerns the ethics of resorting to force rather than a counsellor's skill, and it is preserved in the Dasam Granth, whose compilation is debated among Sikhs; it is used because nothing in the Guru Granth Sahib fits.

entries.source: Posidippus, epigram on the Kairos of Lysippus (Greek Anthology 16.275), summarized via Theoi Project
entries.rationale: Covers only the timing element; a personification rather than a teaching about ministers.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.9 (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: A remarkably close conceptual match; Aristotle is describing a virtue of any practically wise person, not specifically a minister.

entries.source: Cavour wins France as Piedmont's ally against Austria
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of a minister weighing means, timing and method for a difficult undertaking, though the outcome in 1859 fell short of Cavour's full aims.
Very close list of ministerial virtues; Kautilya’s list is much longer and does not single out protecting the people.
A real parallel in appointing capable officers to serve a community, though these are church stewards, not royal ministers.
Classical Islamic political writing often cites this verse for choosing officials, but the scene itself is about hiring a shepherd.
Strong match: Jethro, himself a counsellor, describes the qualities of officials; he stresses integrity more than courage or learning.
Good match for protecting the people through counsel; the story is really a critique of sacrifice, so this is a secondary theme.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: it touches the single quality of protecting others, and in a spiritual sense; no Jain passage found lists a minister's qualities as the Kural does.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Tegh Bahadur, Guru', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Next-best: it illustrates courage and protecting the people, two of the Kural's qualities, but a Guru giving his life is not a minister serving a king, and learning and sustained effort are not covered; the dialogue comes from an 18th-century Gurbilas text quoted by the encyclopedia.
Fits courage and guardianship; Mentor looks after one household, not a kingdom’s people.
Strong match on protecting the people; Cicero does not list the other qualities in this passage.

entries.source: Sardar Patel brings the princely states into the Indian Union
entries.rationale: A strong fit for firmness, protection of the realm and sustained effort; 'learning' is the quality least directly shown by the event.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavat-yana section), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: Good fit for reconciliation and division; the embassy fails, and Krishna is a divine envoy, not a minister.
A clear example of dividing opponents; Paul is defending himself, not advising a ruler.
Matches keeping and reuniting; the verse credits God rather than a minister and does not cover dividing enemies.
An excellent narrative example of a loyal counsellor dividing the enemy camp; the text credits the outcome to God’s design.
Direct match on dividing and preserving alliances, with an actual minister; the Buddha’s own concern is harmony, not conquest.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). Near one-to-one on detaching the enemy's allies; the Kural's further points (keeping one's own side, winning back defectors) are not shown. Jain narrative, not doctrine.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Chali Mukte', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit for the third skill, reconciling those who left; it is the Guru's forgiveness rather than a minister's diplomacy, and it says nothing of detaching the enemy's allies or keeping one's own side loyal.
Clear example of reconciliation by envoys, although in Book 9 it fails.

entries.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War I and III (trans. Lionel Giles)
entries.rationale: Strong match on dividing enemies; Sun Tzu says little about reconciling former allies.

entries.source: Talleyrand splits the victorious allies at the Congress of Vienna
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the first skill named (splitting the enemy's alliance); the kural's other two skills are less directly shown.
Precise match on decisive counsel; Kautilya presents it as one view in a debate and then qualifies it.
Matches the ideal of unambiguous speech; Jesus is talking about oaths and honesty, not political advice.
Strong match for deliberation followed by resolute action; here the ruler consults rather than a minister advising.
Close match on counsel before action; it does not address speaking decisively.
Parallel in method only; the sutta is about religious belief, not counsel to a ruler.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). Shows examination followed by a firm decision; it is a single anecdote of practical wisdom, not a teaching about counsel.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: it praises discernment in general but names none of the Kural's three specific abilities, and the wisdom it means is directed to serving God rather than to counsel in affairs of state.
Good illustration of deliberation before action; Odysseus acts for himself rather than advising a king.

entries.source: Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part III
entries.rationale: Parallel on resolute action after choice; Descartes is writing about personal conduct, not statecraft.

entries.source: The Beveridge Report sets out a plan against the five giant evils
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of thorough study leading to a decisive recommendation, though Beveridge was an appointed adviser rather than a minister.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: Spoken by the epic’s ideal minister and centred on moral steadiness; it says less about speech or method.
Matches the ideal of measured speech only; not about counsel to a ruler.
Strong on consultation as a value; says nothing specific about the qualities of the counsellor.
Direct statement on the value of counsellors; it stresses their number rather than their personal qualities.

entries.source: Subhasita Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.3 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Covers the speech element only; says nothing of dharma-knowledge or practical method.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (quoted with omissions marked). Next-best only: it describes a sage's restrained speech, not an adviser's skill in counsel or knowledge of method.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: it matches only the measured-speech element; knowing what is right and knowing how things are done are not addressed, and the honour meant is honour before God.
Strong match for the eloquent, experienced counsellor, though his advice goes unheeded in this scene.
Close three-part parallel; Aristotle is analysing persuasion rather than the office of minister.

entries.source: Nizam al-Mulk founds the Nizamiyya colleges and writes the Book of Government
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: he fits the learned, capable counsellor well, but his record is not spotless, so the kural's stress on moral knowledge is only partly shown.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Jatugriha section), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: An excellent narrative match with the epic’s model minister; summarized rather than quoted.
Matches the call for shrewdness; it adds moral innocence and says nothing about learning.
Matches the idea of not being outwitted; it stresses learning from experience rather than books.
A close match: courtiers who combine learning and special insight (v. 20 says they were ten times better than the court magicians); the insight is presented as a divine gift.
An excellent match: a minister who defeats every stratagem through wisdom.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson); the four-buddhi list is in Johnson's footnote, paraphrased here. Good fit on inborn plus acquired intelligence, though Abhaya is in fact tricked once in the same episode.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: both join learning to inner understanding, but Guru Nanak's goal is benefiting others, not outwitting stratagems, and he does not speak of natural acuteness as such.
Good example of wit defeating a trick; Palamedes is not a king’s minister, and learning plays no part.
Close on nature plus learning; Horace is writing about poetry, not statecraft or outwitting schemes.

entries.source: Benjamin Franklin answers the House of Commons on the Stamp Act
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of sharp wit combined with deep knowledge defeating hostile questioning; the repeal itself had several causes besides Franklin's testimony.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.33 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Shares the idea that nature constrains action; the Gita’s concern is spiritual discipline, not administration.
Good match on adapting to people as they actually are; Paul’s goal is evangelism, not statecraft.
An analogy of adapting to the audience; the verse is about prophecy, not administration.

entries.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 86b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
entries.rationale: A close proverbial match on conforming to local ways; it is about custom and etiquette, not policy.
Good parallel on adapting to local practice; limited to language and part of a teaching on avoiding conflict.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). A negative example rather than a teaching, and spoken by a hostile king, but it fits the Kural's warning closely.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: both say book learning is not enough, but the Kural adds knowledge of worldly affairs, whereas Guru Nanak points beyond the world to the one thing that counts, God's Name.
A neat illustration of rule adjusted to circumstance; it concerns personal tact, not governance.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.7 (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: A very close conceptual match between theoretical knowledge and experienced grasp of particulars.
Almost a dramatisation of the kural in negative form: an elaborate plan that ignored the real conditions of the land.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva 37 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: A near-exact situational and moral match: the model minister counselling an unheeding king.
Strong on fearless truth-telling to a ruler; John is a prophet, not a court adviser.
Close match on the duty of sincere counsel to rulers; it does not address a ruler who refuses it.
Classic example of a court figure speaking hard truth to a king; unlike the Kural’s king, David repents.

entries.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Strong match on voicing unwelcome but beneficial truths; the Buddha is teaching a prince, not serving a king.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.33-34 (cf. 13.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's 'Pa*ñ**k*âlas' rendered Pañkâlas). Strong fit on giving good counsel to an unwilling king; Citta is a monk and former brother, not a minister, and in the end he leaves.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: it shares the duty of speaking truth to power, but Guru Nanak speaks as a prophet addressing an age, not as a counsellor advising his own king.
Very close narrative match: a counsellor speaks, is rebuffed, and is proved right.

entries.source: Plutarch, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend (Moralia)
entries.rationale: Close in spirit; Plutarch discusses friendship generally, though he repeatedly applies it to rulers and their courtiers.

entries.source: Hai Rui's memorial rebukes the Jiajing Emperor
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: an official delivering unwelcome but beneficial counsel to a ruler who would not heed it.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta section), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: Strong narrative match; Shakuni works against the Pandavas rather than against his own master, although his advice ultimately destroys the Kauravas too.
Strong on betrayal from within the inner circle; Judas is a disciple, not a counsellor.
A direct match on evil counsellors in a ruler’s inner circle.
A close emotional and structural parallel; the link to Ahithophel comes from tradition, not the text.
Good match on a harmful intimate adviser; Devadatta is a monk, not a minister.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The structure (an inner foe worse than an outer one) matches, but the Jain inner foe is one's own soul's misconduct, not a treacherous adviser.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Sahibzada Zorawar Singh', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Strong thematic fit on betrayal from within one's own household; Gangu was a cook, not a minister, and the comparison with the outer army is an interpretive gloss, not stated by the source.
Strong on the danger of the enemy within; Sinon is an infiltrator, not a trusted minister.

entries.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
entries.rationale: Close on the self-serving minister; it lacks the Kural’s comparison with external enemies.

entries.source: The fall of Sejanus, Tiberius's trusted prefect
entries.rationale: A very close fit, with the caveat that the full extent of Sejanus's plot is debated by historians because the ancient sources are hostile to him.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Shares the value of skill in action; the Gita’s context is freedom from karmic reaction, not administrative competence.
Strong image of unfinished work; Jesus blames poor planning, whereas the Kural blames poor execution after good planning.
Parallel on the gap between words and deeds; the Qur’an treats it as a moral failure, the Kural as a lack of competence.
Good match on action over study; it concerns religious practice rather than executive skill.
Close image of fine words without results; the verse concerns practising the Dhamma, not carrying out policy.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best: it concerns failing to finish from lack of zeal, but nothing about prior planning or ministers.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: both contrast good intentions with failed execution, but Guru Nanak speaks of moral conduct and inner impurity, not of a lack of executive skill in carrying out planned work.
Good mythic picture of incomplete execution; Epimetheus fails through lack of foresight as much as lack of skill.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.8 (trans. W. D. Ross)
entries.rationale: Parallel on action over mere potential; Aristotle’s subject is happiness, not administrative execution.

entries.source: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 1 is left unfinished
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of good design without completed execution, though funding and a dispute with the engineer, not only Babbage's own management, stopped the work.

entries.source: Rigveda 10.125 (Vak Sukta), trans. R. T. H. Griffith
