entries.rationale: A reasonable but partial fit, since Jefferson's silence reflected his temperament and dislike of debate as much as deference to elders.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Sections 132-134 (story of Ashtavakra), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: Dramatic parallel of failure before a learned court. The story is about formal debate, not a counsellor’s verbal slip.
Matches the gravity of slips in speech, but without the Kural’s focus on a learned audience.
Striking match of the slip-and-fall image. The hadith’s stakes are eschatological, while the Kural’s are social.
Very close image. Ben Sira belongs to Jewish wisdom literature and is quoted in the Talmud, but is outside the Hebrew canon.
Good dramatic parallel. The setting is a debate, not a counsellor’s address.

entries.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.14.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Next-best match: it stresses care and accuracy in speech, but not the Kural's particular danger of erring before an expert audience.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the salok is about harsh or insipid speech in general, not a single slip before a learned audience.
The punishment is for arrogance as much as for error, so the parallel is partial.
A related theme of exposure before the wise. Plato’s point is about ignorance of one’s ignorance, not court speech.

entries.source: Benjamin Disraeli's maiden speech is shouted down in the House of Commons
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of a slip before a demanding audience, though the hostility Disraeli faced had political as well as rhetorical causes.

entries.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Book 3 (trans. F. Max Müller)
entries.rationale: A close narrative parallel of learning shown before a learned assembly.
A good illustration of learning recognised by the learned. Luke’s purpose is Christological.
Shares the idea that understanding requires capable hearers. The context is religious remembrance.

entries.source: Proverbs 27:17 (KJV), as applied in Babylonian Talmud Taanit 7a
entries.rationale: Strong through the Talmudic reading. The verse itself concerns friends in general.

entries.source: Milindapanha, Book 2, ch. 1 (trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, The Questions of King Milinda)
entries.rationale: A close parallel on the right kind of audience for learned discourse.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the Jain simile is about the learned person as the vessel of knowledge, not about the audience as the setting where learning becomes visible.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on worth recognised only by qualified judges; the jewel in Gurbani is the Name, not scholarly learning.
A good illustration. The Phaeacians are admiring hosts rather than critical examiners.
Close on learning revealed through capable company. The letter’s authenticity is debated.

entries.source: Hilbert and Klein bring Emmy Noether to Gottingen
entries.rationale: A strong fit for learning recognised by expert judges, though sources differ slightly on whether she arrived in 1915 or 1916.
Strong on the receptive hearer. The Upanishad does not use the watering image.
Very close, image and meaning alike, though Jesus uses seed where Valluvar uses water.
An almost exact parallel of image and meaning.

entries.source: Mishnah Chagigah 2:1 (Sefaria, William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz edition)
entries.rationale: A precise match on the kind of hearer. The Mishnah is restricting esoteric teaching rather than praising ordinary speech.

entries.source: Saddharma-pundarika (Lotus Sutra), Chapter 5 ‘On Plants’, trans. H. Kern
entries.rationale: A very close image. The Lotus Sutra stresses the rain falling on all equally, whereas the Kural focuses on the ready bed.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on speech bearing fruit in a receptive hearer; the Jain image is horsemanship, not watering a garden bed.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 354, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: the garden-and-watering image is shared, but in Gurbani the watering is love for God within the hearer, not a speaker addressing a receptive audience.
An illustrative narrative match only. Homer uses no agricultural image.
A strong parallel in both image and thought. It is paraphrased here because the passage was not re-verified verbatim.

entries.source: Einstein translates and extends Satyendra Nath Bose's paper
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of the kural, with the same paper meeting silence in one place and immediate growth in the hands of a receptive expert.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.67 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: A close parallel. The Gita concerns sacred teaching, not council speech.
Matches on leaving the unreceptive alone. The disciples do try once, whereas the Kural advises not speaking at all.
Good match on withdrawing from unworthy company. The verse is about ill speech, not wasted wisdom.
Close in spirit. Proverbs 26:5 gives the opposite advice, and the pair is famously paradoxical.

entries.source: Ananda Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 44.10 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: A parallel of skilful silence. Vacchagotta is confused rather than base, so the ‘mean assembly’ element is missing.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: it forbids mixing with mean men in general, not specifically speaking good things before them.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (pauri 19), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong practical parallel, though Gurbani speaks of arguing with fools rather than of choosing which assembly to address.

entries.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Cock and the Jewel’ (trans. G. F. Townsend)
entries.rationale: A close image of worth wasted on the unappreciative. Aesop is Greek fable rather than myth proper.

Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Carter translation). Strong match on not speaking good things to an unfit audience. Epictetus' reasons are humility and the risk of speaking undigested doctrine, rather than the unworthiness of the assembly as such.

entries.source: Pablo Casals refuses to perform in countries that recognised Franco's regime
entries.rationale: A next-best fit: Casals's boycott was a political protest against governments rather than a judgement on the quality of particular audiences.
A very close parallel in thought and in its image of waste. Manu’s wording is far more severe.
An almost identical teaching and image. Matthew adds the danger of retaliation.
Matches on speech wasted on the unreceptive. The Qur’an’s context is disbelief, not social rank or learning.
A direct parallel in meaning.

entries.source: Ayacana Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 6.1 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: A close concern with wasted teaching. The Buddha’s compassion finally overrides it, whereas the Kural’s counsel stands.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Next-best match: the imagery of good things versus filth is similar, but the Jain verse blames the unworthy receiver and gives no warning to the speaker about choosing an audience.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit, with the same image of wasted nectar; Kabir stresses the unchanging nature of the recipient rather than the unclean place, and the 'unreceptive hearer' reading comes from commentary.
An evocative match of wasted truth. The cause is a divine curse, not the hearers’ low quality.

entries.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.5 (trans. W. D. Ross), quoting Heraclitus (DK B9)
entries.rationale: A vivid parallel of value lost on the wrong recipient. Aristotle uses it to make a point about pleasure, not speech.

entries.source: Mendel's laws of heredity are presented in Brunn and then overlooked
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit for wisdom wasted on an unready audience, though historians debate how fully Mendel was ignored and the Brunn society was not an unworthy assembly.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: It pairs pure speech with study as the Kural does, but it says nothing about fear of an audience.
The verse is about fitting one’s speech to each listener. Fear of the assembly is only implied.
A strong match on steady, understandable speech before power. The Qur’an credits God as the source of that confidence, where the Kural credits learning and purity.
It overlaps with the Kural on skilled, well-placed speech among scholars. It is about good manners rather than fear.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarājakumāra Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
entries.rationale: It closely matches the idea of classifying speech and timing it well, but it does not address fear of an audience.

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It closely matches fearless, disciplined speech, but the Jain verse says nothing about first sizing up what kind of assembly one faces.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit linking wisdom and fearlessness, though the salok concerns fearlessness in all of life, not specifically speaking in an assembly.
The two agree on assured public speech. Hesiod credits divine gift where the Kural credits learning and purity.
A close structural parallel. Plato stresses method more than courage.

entries.source: Frederick Douglass delivers What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
entries.rationale: A strong example of commanding an assembly with mastery of words; how deliberately he sized up this particular audience is inferred from the structure of the speech rather than documented.

entries.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.1-3.9 (trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15)
entries.rationale: A very close match. Rank among scholars is decided by answering before scholars.
Close on speaking well before scholars. Luke emphasises understanding, not courage.
The shape matches: knowledge is shown before knowers. But the point of the verse is God’s knowledge, not human rank.
A strong narrative parallel. The Talmud then adds a humbling twist when Hillel himself forgets a law.
It matches on skilled exposition. It does not mention a learned audience or fear.

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It is strong on making teaching reach the hearer, but the setting is a teacher and pupil, not a learned assembly, and the Kural's 'most learned of the learned' ranking is missing.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 938, Raag Ramkali, Siddh Gosht, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit for speaking before a learned assembly, though the dialogue aims at spiritual truth rather than at showing one's learning.
A vivid match: an unimpressive-looking man proves supreme by speaking before elders.
The two ideals are close. Quintilian stresses moral character, which sits closer to 721’s ‘purity.’

entries.source: David Hilbert presents his problems to the International Congress of Mathematicians
entries.rationale: Very close to the kural: a master presenting ideas to his peers in a way that took hold of the whole field.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta sub-parva), trans. K. M. Ganguli
entries.rationale: An unusually direct parallel: brave warriors are silent in the council hall.
Strong on rare boldness before an assembly. Acts attributes it to their time with Jesus rather than to learning.

entries.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4344 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
entries.rationale: A very close match in how it ranks spoken courage above martial courage.
Her courage is to speak in a royal court, not in a learned assembly. The spirit is the same.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikaya 12, Mahāsīhanāda Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
entries.rationale: Close on fearlessness in assemblies. There is no contrast with the battlefield.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It shares the pairing of learning and fearlessness, but it lacks the Kural's sharp contrast between battlefield courage and courage in an assembly.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Strong on fearless speech, but it is truth spoken before violent power, not composure in a debating council, and the link to Babur rests on the hymn's content and tradition.
Nestor praises both courages together. The surrounding silence of the other kings shows that council courage is the rarer of the two.

entries.source: Plutarch, Life of Demosthenes 20 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)
entries.rationale: It inverts the Kural’s case. It confirms the two courages are distinct, but here the council courage is the one present.

entries.source: Margaret Chase Smith delivers her Declaration of Conscience
entries.rationale: Almost a dramatisation of civil courage before an assembly, the kural's central contrast.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: A good match for the ‘learn from the greater’ half. It lacks the ‘speak before the learned’ half.
A near one-to-one narrative match for both halves of the couplet.
Strong on learning from the one who surpasses. There is no public-speaking element.
Close in spirit, although Ben Zoma says ‘every person,’ not only those who are greater.
It matches the learning-from-the-wiser idea. It says nothing about speaking before an assembly.

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.15; cf. I.14.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The learn-from-those-who-know half fits well, but the Jain verse is about monastic instruction rather than speaking in an assembly.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 766, Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A good fit on mutual giving and taking, though Gurbani speaks of sharing virtues rather than scholarly knowledge.
A close match that even includes the shyness the chapter warns against.
The method matches but the outcome does not: Socrates rarely found anyone who actually knew more.

entries.source: Andrew Wiles announces, then repairs, his proof of Fermat's Last Theorem
entries.rationale: Strong fit for presenting before peers and then learning from their scrutiny; the help came from a former student rather than a more learned senior, a small difference from the kural's wording.
It matches the very discipline the traditional commentary names.
Close on readiness to answer. It does not prescribe formal logic.
It shares the ideal of good argument but does not mention fear or the study of logic.
A very close functional match: learning aimed at readiness to reply.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarājakumāra Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
entries.rationale: A close match on mastery producing ready answers to learned questioners.

entries.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.6, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Pramana as the means of valid knowledge fits the commentators' reading of this Kural well, though the sutra is about knowing the categories of reality, not about debate.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: both want disciplined, applied learning, but Gurbani's goal is benefiting others, not winning debates through logic.
It matches on deliberate training for council speech. Logic as such is not mentioned.
Paraphrased because the exact wording could not be verified against a live source. The point is close.

entries.source: Thurgood Marshall, trained at Howard, wins Brown v. Board of Education
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit for trained reasoning producing confident advocacy, but the sources do not describe his courtroom exchanges in detail, so the link to fearless replies is general.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 1.29 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: A vivid match for the sword half. Arjuna’s fear is moral anguish rather than ordinary cowardice.
A close parallel: fear leads to burying something valuable.
The image of useless learning is exact. The verse is about failing to act on scripture, not about fear.
It shares the problem of fear blocking speech. The resolution is divine help, not human training.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.101, Sārajja Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
entries.rationale: It supports the Kural from the opposite side: learning is meant to produce confidence.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.16 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Learning and fearlessness are joined in one image, but there is no counterpart to the Kural's pairing of a sword with books.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: courage is the shared point, but the verse is about devotional self-surrender, not about weapons or learning.
A direct illustration of the sword half of the couplet.
A remarkably close structural parallel between the two kinds of defence.

entries.source: Copernicus withholds On the Revolutions until the end of his life
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit, though his reasons for delay are inferred by historians from the preface rather than stated as plain fear, and his work was eventually published.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: An unusually exact cultural parallel. Klība and pēṭi belong to the same imagery.
A suggestive narrative parallel. Peter’s failure is denial under questioning rather than scholarly timidity.
It covers only the battlefield image and says nothing about learning.
A close match for the image. The application to learning is left to the reader.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.75, Yodhājīva Sutta (trans. Bhikkhu Sujato)
entries.rationale: Strong on the warrior image. The Buddha applies it to spiritual life rather than to learning.

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.3.1-2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The coward-in-battle image is shared, but the Jain passage is about a monk's resolve under hardship, not about learning wasted through fear of an assembly, and it has no sword simile.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maru, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable contrast-parallel; Kabir's battle is largely inner or in defence of the weak, and he says nothing about learning.
A good illustration of armed men paralysed by fear. The fear is overcome quickly.
A close psychological parallel. Epictetus also offers a Stoic cure that the Kural does not.

entries.source: Henry Cavendish's electrical discoveries stay unpublished for a century
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of valuable knowledge kept from others; the sources consulted do not state that fear of the scientific community was his reason.

entries.source: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.9 and 1.11 (trans. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East 15)
entries.rationale: A close match on the duty to teach what one learns. It does not speak of assemblies or fear.
A well-known image for the same point about unshared gifts.

entries.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 3658 (graded hasan sahih by al-Albani)
entries.rationale: It shares the point that knowledge must be passed on. The hadith condemns deliberate concealment, not inability.
Close on the need to convey knowledge. Here the problem is solved by a spokesman rather than by the scholar’s own courage.
The Dhammapada’s ‘use’ is practice, where the Kural’s is public speech. Both say learning left unused is wasted.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: the verse shares the idea that learning should serve others but does not call learning useless when it is not communicated.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa, Asa ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: both call vast learning useless without something more, but Gurbani's missing element is the Name, not skill in public speech.
Odysseus contrasts looks with speech, where the Kural contrasts learning with speech.
A genuine historical case. Unlike the Kural’s scholar, Isocrates made his learning useful through writing.

entries.source: Josiah Willard Gibbs's great work on thermodynamics goes long unappreciated
entries.rationale: Partial fit: Gibbs did publish and was admired by a few, and his difficulty lay in style rather than any fear of speaking, though the delay in his influence matches the kural's warning.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Vidura Niti (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Very close in spirit. The exact verse number varies between editions.
A close match: learned insiders silenced by fear of the assembly.
The Qur’an praises the positive side. The Kural condemns the failure.
The two share the ‘fear no face’ ethic, applied here to judges.
It supports the link between wisdom and fearlessness. It also warns against mere talkativeness.

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.3.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: it condemns giving way before people's insults, but it says nothing about learning and makes no comparison with the unlearned.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Maajh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable: the same 'learned yet a fool' verdict, but the failing Gurbani names is ego and greed, not timidity.
A positive counterpart to the Kural rather than a direct parallel.

entries.source: Plutarch, Life of Demosthenes 6 (trans. Bernadotte Perrin)
entries.rationale: A very close case: real ability thrown away through fear of the assembly.

entries.source: Gauss keeps his ideas on non-Euclidean geometry private
entries.rationale: Fits the idea of the learned dreading the assembly, though calling Gauss lower than the unlearned would be unfair, so the kural's harsh ranking is not matched.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Both give the same ‘worse than death’ verdict on fear. The Gita is about duty in battle, not speech.
The verbal parallel is striking, but the context is spiritual lukewarmness.
The life-and-death imagery matches. The verse is about faith, not public speech.
Close in feeling. Jeremiah’s silence comes from weariness under persecution rather than stage fright.
The imagery matches but the cause differs: heedlessness rather than fear of the assembly.

entries.source: Sutrakritanga I.14.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It is the positive counterpart of the Kural's point, but it has no 'living dead' image and does not mention fear of the assembly.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best: the 'alive only in name' rhetoric is shared, but Gurbani's test of being alive is the Name, not sharing learning.
Achilles withdraws out of anger, not fear, but the result is the same wasted life.
A close match in value judgement. Seneca speaks of sharing, not fear of assemblies.

entries.source: Fermat's marginal note and his unpublished mathematics
entries.rationale: Fits the failure to pass on learning, but Fermat's reluctance came from temperament and lack of interest in publishing rather than documented fear of an assembly.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, Sarga 6 (description of Ayodhya)
entries.rationale: Close thematic match. Valmiki describes the ideal city in far more detail, and the Kural’s precise three-part definition is its own.
Matches only one of the Kural’s three elements (the right kind of wealthy person). Paul says nothing about harvests or the definition of a country.
Strong on abundance and ‘a good land’. The Qur’an stresses gratitude to God, while the Kural adds worthy people and merchants.
Very close on the unfailing harvest. Deuteronomy does not mention the worthy people or the wealthy class the Kural adds.
Good fit for the picture of an ideal prosperous realm, though the sutta links prosperity to moral renewal rather than listing its parts.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §90 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (quoted up to the semicolon). It lists the same signs of prosperity, but as an auspicious omen in a story, not as a definition of a good country, and it says nothing about people of worth.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Arjan Dev, Guru
entries.rationale: A strong practical parallel to the Kural's three constituents of a land, though it describes the founding of one sacred city, not a teaching about countries in general.
Near-exact image for the first element of the Kural. It describes a royal garden rather than a whole country.
Same method of defining a polity by its essential parts. Aristotle’s list is longer and includes arms and religion.

entries.source: Emperor Zhenzong distributes drought-resistant Champa rice
entries.rationale: Illustrates only the first of the kural's three marks, unfailing harvests; the worthy people and prosperous merchants are not part of this story.
Close in its list of what makes a territory desirable. Manu’s verse also includes ethnic and political criteria that the Kural does not share.
Good image of a land desired for its richness. The same verse warns of its coming destruction, which runs against the Kural’s ‘free from calamity’.
Matches the pairing of abundance and freedom from disaster. The Qur’an makes both depend on faith, which the Kural does not say.
Strong on desirability through abundance. The spies go on to report that the land is strongly defended, which is a different emphasis.
The prosperity is described in detail, but the sutta’s aim is to show that it does not last, which is the reverse of the Kural’s aim.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.49 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a contrast, not a parallel: Jainism names the same riches of the land but treats craving for them as bondage, so the fit is weak.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 783-784, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Close in imagery of abundance and freedom from harm, but the hymn speaks of the gift of the Name and spiritual contentment (as Sahib Singh's commentary stresses), not the economy of a kingdom, and it lacks the Kural's note that such a land is coveted by others.
Good fit for the idea of a land that invites others to want it. The island is empty and uncultivated, so it lacks the rest of the Kural’s picture.
An indirect match. Plato explains why rich lands are coveted, while the Kural simply treats being coveted as a sign of wealth.

entries.source: Augustus annexes Egypt and makes it Rome's granary
entries.rationale: A strong fit for a land coveted for its abundant harvests; the 'free from calamity' element is implied by Egypt's reliability rather than documented here.
Matches the tax element only, and from the king’s side rather than the land’s. The burden of incoming people is not addressed.
Clear match on paying dues to rulers. Paul does not speak of a land’s capacity to carry sudden burdens.
Very close to Parimelazhagar’s reading of the burden as incoming people. The Qur’an praises self-sacrifice, while the Kural praises a land rich enough to cope.
Good fit for a land that supports both people and king. Later chapters show Solomon’s taxes as oppressive, which complicates the picture.
Close on the link between a thriving land and full royal revenue. The sutta speaks to the king, while the Kural praises the land.

entries.source: 'Basic Positivity of Ahimsa', in The Jaina Path of Ahimsa (online book, jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainworld.com. Next-best only: this is a secondary summary of individual lay charity and has nothing to say about a land's capacity or about paying the ruler's dues.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Amar Das, Guru
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the langar's open hospitality and the offering system mirror the two halves of the Kural, but the setting is a religious community, not a state paying taxes to a king, and the Akbar visit rests on tradition ('is said to').
Interesting parallel of a people sharing the cost of a stranger, but it concerns one guest, not a mass of newcomers.
Almost point for point the same idea, and likely from a shared Indian tradition of statecraft.

entries.source: The Edict of Potsdam opens Brandenburg to Huguenot refugees
entries.rationale: Closely matches the commentators' reading of absorbing refugees; the kural's second point, still paying the ruler his full dues, is reversed here by the generous tax exemptions.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 128 (Rama’s reign)
entries.rationale: Strong match on freedom from famine, disease and fear. Valmiki attributes it to Rama’s righteousness rather than to the land itself.
The same triad of evils, but described as signs of the end rather than as the absence that marks a good land.
Close on hunger and enemies. Disease is not mentioned, and the verse calls for gratitude to God.
Very close on famine and enemies; disease is covered later in the chapter’s curses rather than here.

entries.source: Sutta Nipata 2.1, Ratana Sutta, with its commentary (Piyadassi’s introduction)
entries.rationale: A striking parallel triad. The third danger is non-human beings rather than human enemies, and the story comes from the commentary, not the sutta itself.

entries.source: Jain Heritage Centres, 'Chandragiri' (Shravanabelagola), jainheritagecentres.com, summarising the Bhadrabahu tradition and Shravanabelagola inscriptions
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on jainheritagecentres.com, a secondary web source; the event is traditional and partly legendary. It covers famine only (not disease or enemies) and is a narrative, not a teaching about what makes a good land.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Arjan Dev, Guru
entries.rationale: A strong thematic fit on famine and disease; the Kural's third evil, destructive enemies, is not covered by this account, and the Kural describes a condition of the land rather than relief work.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 225-230 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Very close. Hesiod makes the blessing depend on justice, a link the Kural keeps for the chapter’s last verse.
Shares the concern with famine and disease; hostile armies are dealt with elsewhere in the Arthashastra.

entries.source: War, crowding and plague strike Athens
entries.rationale: A negative illustration that matches the kural's triad of hunger, disease and enemies very closely.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 107 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Direct parallel on the peril of internal enmity and faction, in a passage about the same kind of groups (gana) the Kural calls kuzhu.
Very close on the destructiveness of internal division. Jesus uses it as an argument, not as advice on statecraft.
Good match on the danger of internal dispute. The verse is addressed to a community at war rather than to a settled land.
Strong parallel on internal hatred bringing ruin; the Talmud frames it as a sin before God as well as a political failure.

entries.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.4 (trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story)
entries.rationale: Close fit. The sutta states the positive condition (concord) that the Kural states negatively (no factions).

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.28 and 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: it names the threat of robbers and the duty of public safety, but the Jain voice is sceptical of the state's remedy and says nothing about factions.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 74, Siree Raag, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on internal peace; the hymn is primarily about the inner victory over the five passions under God's rule, and it does not single out factions or chieftains as the Kural does.
Clear thematic parallel; it is a prayer in drama rather than a definition of a good country.
Very close on factions as the sickness of a state, though Plato traces faction mainly to the gap between rich and poor.
A clear negative illustration of an internal plot against the ruler; the kural's warning about rival factions in general is only partly reflected.

entries.source: Vishnu Purana 1.13 and Bhagavata Purana 4.18 (story of Prithu)
entries.rationale: Matches the theme of fruitfulness restored after disaster, but credits a king rather than the land’s own resilience.
Shares the image of withstanding disaster, but it is a parable about personal faith, not about a country.
Good match on resilience through reserves. The Qur’an’s focus is Joseph’s wisdom rather than the land.
Captures abundance in a time of ruin, but the blessing belongs to one man, not to a whole country.

entries.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.28 (trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story)
entries.rationale: Shares the idea of the foremost city exposed to ruin, but says nothing about keeping its wealth after harm.

entries.source: Tattvartha Sutra 3.28, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The parallel is cosmological, not political: these regions are stable because of the structure of time, not because of resilience to harm by enemies.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Des Raj, Bhai (by Sarmukh Singh Amole)
entries.rationale: A reasonable historical illustration of recovery after ruin, but it concerns one city and shrine rather than a whole land, and it is an event, not a teaching.

entries.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Good image of recovery. In the myth the earth is barren for a time, whereas the Kural’s best land does not lose its richness at all.
Strong on resilience under attack; Machiavelli writes about a single fortified city rather than a whole country.

entries.source: Tokyo is rebuilt after the Great Kanto Earthquake
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of resilience after ruin, though the reconstruction was scaled back from Goto's original plan for lack of funds.
Close on hills and water as defences; Manu is concerned with the fort alone, while the Kural also values water for life.
Water and security are both present, but the psalm’s river and defence are largely spiritual.
Same features (mountains and rivers), but cited as signs of God rather than as parts of a well-ordered country.
Matches the idea of hills as protection; water and fortress are not mentioned.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Close on water supply and fortification as the basis of security. The sutta uses them as a metaphor for spiritual practice.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.18 and 9.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (verse 20 quoted only to its first clause). It matches the fortress only; the waters and hills of the Kural have no counterpart, and the Jain move is to spiritualise rather than endorse fortification.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 7, Japji Sahib (pauri 34), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: both texts list natural features of the land, but Japji Sahib speaks of the cosmos as a field for righteous action and says nothing of hills, rivers or fortresses as the strength of a kingdom.
Striking match on the two kinds of water and the hills; there is no fortress in the passage.
Remarkably close, down to the two sources of water; Aristotle adds health and air.

entries.source: King Kassapa I builds his capital on the rock of Sigiriya
entries.rationale: Shows hill, water and fortress combined, but at the scale of a single royal site rather than a whole country, and Kassapa lost his throne in 495 despite it.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 68 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Strong on security. It covers only one of the five ornaments, and ‘case’ is a typo for ‘ease’ in the online Ganguli text.
Very close list of a land’s blessings; health is not named directly.
Matches security and harvest; health, wealth and joy are not mentioned.
A classic image of the ideal land; health and wealth are implied rather than stated.
Shares health, wealth and happiness as goods, but speaks of the individual, not the country.

entries.source: Shanti Path (Hindi Shanti Path of Digambara worship), verse 7, English rendering at frontdesk.co.in ('Shanti Path with Meaning', 2025)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on frontdesk.co.in, a web translation of a liturgical prayer, not canonical scripture. It covers nearly all five of the Kural's ornaments; the Sanskrit counterpart (kṣemaṃ sarvaprajānāṃ...) was seen only in search results.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 345, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A near match to the Kural's list of a land's ornaments; the difference is that Begampura is a spiritual city of God's kingdom, and its freedom from taxes stands in tension with the Kural's praise of lands that pay their ruler's dues.
Parallel in listing the goods that adorn a society, but the Horai are moral and civic qualities, not material ones.

entries.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric, I.5, 1360b (tr. W. Rhys Roberts)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive (Rhys Roberts). Partial match: Aristotle's list is mainly of an individual's happiness, and harvests are absent, but health, prosperity, enjoyment and security all appear, and the chapter applies some of them to states.

entries.source: The first Human Development Report introduces the Human Development Index
entries.rationale: A reasonable parallel in spirit; the index's components overlap with only some of the kural's five ornaments, and security is not among them.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Bhishma Parva, Jambu-khanda section (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Good image of effortless abundance, but it is a mythical paradise rather than a real country.
Nice verbal echo; the parable is about the growth of God’s kingdom, not about the richness of a land.
Close on wealth that comes of itself; the verse’s main point is the loss of it through ingratitude.
Nearly the same comparison; Deuteronomy adds that the rain depends on God’s care and Israel’s faithfulness.
Close image of unsought abundance; the sutta places it in a lost golden age and treats its loss as a moral lesson.

entries.source: Tattvartha Sutra 3.37, with Pujyapada's Sarvarthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. A close match to wealth that comes unsought, but it is cosmology rather than advice on statecraft, and Jainism does not rank such lands highest spiritually.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 10, So Dar (Rehras), Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial: both speak of wealth that comes without straining, but the Kural praises a naturally rich land, while Guru Arjan warns against anxious scheming; Sikh commentators such as Sahib Singh stress that honest effort (kirat) remains a duty.

entries.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 116-119 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
entries.rationale: Very close on unsought abundance, though Hesiod describes a vanished age rather than a present country.
Parallel image; Plato questions whether such ease makes people happy, which the Kural does not ask.

entries.source: Oil is struck at Burgan, Kuwait
entries.rationale: Next-best fit: the wealth was a natural endowment, but it still had to be sought through years of exploration and drilling, which the kural contrasts with true natural plenty.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 68 (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Very close; the Mahabharata stresses fear of anarchy, while Parimelazhagar’s reading stresses harmony between ruler and people.
Close in spirit; Proverbs stresses justice and bribery, the Kural harmony between king and land.
Matches the ruler’s responsibility for his people; it does not say that a land’s wealth is worthless without him.
Close on the necessity of government; the Mishnah speaks of order, the Kural of harmony between king and land.
Very close on the ruler’s effect on the land; the sutta makes the link cosmic, while the Kural keeps it practical.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §§210-211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. It shows the Jain ideal of a beneficial first king, but it does not say that a land is worthless without a fitting ruler; Rishabha in the end renounces kingship.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Ashtapadi, Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: A strong fit on the ruin that follows unfit rule; Guru Nanak frames the disaster ultimately within God's will (hukam), a dimension the Kural does not share.
Very close; Homer states the positive case (good king, fruitful land), the Kural the negative.
Same structure of argument; Plato demands wisdom in the ruler, the Kural harmony between ruler and land.

entries.source: The reign of Charles II, last Habsburg king of Spain
entries.rationale: A strong illustration of riches without effective rule, though historians note that many of Spain's problems predated his reign.

entries.source: Manusmriti 7.74 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
entries.rationale: Strong match on the fort’s value; Manu stresses defensive multiplication rather than the Kural’s attack-and-refuge pairing. The spelling ‘posses’ is as printed in the online Bühler text.
Jesus is using a parable about spiritual power, not teaching statecraft; the parallel is to the image only.
Covers the defensive half of the couplet well but not the attacker’s use of a fort.
Illustrates the defensive value of walls; the Kural’s claim that forts also serve attackers is not addressed.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Close structural parallel, though the sutta uses the fort as a simile for spiritual qualities.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); the verse states the Kural's view of the fort as a king's essential asset, but the Jain text puts it in the mouth of the tempter and does not endorse it, so the fit is partial.
A reasonable historical parallel; Sikh teaching permits arms only in defence of the faith and the oppressed, so the Kural's picture of a fort as a base for attacking others fits only in part.
Paraphrased narrative; the dual use is drawn from the story, not stated as a teaching.
Strong conceptual match on the fort as a flexible asset.

entries.source: Edward I builds his castles in north Wales
entries.rationale: Strong fit, since the castles were explicitly instruments of conquest and places of refuge at once, though the event is a building programme rather than a single dramatic moment.

entries.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 2.3 ‘Construction of Forts’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)
entries.rationale: Near one-to-one match of the four natural defenses; Kautilya’s ‘desert’ corresponds to the Kural’s open land.
Covers hill and water; forest and open land are absent, and the verse is a prophetic promise, not military advice.
The verse is about divine provision generally, not fortification; the overlap is in the natural features named.
Matches on water as a defensive resource only.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Only the water element matches; the sutta’s moat is man-made rather than a natural feature.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.3, part 10 ‘Description of a samavasaraṇa’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Both sentences verified verbatim against Johnson's translation on wisdomlib.org; Jain scripture has no teaching on the natural defences of a fort, so this is a next-best structural echo only (no hill or forest belt is described).

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 481, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Next-best only: Kabir shares the image of water as a fortress's defence but uses it to teach impermanence and the need for the Name, the opposite of the Kural's practical praise of natural defences.
Paraphrase; only the water and narrow-approach features correspond to the Kural’s list.
Strong on water; Aristotle does not list hill and forest as the Kural does. The quote is cut before the words ‘by war’.

entries.source: Rajput rulers build the hill forts of Rajasthan among hills, rivers, forest and desert
entries.rationale: Very close fit, since the kural's own list of natural defences matches UNESCO's description, though the event is a long building tradition rather than one dated moment.

entries.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra 2.3 ‘Construction of Forts’ (trans. R. Shamasastry)
entries.rationale: Very close technical parallel and a likely example of the kind of ‘nool’ the Kural cites.
A symbolic vision, not a building specification; matches height, size and guarded access.
Strong on height and solidity; breadth is not mentioned.

entries.source: Psalms 48:13-14 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 48:12-13)
entries.rationale: Praises fortifications but gives no technical criteria. The translation notes that the meaning of ‘go through’ is uncertain.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Close match on three of the four qualities.

entries.source: Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’, section on the twelve vratas (jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on the jainworld.com page; this is a secondary scholar's summary of the traditional simile, and it uses the town wall as a metaphor without listing its qualities, so the match is partial.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1161, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Close in its picture of an impregnable wall, but allegorical: the fortress is the self ruled by maya and ego, which Kabir wants to see conquered, not defended.
Paraphrase; it supports the need for high walls in general, not the four specific qualities.
Matches the concern with strength against attack; Aristotle gives no fourfold list. A missing space in the online text has been restored.

entries.source: Theodosius II builds the land walls of Constantinople
entries.rationale: Close illustration of all four qualities of a wall, although the precise dimensions come from one of the two sources.
Matches the spacious interior; says nothing about breaking the enemy’s morale.
A spiritual metaphor with only a loose structural parallel.
Good match on a narrow sealed gap that defeats attackers; interior space is not mentioned.

entries.source: Nehemiah 4:13-14 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:19-20)
entries.rationale: Shows the problem of a long perimeter; the Kural states the design ideal instead.
A general image of vigilant guarding, used as a simile for self-discipline.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, no. 7, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim (including the source's hyphen spacing) on jainworld.com; the design principle of few exits is a genuine parallel, but it concerns a layman's house, not a royal fort, and says nothing about breaking an attacker's spirit.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1161, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Partial and allegorical: the demoralising fortress is the self's bondage to maya, and the hymn goes on to show it taken by divine love, so the sympathy runs opposite to the Kural's; nothing corresponds to the Kural's narrow perimeter and spacious interior.
Historical rather than mythological, and a pass rather than a fort, but the principle matches closely.

entries.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.5 (trans. Lionel Giles)
entries.rationale: Strong match on the fort breaking the besieger’s morale.

entries.source: The garrison of Kumamoto Castle holds out against the Satsuma army
entries.rationale: Good on a fort wearing down the attackers' momentum, but the sources do not detail the specific design of a short perimeter around a large interior that the kural stresses.
Near-direct match on provisioning.
A parable about counting the cost of discipleship; the link is to planning resources, not to storing food for a siege.
Provisioning against famine, not siege; the parallel is limited to storing food.
Very close match on a strengthened and provisioned fort.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Very close match on provisions and ease for the defenders.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22, first half (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (quotation stops mid-sentence at the ellipsis); the impregnability theme fits strongly, but the Jain fortress is spiritual and the Kural's stress on stored provisions has no counterpart.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
entries.rationale: A strong historical illustration, though a negative one (the fort's stores ran out), and sources differ on dating the siege to 1704 or 1705.
Historical narrative, not myth. It matches on provisions, but the city did fall.
Near one-to-one match on two of the three conditions; provisions are covered elsewhere in the same chapter.

entries.source: Hunger forces the surrender of Vicksburg
entries.rationale: Strong illustration by negative example, since the defences held against assault but the food supply did not.
The ‘fort of men’ matches the human element; Manu gives this as a separate type, not as part of every fort.
A parable about discipleship; only the concern with enough troops carries over.
Close on general readiness; not specifically about fortification.

entries.source: Nehemiah 4:10 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:16)
entries.rationale: Strong on the human element; supplies are not in view.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Close match; the sutta separately lists the stores, just as the Kural pairs the two.

entries.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.3, part 10 ‘Description of a samavasaraṇa’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)
entries.rationale: Both sentences verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; the guardians are celestial door-keepers of a peaceful preaching hall rather than soldiers of a garrison, so this is an imagistic next-best match.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
entries.rationale: A reasonable fit on the human element of a fort; the Khalsa is first a spiritual order with a code of conduct, not a garrison, and the Kural's material stores are not addressed.
Paraphrase; a close dramatic example of defenders placed where they are needed.
Matches the purpose of readiness; not specific about supplies and men.

entries.source: King George VI awards the George Cross to the island of Malta
entries.rationale: Close fit to the kural's pairing of stores and brave defenders, with the island itself serving as the fortress.

entries.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book XIII (trans. R. Shamasastry)
entries.rationale: Paraphrased summary of the book’s scope, not verified against the text line by line.
Spiritual parable; it shows the danger without the Kural’s three methods of capture.
A theological lesson about trusting in forts, which the Kural does not share. The overlap is the collapse from within.
The proverb praises wisdom; the Kural requires resistance to it, so the parallel is the reverse side of the same idea.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Good match on protection against infiltration; the sutta also says the fort resists ‘duplicitous allies’.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the warning against trusting others touches the Kural's concern with treachery, but the verse is about spiritual vigilance and does not address military siege.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
entries.rationale: A strong fit: the event shows siege, assault and treachery as the three ways a fort is lost; the Zafarnamah is in the Dasam Granth tradition, but here it is only cited as history through the Encyclopaedia, not quoted as scripture.
Paraphrase; a classic example of the Kural’s three methods of capture.

entries.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.4 (trans. Lionel Giles)
entries.rationale: Matches the difficulty of siege; Sun Tzu elsewhere relies on spies, the Kural’s third threat.

entries.source: Krak des Chevaliers falls to Sultan Baybars
entries.rationale: Near-dramatisation of the kural's three methods, though the sources differ on how certain the forgery is and whose name it bore, which the entry reflects.
Stresses safety more than victory over the besiegers.
Close match on outcome. The city is saved by wisdom rather than by its walls, which also points ahead to 750.

entries.source: Qur’an 33:9-25 and the sira accounts of the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq)
entries.rationale: Historical paraphrase; the Qur’an credits the victory mainly to God’s help, the wind and unseen forces.
Paraphrase. The biblical text credits deliverance mainly to divine action, not to the defenders.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Matches on invincibility; the sutta does not describe the defenders winning actively.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22, second half (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritic on Saṃsâra normalised); the image of defenders winning from within the fort fits well, but the enemy is karma, not an army, and siegecraft is not described.

entries.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University, Patiala), entry Gobind Singh, Guru
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the defenders held firm as the Kural requires, but they did not defeat the besiegers, and the date is given as 1704 or 1705 in different sources.
Paraphrase; Troy eventually fell, so the example fits the long defense only.

entries.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 4.1 (trans. Lionel Giles)
entries.rationale: Close on the strategy of secure holding followed by victory.

entries.source: The Rats of Tobruk hold the port against Rommel
entries.rationale: Very close fit to defenders holding their ground against a skilled besieger, though Tobruk was a fortified port rather than a single fortress.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.31 (trans. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Speaks of the warrior’s duty in general; forts are not mentioned.
General praise of faithful warriors; no fort is involved.
Good match on defenders as a fort; the verse speaks of God’s love rather than a fort’s fame.

entries.source: Nehemiah 4:12 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; KJV 4:18)
entries.rationale: Matches readiness for action; no battle is actually fought in the passage.
Spiritual metaphor, but the structure (fortify, then fight from it) matches closely.

entries.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the Kural's language of victory in battle but deliberately relativises martial glory, which Jain ahimsa does not celebrate, so it is a partial, contrasting match.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo (Salok), Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the salok exalts the warrior who stands firm, but its field is first the inner battle against vice and the defence of the poor (as Sahib Singh reads it), and it says nothing of fortresses.
Paraphrase; a close narrative example.

entries.source: Plutarch, Life of Lycurgus 19.4 (trans. B. Perrin, LacusCurtius)
entries.rationale: Plutarch himself doubts whether the letters containing the saying are authentic. The saying also rejects walls, which the Kural does not.
Strong fit on fame earned by defenders' deeds; the event belongs to a colonial war of conquest, which the entry states plainly.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 3 (Hanuman’s description of Lanka) and following
entries.rationale: Paraphrased narrative; strong thematic match.
Same structure (the fort alone is not enough), but a different answer to what makes it work.
Strong thematic match on fortified but inwardly weak defenders.
Paraphrase. The rabbinic point concerns spiritual merit rather than military competence.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.63, Nagara Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Allegorical; the match is to the principle that vigorous action inside is decisive.

entries.rationale: A documented example of enduring an extremely long separation, fitting the literal reading; the kural's likely ironic tone (the heroine cannot bear it) is not reflected, and the marriage later ended after Mandela's release.

Paraphrase of the play’s well-known situation, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel for hidden love that will not stay hidden, though Phaedra’s love is illicit, unlike the Kural’s wife’s.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 846, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match by contrast: the Kural honours the heroine's modesty (naan) as a virtue, while Guru Arjan tells the devotee not to be shy before the Lord.
Paraphrase of the opening of the letter, not checked against a translation this session; a close match in psychology, though Phaedra’s love is illicit, unlike the Kural’s wife’s.

entries.source: Stendhal, On Love, chapter on modesty (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of Stendhal’s general argument, not checked against a translation this session; it addresses modesty restraining love but not the specific double bind of the couplet.

entries.source: Charlotte Bronte's letters to Constantin Heger
entries.rationale: Very close to the kural's conflict between concealment and shame, though Bronte loved a married teacher rather than an absent husband.
Paraphrase of a well-known image, not checked against a translation this session; it matches the wasting body but not the twin burden of love and shame.

Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); it captures love-sickness weakening the body, though there is no counterweight of shame and the lovers are not separated.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it pairs two afflictions arising from love, but grief and fear are not the Kural’s love and shame, and the verse counsels detachment.
Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; the shared idea is love as a heavy burden, but the Jain answer is renunciation, opposite to the Kural’s sympathy.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 836, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the image of a body loaded with longing, but has nothing of the Kural's carrying-pole or its balance of love against shame.
Paraphrase of a very well-known poem, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel for love’s physical toll, though it lacks the counterweight of shame.
Paraphrase of a famous passage, not checked word for word this session; the opposition of desire and shame within the lover is a close match, though Plato wants shame to win.

entries.source: Chopin's silent love for the singer Konstancja Gladkowska
entries.rationale: A good illustration of love held in balance with bashful silence, though Chopin is a young man in love rather than a wife in separation, and both sources come from the Fryderyk Chopin Institute.
Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not checked against the As It Is wording this session; the sea-and-boat image matches closely, but the ocean is sin, not love.

Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close image of drowning without support, though the psalm’s distress is persecution, not love.

entries.source: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (Simile of the Raft) (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a famous simile, not quoted from a translation this session; the image of crossing a flood by raft matches closely, but the flood is samsara, not love.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 59, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Paraphrase of a famous episode, not checked against a translation this session; the lost raft and the sea between spouses match, though the sea is literal.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it states the helplessness under passion but not the sea image or the absent beloved.

entries.rationale: The swim matches the kural's image of crossing a sea without a raft, but Byron swam as a sporting feat inspired by a legend, not out of love, so this is a next-best fit.

entries.source: Sutta Nipata 4.1, Kama Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close structural match of rapture against shattering loss, though the sutta’s point is to avoid sensual desire altogether.
