entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 542, Raag Bihaagraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on sleepless, longing eyes, though Guru Arjan does not cast the eyes as the cause of the sickness, and the longing is for God.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; a strong match for love-caused sleeplessness, though Medea’s is new love, not separation.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; a general account of being overpowered by emotion, not specific to love or sleeplessness.

entries.source: Juliette Drouet's fifty years of daily letters to Victor Hugo
entries.rationale: The sheer scale of devotion matches the kural's love greater than the sea, but its focus on sleepless, suffering eyes is not documented in these sources.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; the idea of one’s own faculty as enemy fits, but the Gita speaks of the mind (not the eyes) and has no element of satisfaction in its suffering.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the sowing-and-reaping principle matches the Kural’s logic, though Paul speaks of moral judgment, not a lover’s wry satisfaction.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the laugh-then-weep recompense matches closely, though the verse concerns hypocrites, not a lover’s eyes.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match to the eyes ‘falling into’ the sickness they caused, though Proverbs speaks of malice rather than love.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the self-as-enemy and bitter-fruit ideas match, though the verse speaks of evil deeds and lacks the Kural’s ironic delight.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it supports the idea that the passionate sense suffers, though the Jain point is a call to dispassion, with none of the Kural’s ironic glee.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 89, Sri Raag ki Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: both value the pain of longing, but the Kural's 'sweetness' is ironic satisfaction at the eyes' punishment, which has no counterpart in Gurbani.

entries.source: Sophocles, Oedipus the King, lines c. 1268-1274 (messenger’s report) (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; it shares the motif of the eyes punished as culprits, but in tragedy, not love.
Paraphrase of a well-known argument, not checked word for word this session; the fittingness of deserved suffering fits, but Plato’s concern is moral wrongdoing, not love.

entries.source: Cleopatra meets Mark Antony at Tarsus
entries.rationale: The idea of the one who caused love's suffering being trapped in it too is only loosely present, and the details of the barge come from Plutarch's later account, so this is a next-best fit.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, Hanuman finds Sita in the Ashoka grove (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; strong on a wife’s weeping in separation, though Sita does not curse her eyes.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; it shares the eyes-as-fountain image, but reverses the wish and concerns national mourning.
Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; the tearful eyes of separation-grief match, but the Prophet’s tears are accepted as mercy, with no curse on the eyes.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match in form and feeling, though the absent comforter is God and the grief is national.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; reaping with tears matches the Kural’s image, though the verse is about regretted wrongdoing, which love is not.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the misery of missing what the eye desired fits, though the Jain verse argues against desire rather than voicing a lover’s grief.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1111, Raag Tukhaari, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the tear-filled eyes of longing, but the Kural's mock-curse on the eyes has no parallel, and the love is spiritual.
Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; strong on endless weeping, but the grief is a mother’s and the tears never stop.

Paraphrase of a well-known passage, with the famous line given without quotation marks because it was not checked word for word this session; a close structural parallel of addressing and cursing one’s own eyes, though Leontius’s desire is morbid rather than loving.

entries.source: Rembrandt draws Saskia days after their betrothal
entries.rationale: The drawing documents the loving gaze, but the later aching of the eyes is only implied by Saskia's early death, so the fit is next-best.

entries.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, early cantos (Radha’s jealousy and longing) (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the poem’s well-known situation, not checked against a translation this session; a strong emotional match, though the Gita Govinda is also read devotionally.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close match for restless longing to see the beloved, though the bride does not accuse him of not caring.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the link rests on the Arabic idiom of the eye being cooled by seeing a loved one, which the English rendering hides, and the love is maternal.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match for a beloved who withdraws and a lover who cannot rest without him.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; ‘not to see the beloved is painful’ is almost the Kural’s second line, though the Buddha’s conclusion is to hold nothing dear.
Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not re-read this session; a genuine story of a forsaken bride, though its resolution is renunciation rather than continued romantic longing.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 96, Raag Maajh, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa, three consecutive lines); strong fit on finding no rest without seeing the beloved, though the Kural's complaint that he loves her without caring has no parallel, and Guru Arjan longs for the Guru.
Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; a very close match in both the neglect and the fixed gaze.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it explains the husband’s shallow love, but not the eyes’ longing.

entries.source: Izumi Shikibu asks for one last meeting
entries.rationale: The longing to see the beloved matches the kural well, but the kural's reproach that he loved without truly caring is not reflected in the poem.
Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not checked against a translation this session; a strikingly close two-sided parallel, though the poem is devotional as well as romantic.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close image of love-kept wakefulness, though it lacks the Kural’s explicit sleeplessness in both absence and presence.
Paraphrase of the romance’s general situation, not checked against a translation this session, with no specific passage cited; Islamicate love poetry rather than scripture.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); sleep fleeing the eyes matches, but the cause is hard labour, linked only indirectly to love for Rachel.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the sleepless night is a direct image match, but the verse uses it as a metaphor for samsara, not love.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close structural match for suffering both before and during possession, though framed as a warning against attachment.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 460, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match by contrast only: the Kural's point is that union itself is spoiled by dread of parting, which Gurbani does not share for union with the Lord.
Paraphrase of well-known passages, not checked against a translation this session; the absence half is strong, but the reunion night is joyful rather than anxious.

Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; strong on sleepless longing in absence, though Plato says seeing the beloved brings relief where the Kural says it does not.

entries.source: Franz Kafka's engagements to Felice Bauer
entries.rationale: The pattern of unrest both apart and together fits the kural, but the sources document the broken engagements and letters, not literal sleeplessness, and it is the man's unrest rather than the woman's.
Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; a close match for love betrayed by outward signs, though here before marriage.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the hidden-made-known principle fits, but Jesus speaks of the gospel and judgment, not lovesickness.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the eyes revealing the heart match, though the tears here are of recognition of truth, not love.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); it matches the heart showing in the face, though it lacks the Kural’s theme of an exposed secret.

Paraphrase of the tale’s outline from general knowledge, not checked against a translation this session; the exposed lovesickness fits, though the king’s desire is for another man’s wife and the Jataka condemns it.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (excerpted); a weak, next-best match that explains the arising of sorrow but not its public betrayal by the eyes.

entries.source: Bhai Gurdas, Kabitt Savaiye 411, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (kabitt 411, first and last lines joined by an ellipsis); strong fit on love betrayed as by a beaten drum, though Bhai Gurdas does not name the eyes or tears, and the love is for the Lord.
Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; strong on a hidden love betrayed by outward signs, though Phaedra’s love is illicit and tragic.

entries.source: François de La Rochefoucauld, Maxims, no. 70 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known maxim, not checked word for word this session; a close match for love’s inability to stay hidden, though it does not single out the eyes.

entries.source: Princess Margaret's gesture at the coronation reveals her romance
entries.rationale: A close illustration of private love betrayed in public by an unguarded sign, though it was a gesture rather than the eyes themselves.
Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; consent to parting and silent grief match, though Shakuntala’s pallor is not the focus.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; love-sickness in separation and the problem of whom to tell match well, though the bride has not consented to the parting.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the ‘to whom shall I complain’ motif matches, though Jacob grieves for a son, not a husband.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a general proverb on unsharable grief, not about lovers or consent to parting.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the pain of distance from the beloved matches, though the Buddhist remedy is non-attachment rather than reunion.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the grief of a forsaken bride fits, but Rajimati did not consent to the parting and her story leads to renunciation, not reunion.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 133, Raag Maajh, Barah Maha, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on a separation the speaker brought on herself, but the love is the soul's spiritual longing for God, not a wife's for a husband, and 'actions' means karma, not consent to a journey.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; consent and lonely grief match, though Homer does not dwell on pallor.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it states the general principle her situation denies her.

entries.source: Eva Nansen at home while the Fram drifts through the Arctic
entries.rationale: Next-best: a wife at home through a long chosen separation fits the setting, but the sources do not record her explicitly consenting to the voyage or describe her grief.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; the wasted, pale wife is a close image, though the Kural adds the twist of pride.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the proud bodily mark of a beloved matches structurally, but Paul’s marks are of apostolic suffering, not love-sickness.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a strong parallel of grief changing bodily colour, though the bond is parent and child, not husband and wife.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the love-as-bodily-seal image is a partial match, since the Song’s seal is chosen while the Kural’s pallor is suffered.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; both trace grief to the beloved, but the Buddha counsels release while the heroine treasures the gift.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; offered as a contrast, since Jain teaching would reject the Kural’s idea that the beloved is the giver of the change.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable-to-strong fit on valuing an affliction because of who gave it, but the line is about accepting God's will (hukam), not the playful pride of a lover's pallor.
Paraphrase of a well-known lyric, not checked against a translation this session; Greek lyric poetry rather than myth, and Sappho’s pallor comes from the beloved’s presence, not absence.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it matches love’s bodily cost but not the heroine’s pride in it.

entries.source: Ramesses II honours Queen Nefertari in temple and tomb
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the pride of bearing something the beloved gave is a loose parallel, but honour is the opposite of the kural's pallor of grief; the Britannica support for the Abu Simbel temple is a photo caption.
Paraphrase of the general content of these cantos, not checked against a translation this session; viraha (separation) imagery matches, though the canto references are approximate.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; an inverse parallel built on the same idea of exchanged beauty and grief, not a direct match.
Paraphrase of the romance’s general narrative, not checked against a translation this session; a Persian literary work from Muslim culture rather than scripture.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the full-to-empty exchange matches in shape, but Naomi grieves bereavement, not a lover’s absence.
Paraphrase of well-known verses, not checked against a translation this session; the loss of beauty matches, but Ambapali’s cause is age, not separation.
Paraphrase of a well-attested Jain story, not checked against Johnson’s translation this session; a next-best match about lost beauty, not love-sickness.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib (pauri 25), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), two consecutive lines of pauri 25; reasonable fit on pain received as a gift, though the Kural's ironic 'exchange' between lovers has no counterpart in Japji's teaching on accepting God's will.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; beauty wasted by love matches, though Echo’s love was never returned.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; love-as-lack is a loose fit to a concrete exchange of beauty for pallor.

entries.source: Sappho describes the bodily symptoms of love
entries.rationale: Reasonable: love as a sickness that drains the lover's colour matches closely, but it is a poem rather than an outward event, and its setting is jealousy, not separation from a husband.
Paraphrase of a well-known chapter, not checked against a translation this session; remembrance and praise without relief is a close fit.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; remembrance followed by distress matches, though the psalmist’s longing is for God, not a spouse.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; unceasing remembrance consuming the body is a close parallel, though the love is a father’s.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; praising the absent beloved matches well, though the Song does not raise the puzzle of why pallor still comes.

entries.source: Dvedhavitakka Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 19 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it explains rather than shares her puzzle, and its context is monastic training of thought.
Paraphrase from general knowledge of the sutra, not checked against Tatia’s translation this session; sutra numbering differs slightly between recensions.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 40, Sri Raag, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable but partial fit: it matches the constant speaking of the beloved's virtues, but lacks the Kural's complaint that the pallor came all the same, and the love is spiritual.
Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; the faithful, preoccupied wife matches, but Alcyone’s tragedy is a death, not a temporary absence.

entries.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Definitions of the Affects 32 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known definition, not checked word for word this session; a close philosophical account of why remembrance brings pallor.

entries.source: Queen Artemisia builds the Mausoleum for King Mausolus
entries.rationale: Next-best: devotion to the husband's memory fits, but this is mourning after death, and the kural's point (constant remembrance should have prevented the pallor) has no parallel.
Paraphrase of a well-known chapter, not checked against a translation this session; watching the beloved depart and grief beginning at once is a strong fit.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the watched departure matches, but the Ascension is a joyful theological event, not a lover’s parting.

entries.source: Rumi, Masnavi I.1-2 (paraphrase of R.A. Nicholson’s translation)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of famous opening lines, not checked against Nicholson’s text this session; separation as the origin of grief fits, though Rumi’s beloved is ultimately divine.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the immediate failing at the beloved’s departure matches closely.

entries.source: Nanda Sutta, Udana 3.2, and Dhammapada commentary on verses 13-14 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested story, not checked against a translation this session; the bride’s call after the departing groom is a strong image, but the text says nothing of her pallor.
Paraphrase checked against Jacobi’s text on sacred-texts.com; the departure scene fits, but Jainism presents it as a model of renunciation, not a cause for lament.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1108, Raag Tukhaari, Barah Maha, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong thematic fit on separation showing in the body, though it lacks the Kural's 'there he goes, here it comes' timing, and the bride-and-Husband image is spiritual, not romantic.
Paraphrase of a well-known epistle, not checked against a translation this session; a very close parallel of wife, departure and instant pallor.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; immediate pain of absence matches, though Plato’s lover is in a philosophical, not married, relationship.

entries.source: Ovid's last night in Rome before exile
entries.rationale: Strong: the instant collapse of the wife as the husband departs closely matches the kural, though the account is Ovid's own poetic description and the parting was forced, not a journey she agreed to.
Paraphrase of well-known similes, not checked against a translation this session; sarga numbers are approximate and differ between editions.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the waiting-darkness image matches closely, but the context is spiritual light, not married love.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; only the image of encroaching darkness matches, the verse has nothing to do with lovers.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; it shares the light-shadow-beloved imagery but not the simile of darkness lying in wait.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a shared lamp-and-darkness image only, the theme differs.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares a lamp image and the theme of suffering from attachment, but the simile works differently.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 39, Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: the lamp-and-darkness image is shared and the logic matches (darkness fills any gap in the light), but Gurbani applies it to ignorance and the Guru's wisdom, not to a lover's embrace.
Paraphrase of a well-known legend, not checked against a translation this session; the lamp-darkness-lovers link is striking, though the outcome is death, not pallor.
Paraphrase of a famous maxim, not checked against a translation this session; the flame-and-absence image is close, though the logic differs.

entries.source: Martha Washington joins George at his winter camps
entries.rationale: Next-best: shortening separation fits the kural's fear of any gap, but the sources do not record her motive or any sign of pining in his absence.
Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; the sudden loss of a husband’s presence matches, though Nala truly deserts her.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the bridegroom-taken-away motif fits, but it is a figure for Jesus and his disciples.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); it describes spousal closeness, not the grief of its loss.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match of a night-time reaching for the beloved who is not there.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the pain of not seeing the dear one matches, though the Buddhist lesson is non-attachment.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it explains why the joy is fragile but, as a call to renunciation, does not share the Kural’s tender view of married love.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 30) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on how even a short separation shows at once in the body, though Farid's night apart stands for a lapse in devotion, and the bridal image is spiritual, kept within the tasteful bounds of the original.
Paraphrase of a well-known tale, not checked against a translation this session; a Latin novel retelling a Greek myth; the instant loss matches, but Psyche’s act is a broken prohibition.
Paraphrase of a well-known speech, not checked word for word this session; a strong match for love that cannot bear even momentary separation.

entries.source: Ida Straus stays with her husband on the Titanic
entries.rationale: Reasonable but partial: the refusal of even a brief separation fits, but the setting is a disaster and death rather than the ordinary absences the kural describes.
Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; the misdirected blame fits, though Shakuntala’s case involves a curse, not pallor.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage; the one-sided blame matches structurally, but the context is a charge of adultery, quite unlike a faithful wife’s pallor.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a rebuke of unjust gossip about a woman, though its occasion was a slander, not a husband’s absence.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong match for a woman’s changed complexion being judged without regard to its cause, though the cause is not a lover.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it fits the theme of unfair public blame, though not the specific imbalance between wife and husband.

Paraphrase of a well-attested Jain story (also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya), not checked against Johnson’s translation this session; strong on misdirected blame, though the details differ from simple pallor.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa, Patti, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match and partly a contrast: both are about who gets blamed for suffering, but the Kural protests unfair blame while Guru Nanak counsels self-examination instead of blaming another.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; a Roman epic on Greek-Trojan myth; Dido was not married to Aeneas in the Kural’s sense.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it supplies the principle behind her complaint, not a parallel scene.

entries.source: Catherine of Aragon refuses to accept the annulment of her marriage
entries.rationale: Partial: blame falling on the abandoned wife fits, but Catherine's story is about a deliberate annulment, not a husband's absence, and the event has been used once elsewhere in the book in a related form.
Paraphrase from general knowledge of the sutras, not checked against a translation this session; the sutra numbers are approximate and the text is devotional, not marital.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; patient, self-forgetting love matches the spirit, though the verse is general, not about separation.
Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); self-preference for another matches, but the verse concerns the Ansar and the emigrants, not spouses.
Paraphrase of well-known passages, not checked against the JPS text this session; self-giving love fits, though it is friendship rather than married love.
Paraphrase of a very well-known sutta, not checked against a translation this session; metta is universal and non-attached, unlike the heroine’s particular love.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; her acceptance parallels the Kural’s, but Rajimati turns to renunciation rather than wishing a husband well in worldly life.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on love that accepts its own suffering, but the Kural's wish for the beloved's welfare has no direct match, since God needs no one's good wishes.
Paraphrase of a well-known play; a strong match for a wife accepting suffering for her husband’s good, though Alcestis’s sacrifice is her life.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it states the principle but its example is maternal, not marital.

entries.source: George Washington writes to Martha on taking command of the army
entries.rationale: Reasonable: the husband's gentle persuasion to accept his departure matches closely, but we have his letter, not Martha's reply, so her own acceptance is inferred; Mount Vernon confirms the 1775 circumstances, while the letter's wording comes from the primary source.
Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; sarga numbering differs between editions and the Uttara Kanda is considered a later layer.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; love covering the other’s fault matches the heroine’s choice closely.
Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (excerpt); the virtue of concealing another’s faults matches, though the hadith speaks of fellow believers generally.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match for love that covers the beloved’s fault.
Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; not finding fault with another matches, though the Dhammapada turns attention to oneself rather than to protecting a loved one.

entries.source: Ilango Adigal, Silappatikaram, Puhar Kandam (cantos 4 and 9) (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase from general knowledge, not checked against a translation this session; the epic contains Jain elements and its author is traditionally said to be a Jain monk, but that attribution is debated, so this is a Tamil-Jain-adjacent source rather than canonical scripture.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 728, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it shares the refusal to call another bad and the willingness to bear blame oneself, but it is a general teaching on humility and freedom from ego (haumai), not a wife protecting her husband's name.
Paraphrase of a well-known myth, not checked against a translation this session; self-sacrifice to protect a husband fits, but the situation is far more extreme.

entries.source: Søren Kierkegaard, Works of Love (1847), Second Series, V (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the deliberation’s argument, not checked against a translation this session; a close philosophical match, though Kierkegaard writes of Christian love generally.

entries.source: Eliza Hamilton spends fifty years defending her husband's memory
entries.rationale: Strong: shielding the husband's name despite his unkindness matches the kural's core, though Eliza's work came after his death rather than during an absence.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close match on mutual delight in marriage, though Manu speaks of domestic stability rather than the Kural’s image of love’s fruit.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; near one-to-one on mutual belonging, though without the fruit metaphor.

entries.source: Sunan Ibn Majah 1847 (graded hasan by Darussalam)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong match on mutual love fulfilled in marriage.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); near one-to-one on reciprocal love.

entries.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (paraphrase; cf. tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested sutta; strong fit on mutual marital love, though the Buddhist frame is shared virtue rather than sweetness of desire.

entries.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara, on the vow of brahmacarya-anuvrata (paraphrase; cf. tr. Champat Rai Jain)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a standard Jain teaching on lay chastity; only a next-best match, since Jain texts treat marital love as a limit on desire, not as a fruit to be savoured.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 391, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on the blessing of being loved by the one you love, though the love is spiritual, between the soul and God, and Gurbani has no stoneless-fruit image.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 6.180-185 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; strong fit on reciprocal harmony as life’s highest good.
Paraphrase; good thematic fit on reciprocal conjugal friendship, though Aristotle’s register is analytic rather than lyrical.

entries.source: Robert Schumann and Clara Wieck win the right to marry
entries.rationale: A strong, well-documented example of mutual love valued above all obstacles, though the kural's point is the sweetness of mutuality rather than the struggle to marry.

entries.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14 (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; matches only the rain-sustains-life simile, not its application to love.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); the rain-as-love image matches well, though Hosea’s love is divine, not marital.
Paraphrase of two nearby verses; the pairing is suggestive but the Qur’an does not itself make the comparison.
Paraphrase of a well-known dictum; it matches love as life-giving, but lacks the rain image and is framed from the husband’s side.
Paraphrase; the rain-and-wife pairing is genuine, but the sutta’s point runs against the Kural’s dependence on love.

entries.source: Tiruttakkatevar, Jivaka Chintamani (paraphrase of the epic’s marriage episodes)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase from a Tamil Jain text, used as a next-best match; it lacks the rain image and its arc favours renunciation.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 758, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit, with the same rain-on-the-earth image for welcome grace, though the giver is the Guru and the relationship is spiritual, not that of lovers.

entries.source: Aeschylus, Danaids, fragment 44 (Radt), preserved in Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 13.600b (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; a strong image match on love as life-giving rain.

entries.source: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2, metre 8 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; a cosmic rather than personal love, so only a partial fit.

entries.source: Robert Browning's letters reach the invalid Elizabeth Barrett
entries.rationale: Close fit to the image of life-giving tenderness; sources link her improved health partly to Italy's climate, so the rain-like effect of love should not be overstated.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Savitri episode) (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; it shows confidence born of mutual love, though Savitri’s trial is death rather than ordinary separation.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); love’s endurance fits, though the verse does not single out love that is returned.

entries.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, hadith of Umm Zar‘ (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith, cited without a number because it was not checked live; good fit on a loved wife’s proud confidence.
Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); love’s strength fits, but the verse is not about separation or mutuality as such.

entries.source: Bhariya Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya, Book of Sevens (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; cited without a sutta number because Anguttara numbering varies by edition; partial fit, as the sutta catalogues wives’ conduct rather than mutual love.

entries.source: Shripal Ras (Vinayavijaya and Yashovijaya, 17th c.), story of Shripal and Mayanasundari (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a popular Jain narrative; a partial match, since the story’s confidence rests on religious faith as much as on mutual love.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 245, Raag Gauree, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on the loved bride's confidence that her happiness is secure, though Gurbani grounds it in an undying divine Husband, not a husband who will come home from a journey.
Paraphrase; mutual love sustaining a separated wife fits, though Homer does not phrase it as a ‘boast’.
Paraphrase; a partial fit, since Aristotle goes on to praise loving over being loved.

entries.source: Sullivan Ballou's last letter to his wife Sarah
entries.rationale: The letter shows the husband's side of a secure, mutual love; Sarah's own feelings are not documented in these sources, and the letter reached her only after his death.

entries.source: Kalidasa, Abhijnanashakuntalam, Act 5 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of the play’s famous rejection scene; strong fit, though Dushyanta’s coldness is caused by a curse rather than lack of love.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); the structure matches, but Paul speaks of having love, not of being loved by a spouse.
Verified verbatim on quran.com (excerpt); good fit on the plight of a wife deprived of her husband’s affection, though framed as a rule for husbands.
Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); the one-sidedness is drawn from the wider narrative and the text’s silence, a widely noted reading rather than an explicit statement.

entries.source: Sambula Jataka (Jataka 519) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a canonical Jataka; a strong narrative fit on a revered but unloved wife.

entries.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7 (Jain Ramayana), story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative not checked live in this session; strong fit on the admired but unloved wife.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 528, Raag Dayv Gandhaaree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on admired beauty that counts for nothing without the one bond that matters, but Gurbani's lack is the Name, not a lover's love in return.
Paraphrase; a good fit on abandonment, though Ariadne’s story is desertion rather than lifelong indifference.
Paraphrase; good structural fit, though Aristotle speaks of friendship in general rather than one beloved.

entries.source: Catherine of Aragon is set aside by Henry VIII
entries.rationale: Strong fit: public admiration and a husband's rejection are both documented; her inner feelings are inferred from her conduct and her final letter, not stated in the event.
Paraphrase of a well-known passage; strong fit on the reproach of unreturned love, though theologically Krishna’s love is never truly absent.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; an honest counterpoint rather than a parallel, since Jesus values love without return.
Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (excerpt); near one-to-one on the futility of one-sided love, with the roles of man and woman reversed.
Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); strong fit on love that is not returned within a marriage.
Paraphrase of a canonical episode; good fit on unrequited love, though the sutta uses it only as a prelude to the Dhamma.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 22 (Rathanemi) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a canonical Jain narrative not checked live in this session; good fit on love not returned, resolved in a distinctly Jain way.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), two consecutive lines of one salok; next-best match and partly a contrast: both weigh love against what it returns, but the Kural voices a hurt lover's complaint while Guru Angad condemns love that keeps accounts.
Paraphrase; good fit on unrequited love, though Sappho hopes for magic reversal rather than lamenting futility.
Paraphrase; a partial fit, giving the psychological reason behind the Kural’s complaint.

entries.source: Ivan Turgenev's lifelong devotion to Pauline Viardot
entries.rationale: Next-best fit: Turgenev's devotion is well documented, but how far Viardot returned his feelings is debated, so this is not a clear case of wholly unreturned love.

entries.source: Rigveda 10.191.4 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; matches the ideal of balanced, shared feeling, though the hymn concerns an assembly, not a couple.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); a striking image parallel, but Paul’s imbalance is of faith, not of love.

entries.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book III (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known Masnavi theme, cited by book only; good fit on mutual love, though Rumi’s beloved is ultimately divine.
Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); strong fit on shared burden, though not specific to love.

entries.source: Kusa Jataka (Jataka 531) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a canonical Jataka; good narrative fit on the pain of one-sided love turning to joy.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; an honest contrast rather than a parallel, since Jainism resolves one-sided love through non-attachment.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 658, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong thematic fit on love as a two-sided bond, though it has no carrying-pole image and the relationship is between the devotee and God.
Paraphrase of a late-antique telling of the myth; strong fit on love needing its counterpart.
Paraphrase of a well-known definition; near one-to-one on reciprocity, though Aristotle speaks of friendship rather than romantic love.

entries.source: Goethe falls in love with the engaged Charlotte Buff
entries.rationale: Good illustration of one-sided love's pain beside a mutual couple, though the sweetness of the balanced side is implied rather than described in the sources.
Paraphrase of a well-known canto; strong fit, the same love-god acting on one side only, though the lovers are divine.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; love-sickness fits, but there is no love-god and the love is not one-sided.
Paraphrase; the one-sided seizure of love fits, but the context is illicit desire, not a wife’s longing for her husband.
Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917); love as an independent power fits partly, but there is no one-sidedness or love-god.
Paraphrase; the personified desire matches, but Buddhism treats it as an enemy rather than a god to be reproached.
Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; addresses the same pain but rejects the idea of an external love-god, so only a partial fit.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Saloks Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); weak, next-best match offered as an honest contrast: both speak to desire as a power that causes suffering, but Sikhism does not worship a love-god, and it ranks kaam among the five thieves, while the Kural's Kama is a conventional poetic deity of married love.
Paraphrase of a famous episode; near one-to-one on a love-god making love one-sided.

entries.source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 4.1048-1072 (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase; the love-god’s wound matches, but Lucretius’ remedy runs against the Kural’s longing.

entries.source: W. B. Yeats and his unreturned love for Maud Gonne
entries.rationale: Strong fit for one-sided love; the kural's speaker is a wife addressing the love god, while here the lover is a man who never married his beloved.

entries.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; good fit on enduring separation without word, though Nala’s desertion is caused by misfortune, not lack of love.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a good general fit on the strain of waiting, without the specific love context.
Verified verbatim on quran.com (excerpt); a good fit on enduring separation without word, though the love is a father’s, and Islam praises the patience the Kural half-reproaches.
Paraphrase not checked live; a partial fit on the burden of inner suffering, without the love context.
Paraphrase; a partial fit on enduring unreturned devotion, though Isidasi’s resolution is renunciation.

entries.source: Vimalasuri, Paumacariya (Jain Ramayana), Sita’s banishment and renunciation (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative not checked live in this session; partial fit on enduring abandonment.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1379, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 36) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), both lines of salok 36; reasonable but partial fit: both judge the heart that endures life apart from the beloved, though the Kural is ironic self-reproach and Farid makes longing for God a mark of being truly alive.
Paraphrase; strong fit on enduring long separation without word, though Penelope is never in doubt of Odysseus’ love.
Paraphrase; a reasonable fit on the need for words between those who love, though Aristotle speaks of friends in general.

entries.source: Beethoven's letter to the Immortal Beloved
entries.rationale: Next-best fit: we do not know how the woman felt or whether she ever sent him kind words, so the link to living without a sweet word is an inference from the unsent letter and his single life.
Paraphrase; good fit on the sweetness of the absent beloved’s sound, though Krishna’s love is not withheld.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (excerpt); strong fit on the beloved’s voice as sweetness, though here the love is returned.

entries.source: Attributed to Qays ibn al-Mulawwah (Majnun Layla), Diwan (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a widely cited verse of uncertain authorship; good fit on cherishing traces of an absent beloved, from Arabic love poetry rather than scripture.
Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917); strong fit on the sweetness of the beloved’s voice, though he is coming toward her.
Paraphrase; good fit on the lingering sweetness of the beloved’s words, though the roles are reversed and the sutta’s aim is detachment.

entries.source: Jain doctrine of the samavasarana and divya-dhvani (paraphrase; cf. Tattvartha tradition and the Kalpa Sutra’s account of Mahavira’s preaching)
entries.rationale: A next-best match only; the shared theme is a beloved voice, but the Jain context is devotional, not romantic, and no specific verse was checked live.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 388, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on finding life in merely hearing of the beloved, even matching the commentators' reading of the Kural's 'icai' as fame or praise, though Gurbani never suggests the Lord withholds grace and the love is spiritual.
Paraphrase of a famous episode; good fit on clinging to the words of an unresponsive beloved.
Paraphrase of a famous maxim; a partial fit on love’s indifference to reasons, though Pascal’s context is faith.

entries.source: Dante writes La Vita Nuova in praise of Beatrice
entries.rationale: Good fit for love that delights in the beloved's name and praise without return; Beatrice's own feelings are unknown, and some details of her identity rest on early commentators.
Paraphrase of a famous opening; strong fit on pouring one’s grief out to something that cannot answer.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the urge to tell one’s love-pain fits, but the Song does not judge it futile.

entries.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, opening verses (Song of the Reed) (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a partial fit, since Rumi’s longing is mystical and his listeners are not indifferent lovers.
Verified verbatim on Mechon-Mamre (JPS 1917, excerpt); a close image match on futility, without the love context.
Paraphrase; a good fit on the futility of lament, though the sutta concerns bereavement and offers detachment as the cure.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Lecture 9 (Nami Pravrajya) (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase cited by lecture only, not checked live in this session; a partial fit on the unfillable, applied to greed rather than love.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit as the positive side of the Kural's warning against telling one's pain to the indifferent, though it has no sea image and no address to one's own heart.
Paraphrase of a well-known idyll; a strong fit, even sharing the seashore and the self-address.
Paraphrase; a reasonable fit on the futility of trying to command another’s feelings, though Epictetus is calmer than the Kural’s irony.
Strong match to the image of endless complaint to an unresponsive beloved; scholars debate whether Laura was a real woman, though Petrarch's note and poems are certain.

entries.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Canto 2 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Barbara Stoler Miller)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known canto; strong fit on the sweetness of remembered love, though Radha’s memory is mixed with jealousy and lacks the Kural’s comparison with wine.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; near one-to-one, combining remembering, love and the comparison with wine.

entries.source: Ibn al-Farid, al-Khamriyya (The Wine Ode), opening verse (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry and R.A. Nicholson)

Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a contrasting rather than parallel teaching, offered as the most relevant Buddhist view.

entries.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 14.13 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known verse, not checked live; a contrasting Jain view rather than a parallel.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 337, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), two consecutive lines; reasonable-to-strong fit on love's sweetness beating any drink, though Kabir does not stress joy from memory alone, the love is spiritual, and Sikhism rejects intoxicants outright.

entries.source: Sappho, fragment 16 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Anne Carson)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; strong fit on love remembered as the supreme delight.

entries.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric 1.11, 1370b (paraphrase; cf. tr. W. Rhys Roberts)

Paraphrase of a famous verse; strong fit on remembrance soothing the pain of separation, in a devotional frame.

Verified verbatim via quran.com API; a parallel on the soothing power of remembrance, but the remembered one is God, not a human lover.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); good thematic fit on love easing a long separation, though it does not speak of remembering.
Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; parallel mechanism of comforting recollection in solitude, different object.
Paraphrase from memory of a widely recited hymn, not checked live; only a structural parallel, since Jain devotion is not romantic.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 518, Raag Goojaree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); strong fit on remembrance of the beloved as free of pain, though simran is meditation on God's Name rather than a lover's memories.

entries.source: Sappho, fragment 94 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Anne Carson)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-attested fragment; strong fit on memory as consolation in separation.

entries.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 10.22 (letter of Epicurus to Idomeneus) (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.D. Hicks)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a famous letter; strong fit on remembered joy overcoming pain, though about friendship rather than love.

entries.source: John and Abigail Adams sustain their marriage through letters
entries.rationale: Reasonable fit; the letters show love bridging separation, but they do not show that separation caused no pain at all, as the kural claims.

entries.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, sarga 29 (paraphrase; cf. valmikiramayan.net)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong fit on reading a bodily omen about the absent beloved, though Sita’s omen is fulfilled while the heroine’s fades.

Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; matches only on the sneeze itself, offered as the nearest Islamic treatment.
Paraphrase of a midrashic tradition from memory; the shared element is the sneeze as omen, not love.

entries.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga V.33 (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids and H. Oldenberg, SBE 20)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a Vinaya episode from memory; a direct engagement with sneeze-belief, but sceptical rather than parallel.

entries.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira, the fourteen dreams (paraphrase; cf. tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a famous episode; only a loose parallel on omens, with no romantic content.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 401, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
entries.rationale: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match offered as an honest contrast: Sikhism rejects omen-reading of the kind the Kural's folk belief about sneezing assumes, though both link signs to whether the beloved is remembered.

entries.source: Homer, Odyssey 17.541-547 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Samuel Butler)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a specific passage; strong parallel on sneeze-omen tied to an absent husband.

entries.source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, Proposition 50 and Scholium (paraphrase)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a specific proposition; it explains the Kural’s psychology rather than sharing its feeling.

entries.source: The first transatlantic telegraph cable falls silent
entries.rationale: Next-best only: the kural rests on a folk belief about sneezing and a lover's thoughts, and no documented event matches it; the cable is an analogy for a fading sign of contact, not a love story.

entries.source: Kalidasa, Abhijnanashakuntalam, Act 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a famous scene; strong fit on the asymmetry between known and unknown hearts.
Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; partial fit on holding the absent in one’s heart, without the romantic uncertainty.

entries.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book III (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known teaching; exact verse numbers not checked live, so the citation is to the book only.
Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); strong fit on wishing a place in the beloved’s heart.

entries.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.54 (paraphrase; cf. tr. T.W. Rhys Davids and H. Oldenberg, SBE 13)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a canonical episode; the inner question is implied by later tradition rather than stated in the Vinaya.
Paraphrase from memory, not checked live; matches only on the beloved dwelling in the heart, since the Jina, free of attachment, keeps no one in his.

entries.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1367, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir (salok 55) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)

Paraphrase of the poem’s general content; strong fit on the anxious wife abroad in thought, line numbers not given.

entries.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays 1.28, ‘Of Friendship’ (paraphrase; cf. tr. Charles Cotton)
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a famous essay; it supplies the answer the heroine longs for, about friendship rather than marriage.

entries.source: Napoleon's anxious love letters to Josephine from Italy
entries.rationale: Very close in feeling, though the genders are reversed: here the husband asks whether he has a place in his wife's heart.

entries.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.47.12-21, Bhramara Gita (paraphrase; cf. vedabase.io)

entries.source: Ibn Hazm, The Ring of the Dove (Tawq al-Hamama), chapters on aversion and separation (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Arberry)

entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a short sutta; diagnoses the experience rather than sharing the Kural’s tender reproach.

entries.source: Hemachandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book 7, story of Anjana and Pavananjaya (paraphrase; cf. tr. Helen M. Johnson); also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya
entries.rationale: Paraphrase of a well-known Jain narrative, not re-checked live this session; strong fit on one-sided devotion to an aloof husband.

entries.source: Attributed to Qays ibn al-Mulawwah (Majnun Layla), Diwan (paraphrase)
